But to feel these things when we ought, at the things we ought, toward the people we ought, for the reasons we ought, and in the way we ought — that is the mean, and the best, and the mark of virtue. In the same way, actions too admit of excess, deficiency, and the mean. Virtue is concerned with feelings and actions, and in these excess is wrong and deficiency is blamed, while the mean is praised and gets it right — and praise and rightness both belong to virtue. So virtue is a kind of mean, in that it aims at what is intermediate.

Consider, besides, that there are many ways to go wrong (since, as the Pythagoreans put it, the bad belongs to the unlimited and the good to the limited), but only one way to go right. That is why going wrong is easy and going right is hard — easy to miss the target, hard to hit it. So for this reason too excess and deficiency belong to vice, and the mean to virtue: "Good in one way only, bad in every way."

Virtue, then, is a settled state that issues in choice, lying in a mean relative to us, a mean defined by reason — the reason by which the person of practical wisdom would define it. It is a mean between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. And it is a mean in this further sense: the vices fall short of, or overshoot, what is right in both feelings and actions, while virtue finds the middle and chooses it. So in respect of its essence and the account that states what it is, virtue is a mean; but in respect of what is best and right, it is an extreme — the peak.

Not every action or feeling, however, admits of a mean. Some have names that already imply badness — spite, shamelessness, envy; and among actions, adultery, theft, murder. These and their like are condemned because they are bad in themselves, not because there is too much or too little of them. With them you can never be right; you are always wrong. Rightness and wrongness in such cases do not depend on doing them to the right person, at the right time, in the right way; simply to do any of them at all is to be wrong. You might as well demand a mean, an excess, and a deficiency in acting unjustly, or in cowardice, or in dissipation — for then there would be a mean of excess and a mean of deficiency, an excess of excess and a deficiency of deficiency. But just as there is no excess or deficiency of self-control or courage, because the mean is in a way the peak, so there is no mean of these bad things, and no excess or deficiency of them either; however they are done, they are wrong. In short, there is no mean of an excess or a deficiency, and no excess or deficiency of a mean.

It is not enough, though, to state this in general; we have to fit it to particular cases. In discussions of conduct, general statements cover more ground but say less that is true, while statements about particulars are truer to life — because action deals with particulars, and our account has to square with those. So let us take our particulars from the following table.

With fear and confidence: the mean is courage. Of those who go too far, the man who exceeds in fearlessness has no name (many of these states do not), and the man who exceeds in confidence is reckless; the man who has too much fear and too little confidence is a coward.

With pleasures and pains — though not all of them, and with fewer pains than pleasures: the mean is self-control, and the excess is dissipation. People deficient in the pursuit of pleasure hardly occur, so this character too has no name; but since such a person is conceivable, let us call him insensible.

With giving and taking money, first on the ordinary scale: the mean is generosity, the excess wastefulness, the deficiency stinginess. Here the two extremes go to excess and deficiency in opposite respects: the wasteful man gives out too much and takes in too little, the stingy man takes in too much and gives out too little. (We are giving only an outline and summary here, on purpose; we will draw these distinctions more exactly later.)

With money on the grand scale: there is a mean called magnificence — the magnificent man differs from the merely generous one, since magnificence deals with large sums and generosity with small. The excess here is called tastelessness or vulgar display, the deficiency pettiness; these too differ from the extremes that go with generosity, and we will say later how they differ.
With honor and dishonor, on the great scale: the mean is greatness of soul, the excess is what we might call vanity, the deficiency smallness of soul.

With honor on the small scale: there is a state related to greatness of soul as generosity is related to magnificence — concerned with small honor rather than great. A man may reach for honor more than he should or less than he should; the one who reaches too far is called ambitious, the one who falls short unambitious, and the one who is just right has no proper name. The states have no names either, except that the disposition of the ambitious man is called ambition. This is why both extremes lay claim to the middle ground as contested territory, and why we ourselves sometimes call the right character ambitious and sometimes unambitious, and praise now the one and now the other. Why we do this will be explained later; for now let us go through the rest of the virtues on the plan we have laid down.

With anger: here too there is excess, deficiency, and a mean. They have no settled names, but since we call the right character even-tempered, let us call the mean even temper. Of the extremes, let the man who goes too far be called hot-tempered and his fault hot temper, and the man who falls short spiritless, and his fault a lack of spirit.

There are also three further means that resemble one another but differ. All three have to do with how we behave in words and deeds when we are with others. They differ in that one is concerned with truth in such things, the other two with what is pleasant — one of these in relaxation and amusement, the other across the whole of social life. We should say a word about these too, so as to see more clearly that in everything the mean is praiseworthy, while the extremes are neither right nor praiseworthy but blameworthy. Most of these also lack proper names, but we will try, as before, to coin some, for clarity's sake.

With truth about oneself: the man in the mean we may call truthful, and his state truthfulness. As for misrepresenting oneself, if it tends toward exaggeration it is boastfulness and the man a boaster; if toward understatement it is irony, or self-deprecation, and the man self-deprecating.
With what is pleasant in relaxation and amusement: the mean is wit, and the man witty; the excess is buffoonery, and the man a buffoon; the man who falls short is a boor, and his state boorishness.

With what is pleasant in the rest of social life: the man who is as he should be is friendly, and his mean friendliness; the man who overdoes it, if from no motive of his own, is obsequious, and if to get something out of it, a flatterer; the man who falls short and is unpleasant in everything is contrary and quarrelsome.

There are means in our feelings and in matters involving feeling as well. Modesty, for instance, is not a virtue, but the modest person is praised. Here too one person is said to be in the mean, another in the excess — like the bashful man who is overcome with shame at everything — while the person who feels no shame at all is shameless; the one in between is modest. And righteous indignation is a mean between envy and spite. All three have to do with the pleasure or pain we feel at what happens to our neighbors: the man with righteous indignation is pained at undeserved good fortune; the envious man overshoots him and is pained at anyone's good fortune; and the spiteful man falls so far short of being pained that he actually rejoices at others' misfortune. But there will be another occasion to discuss these, and justice too, since justice is spoken of in more than one sense; afterward we will treat each precisely and show how they are means. We will do the same for the intellectual excellences.

Since there are three dispositions in each case — two of them faults, one in the way of excess and one in the way of deficiency, and one of them right, the mean — they are all in a way opposed to one another. The extremes are opposed both to the mean and to each other, and the mean is opposed to the extremes. Just as the equal is larger compared to the smaller and smaller compared to the larger, so the mean states are excessive compared to the deficient ones and deficient compared to the excessive ones, in feelings and in actions alike. The brave man looks reckless next to the coward and cowardly next to the reckless man; the self-controlled man looks dissipated next to the insensible man and insensible next to the dissipated; the generous man looks wasteful next to the stingy man and stingy next to the wasteful. So the extreme characters each push the man in the middle toward the other side: the coward calls the brave man reckless, the reckless man calls him a coward, and so on. And because of this mutual opposition, the extremes are more contrary to each other than either is to the mean, since they stand farther from each other than from the middle — just as the larger and the smaller stand farther from each other than either does from the equal.

There is this too: some extremes bear a certain resemblance to the mean — recklessness to courage, wastefulness to generosity — but the extremes are utterly unlike each other. Now things that stand farthest apart are defined as contraries, so the farther apart, the more contrary they are. In some cases it is the deficiency that is more opposed to the mean, in others the excess. Cowardice, the deficiency, is more opposed to courage than recklessness, the excess; but dissipation, the excess, is more opposed to self-control than insensibility, the deficiency. There are two reasons for this. One comes from the nature of the thing itself: when one extreme is nearer and more like the mean, we set not it but the other against the mean as the true opposite. Since recklessness seems nearer and more like courage, and cowardice less like it, we set cowardice rather than recklessness against courage, because what stands farther from the mean seems more contrary to it. The other reason comes from ourselves. The things we are naturally more inclined toward seem more opposed to the mean. We are naturally inclined more toward pleasures, and so we slide more readily into dissipation than into decorum. We call "more contrary," then, the extreme we tend to drift into — which is why dissipation, the excess, is more contrary than insensibility to self-control.

So we have now said enough about how excellence of character is a mean; how it lies between two faults, one of excess and one of deficiency; and how it is such because it aims at the middle in both feelings and actions. This is also why being good is hard work. In each case finding the middle is hard, just as finding the center of a circle is not something anyone can do, but only the one who knows how. Anyone can get angry — that is easy — and anyone can give away money or spend it; but to do these to the right person, in the right amount, at the right time, for the right reason, and in the right way — that is not something anyone can do, and it is not easy. That is why doing it well is rare, and praiseworthy, and fine.

So the man aiming at the mean should first steer clear of the extreme more opposed to it — as Calypso advises in Homer, "Keep the ship clear of this spray and surge." For of the two extremes one is always more of a mistake than the other; and since hitting the mean exactly is so hard, the next-best course, as they say, is to take the least of the evils. We will do this best by the method just described. We should also watch for our own natural bias, which differs from person to person and shows itself in the pleasures and pains we feel. And we should drag ourselves off in the opposite direction, for by pulling well clear of where we go wrong we will arrive at the middle — the way people straighten warped timber. In everything, we should be most on guard against what is pleasant, and against pleasure itself, since we are not impartial judges of it. We ought to feel toward pleasure the way the elders of Troy felt toward Helen, and say of it what they said of her — for if we send it away, we will go wrong less often.

In short, by taking these precautions we will best be able to hit the mean. Still, this is no doubt hard, especially in particular cases. It is not easy to determine exactly how, with whom, for what, and for how long one should be angry; we ourselves sometimes praise people who fall short and call them even-tempered, and at other times call the hot-tempered manly. And the person who deviates a little from what is right, whether toward too much or too little, is not blamed; only the one who deviates a good deal is, since he cannot go unnoticed. But just how far and how much someone has to go to be blameworthy is not easy to fix in words — no easier than anything else that is a matter of perception. Such things lie among the particulars, and the judgment rests with perception. This much, at least, is clear: the mean state is praiseworthy everywhere, but we have to lean sometimes toward excess and sometimes toward deficiency, since that is the easiest way to hit the mean — and so to get it right.

Virtue has to do with how we manage our feelings and our actions, and praise and blame attach to actions that are voluntary, while for the involuntary we make allowances and sometimes even feel pity. So anyone trying to understand virtue has to draw the line between what is voluntary and what is not. The distinction matters for lawmakers too, when they decide whom to honor and whom to punish.

Involuntary actions seem to come in two kinds: those done under compulsion, and those done out of ignorance. An action is compulsory, strictly speaking, when its source lies outside the agent and the agent contributes nothing to it — better, the person undergoes it rather than does it. Picture a wind carrying you off somewhere, or men who have you in their power hauling you along. But there are harder cases. Suppose you do something out of fear of something worse, or for some honorable reason — say a tyrant who holds your parents and children orders you to do something shameful, and they live if you comply and die if you refuse. Here it is genuinely open to question whether the act is voluntary or involuntary. The same goes for jettisoning cargo in a storm: in the abstract, no one throws away his own property; but to save himself and everyone aboard, anyone with sense would.

The truth is that such acts are mixed, but they are closer to voluntary than to involuntary. At the moment they are done, they are chosen, and the point of an action has to be judged against the actual circumstances. We should call an act voluntary or involuntary by reference to the moment of acting. And in these cases the person acts voluntarily, because the source of the movement — the working of his own limbs — lies within him; and where the source is in him, it is up to him whether to act or not. So such acts are voluntary, even if, considered in the abstract, they are involuntary, since no one would choose any such thing for its own sake. For acts like these people are sometimes even praised, when they put up with something disgraceful or painful to win something great and noble. But if it is the other way around — disgrace endured for nothing noble, or for some trifle — they are blamed, since only a low character endures real disgrace for no fine end. And for some acts there is no praise, only forgiveness: when a person does what he should not because the pressure overstrains human nature and goes past what anyone could bear.

But some acts, perhaps, can never be excused by compulsion; a person should die first rather than do them. The pleas of compulsion that Euripides puts in the mouth of Alcmaeon, to excuse killing his own mother, are simply absurd. Still, it is sometimes hard to judge what should be chosen at what cost, and what endured to avoid what, and harder still to stand by the judgment once made — because usually the alternatives are painful and the act demanded is base, and so we get praise or blame depending on whether a person gave in or held out.

So which actions should we call compulsory? Simply those whose cause is external and to which the agent contributes nothing. As for actions that are in themselves the kind no one would want, but are chosen here and now over some worse alternative, and whose source lies in the agent — these are involuntary in the abstract but voluntary here and now, in preference to the alternative. And they are more like voluntary actions, because action is made of particular concrete steps, and those steps are voluntary. (Exactly what should be chosen over what is not easy to lay down, since the particular cases differ so much.)

Someone might object that pleasant and noble things compel us too, since they are external and they do pull us; but then every action would be compulsory, since these are what move all of us in everything we do. That is wrong. People who act under real compulsion, against their will, act with pain; people who act for the sake of something pleasant or noble act with pleasure. It is absurd to blame the outside thing instead of yourself for being so easily hooked by it — or to take credit for the noble acts and pin the base ones on pleasure. So compulsion is this: when the source is outside, and the person compelled adds nothing.

Now, not everything done out of ignorance is, strictly, involuntary. An act is involuntary only when it is followed by pain and regret. Someone who did something out of ignorance but is not bothered by it didn't act with his will, since he didn't know what he was doing — but he didn't act against it either, since he is not sorry. So within the class of those who act out of ignorance, the one who regrets it afterward we count as having acted involuntarily; the one who feels nothing, since his case is plainly different, we will call a non-voluntary agent. The two deserve different names because they really are different.

There is also a difference between acting because of ignorance and acting in a state of ignorance. We don't usually blame a drunk man's or an angry man's ignorance for what he does; we blame the drink or the anger. He acts not knowingly, but in ignorance. And of course every bad person is ignorant of what he ought to do and avoid — that very failure is what makes people unjust and worthless. But we don't call an act involuntary just because someone was ignorant of what was good for him. Ignorance in our choices doesn't make us excusable; it makes us depraved. Nor does ignorance of the general principle excuse us, since for that we are blamed. What excuses is ignorance of the particulars — the specific circumstances the action is made of and concerns. These are where pity and forgiveness come in, because the person who is ignorant of one of them is acting involuntarily in the full sense.

It may help, then, to spell out these particulars: who is acting, what he is doing, about what or in what, sometimes with what (an instrument, say), to what end (rescuing someone, for example), and in what manner (gently or hard). No one in his right mind could be ignorant of every one of these — least of all of who is acting, since that's himself. But what he is doing he can be ignorant of, as when people say something "slipped out," or as Aeschylus said of the Mysteries, that he hadn't known it was forbidden to speak of them; or as in that recent catapult accident, where the man said he was only demonstrating how it works. Or someone might take his own son for an enemy, as Merope did; or think the pointed spear had a button on it, or that the stone was pumice; or kill a man with a drink meant to save him; or land a real blow while only meaning, as in sparring, to show someone a move. Since ignorance is possible about any of these particulars that make up the action, the person ignorant of one of them is held to have acted involuntarily — and most clearly so when he was ignorant of the most important ones, which are taken to be the circumstances of the act and its result. But for ignorance to make an act involuntary in this way, the act must also be followed by distress and regret.

Since an involuntary action is one done under compulsion or out of ignorance, a voluntary action looks to be one whose source is in the agent himself, who knows the particular circumstances the action is made of. It is a mistake, by the way, to call actions done from anger or appetite involuntary. Take it as true and, first, no animal but a human being would ever act voluntarily, and neither would children. Next, are we to say that nothing we do from appetite or anger is voluntary — or only that the noble things we do that way are voluntary and the shameful ones aren't? That last is ridiculous, since the cause is one and the same. And the first is strange too: we are not supposed to call involuntary the very things we ought to want. There are things it is right to be angry about, and things we ought to desire — health, for instance, and learning. Besides, what is genuinely involuntary is felt as painful, while acting on appetite is felt as pleasant. And why should it matter, for the voluntariness, whether a wrong is done by cold calculation or in the heat of anger? Both are to be avoided, and the non-rational feelings are no less part of a human being than reason is — so the actions that spring from anger and appetite are no less the person's own. Treating them as involuntary makes no sense.

Having marked off voluntary from involuntary action, the next thing to examine is choice — prohairesis — since it seems more bound up with virtue than action is, and a surer test of character. Choice is plainly voluntary, but the two are not the same: voluntary is the wider term. Children and animals share in voluntary action but not in choice, and we call sudden acts voluntary without crediting them to choice. Choice is not the same as appetite or anger or wish or any kind of opinion either. It isn't appetite or anger, because animals share in those but not in choice. The man who lacks self-control acts from appetite, not from choice; the self-controlled man, the reverse. Appetite can run against choice, but not against appetite. And appetite is about the pleasant and the painful, while choice is about neither as such. Still less is it anger, since acts of anger seem the least connected of all to choice.

Nor is choice the same as wish, close as the two are. We can't choose what is impossible — anyone who said he was choosing it would seem a fool — but we can wish for the impossible, for immortality, say. We can wish for outcomes we ourselves could never bring about, like a particular runner or actor winning; but no one chooses such things, only what he thinks he can do something about himself. And wish is aimed more at the end, choice at the means: we wish to be healthy, but we choose the things that will make us healthy; we wish to be happy and say as much, but it sounds wrong to say we choose to be happy. In short, choice seems to be about what lies in our own power. Nor is it opinion. Opinion ranges over everything — the eternal and the impossible as much as what's in our power — and opinions are true or false, not good or bad the way choices are. Probably no one identifies choice with opinion flat out; the claim is that it's the same as a certain kind of opinion. But it isn't, because it's by choosing good and bad things that we become a certain kind of person, not by holding opinions about them. We choose to take a thing or avoid it; we form an opinion about what a thing is, or what it's good for, or how — but we don't form an opinion to take or avoid. Choice is praised more for aiming at the right object, opinion for being true. We choose things we are fairly sure are good; we form opinions about things we don't really know. And the people best at choosing aren't always the ones best at judging: some see the better course and yet, through some flaw of character, choose against it. Whether opinion comes before choice or alongside it doesn't matter; that's not the question. The question is whether choice is a kind of opinion, and it isn't.

So if choice is none of these, what is it? It is clearly voluntary, but not everything voluntary is chosen. Then is it this: the voluntary that has been thought through beforehand? For choice involves reasoning and weighing things out. The very Greek word for it points this way — pro-hairesis, what is taken before, chosen ahead of the alternatives.

So: do we deliberate about everything — is anything at all a possible object of deliberation — or are there things we don't deliberate about? (By "object of deliberation" let's mean what a sensible person would weigh, not what some fool or madman might.) No one deliberates about the eternal — the order of the universe, say, or the fact that the diagonal and the side of a square can't be measured by a common unit. Nor about things that move but always come out the same way, by necessity or by nature or by some other steady cause, like the turning of the seasons or the rising of the sun. Nor about what varies at random, like droughts and rains, nor about chance events, like stumbling on buried treasure. Not even about all human affairs: no Spartan deliberates about the best constitution for the Scythians, because none of that is within his power. We deliberate about the practical things that are in our own power — which is what's left after all those exclusions.

The causes of things seem to be nature, necessity, chance, and on top of these our own minds and everything in our power. And just as people in general deliberate about what people in general can do, each of us deliberates about what each of us can do. We don't deliberate about the exact, self-contained sciences — how to form the letters of the alphabet, say, where there's no doubt how it's done. We deliberate about the things that depend on us but don't always come out the same way: medicine, for instance, or making money; more about navigation than about athletics, since navigation has been worked out less precisely; and more about the arts than the sciences, since we're less sure of the arts. Deliberation, then, belongs where things fall under general rules but it's still uncertain how a particular case will turn out — wherever there's some open question. For the big decisions we bring in others to help, distrusting our own judgment to settle them alone.

We deliberate not about ends but about the means to them. A doctor doesn't deliberate about whether to cure, nor a speaker about whether to persuade, nor a statesman about whether to make good laws; no one deliberates about his end. They set down the end and then ask how, by what means, it can be reached. If it can be reached several ways, they work out which is easiest and best; if only one way, then how to do it by that means, and that means by what further means, until they arrive at the first cause — which is the last thing found. Someone deliberating seems to search and analyze the way you'd analyze a geometric figure to solve it. Not every search is deliberation — the mathematician's isn't — but every deliberation is a search, and the last step in the analysis is the first in the doing. If in searching they hit something impossible, they give it up — if money is needed, say, and can't be had; if it looks possible, they set about it. By "possible" I mean what can be done through ourselves — including what's done through our friends, since in a sense the source of that still lies with us.

So a person is the source of his own actions, and deliberation is about what he himself can bring about, and actions are done for the sake of other things. Hence it isn't the end we deliberate about, but the means. Nor is it the particular facts of the moment — whether this here is bread, or whether it's been baked properly; those are matters for perception, and if you had to deliberate about everything you'd go on forever. The object of deliberation and the object of choice are the same, except that the object of choice has already been settled — singled out as the thing preferred after deliberation. For each of us stops asking how to act once he has traced the starting point back to himself, to the part of him that governs; that is the part that does the choosing. (The old kingships Homer wrote of show this nicely: the kings would announce to the people what they had already decided.) Since the object of choice is something in our power that we want and have deliberated about, choice is a deliberate reaching for something in our power: we deliberate, then settle on it, then reach for it in line with the result. Let that stand as a sketch of choice and its object — the means to our ends.

Wish, as we said, is for the end. Some hold its object is the genuine good; others, whatever strikes a person as good. Those who say its object is the real good run into this: that what a person wishes for when he chooses wrongly is then not really an object of wish at all (since on their view, if it's wished for it must be good, and in this case it's bad). Those who say its object is whatever strikes one as good run into the opposite trouble: that nothing is naturally an object of wish, only whatever seems good to each person — and different people are struck differently, sometimes by opposite things. If neither view satisfies us, perhaps we should say: in plain truth, the object of wish is the genuine good, but for each person it is whatever strikes him as good. For the good person, then, the object of wish is what is truly good; for the bad person, it can be anything at all — just as, in the body, what is healthy for the healthy is what's truly healthy, while other things are "healthy" for the sick. Same with bitter and sweet, hot and heavy, and the rest. The good person judges each case rightly, and in each the truth appears to him. Each character has its own range of fine and pleasant things, and what most sets the good person apart may be just that he sees the truth in every case, being himself a kind of standard and measure of it. Most people are led astray by pleasure: it isn't really good, but it strikes them as good, so they go after the pleasant as good and shun pain as bad.

Now the end is the object of wish, and the means are the objects of deliberation and choice; so the actions concerning the means are matters of choice, and therefore voluntary. The activities that exercise the virtues concern the means — so virtue is up to us. And so is vice. Wherever it's in our power to act, it's in our power not to act, and the reverse; so if doing the fine thing is in our power, so is not doing it, and if not doing the base thing is in our power, so is doing it. If doing and not doing the fine or base thing is up to us, and that is what being good or bad consists in, then being a good person or a bad one is up to us.

The old saying that "no one is wicked willingly, or blessed against his will" is half right and half wrong. No one is blessed against his will, true; but wickedness is voluntary. Otherwise we'd have to deny what we just argued — that a person is the originator and begetter of his actions as much as of his children. And if that's plainly so, and we can't trace our actions back to any sources beyond the ones in us, then the things whose sources are in us are themselves in our power and voluntary.

This is borne out by what people actually do — by private individuals and by lawmakers, who punish and chastise wrongdoers (unless they acted under compulsion or out of ignorance they didn't cause) and honor those who do well, on the theory that this encourages the one and restrains the other. No one is encouraged to do what isn't in his power — it's useless to talk someone out of feeling hot, or pain, or hunger; he'll feel it all the same. And here's a stronger point: lawmakers punish the ignorance itself, when a person caused it. Drunks pay a double penalty, because the source was in the man himself — he could have not gotten drunk, and the drunkenness caused the ignorance. They also punish people who are ignorant of laws they ought to know and easily could; and likewise in every case where the ignorance is thought to come from carelessness, on the grounds that it was in the person's power not to be ignorant, since he could have paid attention.

Suppose someone is the kind of person who can't pay attention. Well, people make themselves that kind of person by living carelessly, and they make themselves unjust or undisciplined by doing wrong or by spending their days drinking and the like — because the particular things we do shape the kind of person we become. You can see this in anyone training for a contest or a skill: they keep doing the thing. To plead that you didn't know habits are built out of repeated acts is the mark of someone hopelessly dull. And it's beside the point to say that the unjust or the self-indulgent man doesn't wish to have those vices. If a man knowingly does the things that make him unjust, he is unjust voluntarily, even though he can't simply wish himself back to being just. The sick man can't wish himself well — yet he may be ill voluntarily, if his illness came from loose living and ignoring his doctors. There was a time he could have not been ill; now that he's let himself go, he can't. Once you've thrown a stone, you can't call it back — and yet the throwing was up to you, since the source was in your hand. In the same way the unjust man and the man without self-control could have avoided becoming what they are, so they are what they are voluntarily; but now that they've become it, they can no longer be otherwise.

It isn't only diseases of the soul that are voluntary; bodily ones are too, in some people, and we blame them accordingly. No one blames a man for ugliness he was born with, only for the kind that comes from neglect and never exercising. The same with weakness and disability: no one would reproach a man blind from birth or from illness or an accident — we'd pity him — but everyone blames the man whose blindness came from too much wine or some other excess. So among bodily defects, the ones in our power are blamed and the others aren't; and if that's right, then among defects of the soul too, the ones we blame must be the ones in our power.

But here is an objection. Everyone, you grant, aims at what strikes him as good, and no one controls how things strike him; the end appears to each according to the kind of person he is. If a man is somehow responsible for his own character, then he's responsible too for how things strike him. But if he isn't, then no one is the cause of his own wrongdoing; he does wrong out of ignorance of the true end, thinking that this is how he'll secure what's best. Aiming at the end, the objection goes, is no one's own choice; you have to be born with a kind of inner eyesight that judges rightly and chooses the truly good, and the person who has this by nature, well and fully, is the one truly favored — for it's the greatest and finest thing, something you can't get or learn from anyone else but have just as nature gave it. If all this holds, how is virtue any more voluntary than vice? For both the good man and the bad, the end appears and is fixed by nature, or however you want to put it, and they refer everything else to it.

But take it either way. Say the end doesn't appear to each by nature alone, but something also depends on the person himself — then vice is as voluntary as virtue, since the bad man too has a hand in how the end appears to him. Or say the end is fixed by nature, but virtue is still voluntary because the good man does everything toward it voluntarily — then vice is just as voluntary, since the bad man's own agency is in his actions just as much, even if not in the setting of the end. So if, as people say, the virtues are voluntary (we are at least partly responsible for our characters, and it's because we are a certain kind of person that we take the end to be a certain kind of thing), then the vices are voluntary too. The cases are exactly alike.

So we've covered the moral virtues in general — that in outline they are mean states and settled dispositions, how they're formed, that they're naturally exercised on the same circumstances that formed them, that they're in our power and voluntary, and that they follow what right reason directs. Note, though, that actions and dispositions aren't voluntary in the same way. We are in command of our actions from start to finish, knowing the particulars. With dispositions we command only the beginning; the steady accumulation that builds them is no more noticeable than the slow advance of a disease. Still, they are voluntary, since it was up to us to use our circumstances one way rather than another.

Now let's take up the moral virtues one at a time — what each is, what it deals with, and how. Their number will come clear in the process. Start with courage. We've already said it's a mean state regarding fear and confidence. What we fear is, obviously, the fearful — broadly, evils — which is why fear gets defined as the expectation of evil. We fear all sorts of evils: disgrace, poverty, illness, friendlessness, death. But not all of these are the brave man's concern. Some things it is right and noble to fear and base not to fear — disgrace, for one. The man who fears disgrace is decent and has a sense of shame; the man who doesn't is shameless. (Some call that man brave by a loose analogy, since he resembles the brave man in being unafraid.) But poverty and illness — anything that doesn't come from our own vice or fault — these a man shouldn't fear; and yet being unafraid of them doesn't make him brave in the strict sense. We use the word for him too, by resemblance: some men are cowards in the dangers of war but generous with money and steady in the face of losing it. Nor is a man a coward for fearing insult to his wife and children, or fearing envy; nor is he brave for being unflinching about a flogging.

What sort of fearful things, then, is the brave man concerned with? Surely the greatest, since no one stands up to the terrible better than he does. And the most terrible thing is death, because it's the end of everything, and the dead man is thought to have no share in good or evil any longer. Yet even death is not the brave man's concern in every form — not death at sea or from disease. In what form, then? Surely the noblest. And that is death in war, since it's death in the greatest and noblest danger — confirmed by the honors cities and rulers give it. So the man most properly called brave is the one who is fearless in the face of a noble death and the sudden threats of death that war brings. Not that he won't be steady at sea or in sickness too — but not in the way sailors are. The brave man may give himself up for lost there and recoil at that kind of end, while sailors stay cheerful and hopeful out of experience. Courage shows where there's something a man can do to save himself, or where death would be noble — and neither holds for drowning or disease.

What's fearful isn't the same to everyone. There's a kind of terror, as we say, beyond human endurance — fearful to anyone with sense. The fearful things on a human scale differ in size and degree, and so do the things that inspire confidence. The brave man isn't thrown off balance — only so far as he's human, of course. He'll fear such things, but he'll stand up to them as he should, as reason directs, for the sake of what's noble, since that's the end of the virtue. It's possible to fear these things too much, or too little, or to fear what isn't really fearful as if it were. The brave man goes wrong in none of these ways. He stands his ground, fears, and is confident toward the right objects, for the right reason, in the right way, at the right time — for he feels and acts as he should and as reason directs. The end of each activity is whatever accords with the disposition behind it; for the brave man, that's courage, and courage is noble — so the end is noble too, since the end takes its character from the disposition. Honor, then, is what moves the brave man to stand fast against terror and to do what courage demands.

On the side of too much: the man who fears nothing at all has no proper name (many of these states don't), but if he feared nothing — not earthquake, not the high seas, as they say of the Celts — he'd be a madman, or numb to pain. The man with too much confidence toward the fearful is reckless. He tends to be a boaster, faking the courage he doesn't have: he wants to seem to stand toward danger the way the brave man really does, and copies him where he can. So most of the reckless turn out to be a strange mix of bravado and cowardice — loud beforehand, but failing to hold when the real danger comes. The man who feels too much fear is the coward: he fears the wrong things in the wrong ways, on down the line. He's short on confidence, but it's in the experience of pain that he's most exposed — a despairing sort, afraid of everything. The brave man is the opposite, since confidence belongs to the hopeful. So the coward, the reckless man, and the brave man all face the same things but stand differently toward them: the first two overshoot and fall short, the last hits the mean and acts as he should. The reckless are rash, eager before the danger and gone once it's on them; the brave are sharp in the moment but quiet and steady before it.

Courage, then, is a mean state regarding the things that inspire confidence and fear, in the circumstances described, and the brave man chooses his course and holds his ground because doing so is noble, or because failing to is base. But to die in order to escape poverty or heartbreak or anything merely painful is not the act of a brave man but of a coward. Running from what's hard is softness, and the suicide faces death not because it's noble but to get clear of an evil.

True courage is roughly what we've described. But five other dispositions also get called courage in ordinary talk. First, and closest to the real thing, the courage of the citizen. Citizens face danger, it's thought, because of the penalties and disgrace the laws fix on cowardice and the honors they give the brave — which is why the bravest peoples are the ones where cowards are shamed and the brave are honored. This is the courage Homer gives Diomedes and Hector. Hector says, "Polydamas will be the first to heap disgrace on me"; Diomedes, that Hector will boast in Troy of beating him. This comes nearest to real courage, because it springs from a virtue — from shame, from longing for what's noble (that is, for honor), and from avoiding disgrace, which is base.

You might put in the same rank men who stand firm under their commanders' compulsion. But they're lower, because what moves them is fear, not a sense of honor, and what they flee is pain, not disgrace. Commanders do compel their men. As Hector says, "Any man I find skulking far from the fight will have no hope of escaping the dogs." Commanders who post steady troops behind doubtful ones, or beat men who flinch, or draw their line up against a trench or some other barrier, are all doing the same thing: using force. But a man should be brave from a sense of honor, not under compulsion.

Second, experience and skill pass for courage — which is why Socrates even thought courage was knowledge. In war this shows up in seasoned soldiers. There are many things in war that aren't really dangerous, and these men have seen them so often that they look brave to people who don't know how harmless they are. Their skill also lets them strike without being struck, since they handle their weapons well and carry the best for attack and defense — like armed men against unarmed, or trained athletes against amateurs, where the best fighters aren't the bravest but the strongest and fittest. But the regulars turn coward the moment the danger outruns their advantage — when they're outnumbered and outsupplied. Then they're the first to run, while the citizen militia stand and die where they are, as actually happened at the temple of Hermes: to the militia, flight was disgraceful and death better than safety bought that way, while the regulars had gone in trusting their edge and ran once they saw they'd lost it, fearing death more than disgrace. That is not the brave man's way.

Third, plain animal spirit gets called courage. Men driven by raw spirit are thought brave, the way a wounded beast charges — and the truly brave do have plenty of spirit, since nothing drives at danger like it. Hence those phrases all through Homer: "he put strength in his spirit," "roused his strength and his spirit," "and the keen strength flared in his nostrils," "his blood boiled" — all of them naming the way animal spirit rouses and surges. But the truly brave act from a sense of honor, with spirit as their ally; beasts act from pain — because they've been hurt or scared. Leave them alone in their forest or marsh and they don't attack. They aren't brave for rushing at danger when goaded by pain and spirit, with no eye to the risk — by that measure a hungry donkey would be brave, since you can beat it and it won't leave the feed; and dissolute men do plenty of bold things out of lust. So men goaded into danger by pain and raw spirit aren't brave. Still, this spirited temper is the most natural of the lot, and would be real courage if you added deliberate choice and the right motive. Men feel pain at an insult and pleasure in revenge, and those who fight from that may be good fighters, but they aren't brave — they act on the feeling of the moment, not from a sense of honor and not as reason directs. Yet they resemble the brave.

Fourth, the merely confident aren't brave either. Their boldness in danger comes from a string of wins over weak opposition. They resemble the brave in being confident, but the brave are confident for the reasons given, while these are confident from settled conviction that they're stronger and won't be hurt — much as drunk men grow bold. When things turn out otherwise, they run. But it was the brave man's mark to stand against what is, or seems, fearful to a human being, because it's noble to do so and base not to. So it counts as greater proof of courage to be unshaken in sudden terror than in danger you saw coming, since the steadiness then comes from a fixed character rather than from preparation. Foreseen dangers you can face by calculation; the sudden ones you face from the kind of person you've become.

Fifth and last, those acting in ignorance look brave, and aren't far from the merely confident — but they're lower, since they have nothing real behind them. The confident at least think well of themselves and so hold the field a while, whereas men who've been deceived bolt the instant they learn the truth, as the Argives did when they ran into the Spartans, taking them for the men of Sicyon.

So we've said what kind of men are brave, and what kind only seem to be. One more point: though courage has to do with both confidence and fear, it's far more about fear. The man who keeps his head under what's painful, and stands toward it as he should, has a better claim to be called brave than the man who's right about what inspires confidence. So it's for enduring painful things that men are called brave. Courage involves pain, and is rightly praised for it, since standing up to pain is harder than holding back from pleasure.

It isn't that the end of courage isn't pleasant — it is, but the surrounding circumstances bury it. Take the games: for the boxers the end is pleasant — the crown, the honor — but the blows they take hurt flesh and blood, and all the training is hard, and with so many such drawbacks the small prize starts to look like no pleasure at all. So with courage: death and wounds will be painful to the brave man, and against his will. But he endures them because it's noble to, or base not to. And the more complete his virtue and his happiness, the more it will pain him to die — for life is most worth living to a man like that, and he knows he is being robbed of the greatest goods, which is a bitter thing. He's no less brave for feeling it; he may be more so, for choosing the honor of war over keeping those goods safe. Acting with pleasure isn't true of every virtue, except so far as a man is reaching his end. And maybe the best soldiers aren't men like this, but men who are less truly brave and have nothing else worth keeping — men quick to meet danger and ready to trade their lives for a small gain. Let that be enough about courage; from what's been said, its nature isn't hard to grasp at least in outline.

Next, temperance — self-mastery — which seems to come right after courage, since these two are the virtues of the non-rational part of the soul. We've already said it's a mean state concerning pleasures (it has to do with pains too, but less, and differently), and self-indulgence has the same field. So let's settle which pleasures. Divide them into the mind's and the body's. Loving honor or learning are pleasures of the mind: a man takes pleasure in whichever of these he's inclined to love, with his body untouched and only his intellect engaged. We don't call people temperate or self-indulgent over pleasures of that kind, or over any that aren't bodily. People who love telling long-winded stories and gossiping their days away over nothing we call chatterboxes, not self-indulgent; nor do we call a man self-indulgent for grieving over lost money or friends.

So temperance is about bodily pleasures — but not even all of those. People who delight in what they see — colors, shapes, a painting — aren't called temperate or self-indulgent, though here too one can take the right amount of pleasure, or too much, or too little. Same with hearing: no one calls a man self-indulgent for being wild about music or theater, or temperate for enjoying them rightly. Nor for pleasures of smell, except by association. We don't fault a man for enjoying the scent of fruit or roses or incense; we fault him for loving the smell of perfumes and rich cooking, since these recall to the self-indulgent man the objects of his cravings. (You can watch other men enjoy the smell of food when they're hungry too — but to enjoy it in that craving way is the mark of the self-indulgent, for whom these are objects of desire.) Even animals don't take pleasure through these senses except by association: a dog enjoys not the scent of a hare but the eating of it, and only smells out how near it is; the lion likes not the lowing of the ox but the meal, and the lowing only tells him it's close. He takes no pleasure in merely seeing or finding a deer or a wild goat — only in the prospect of the meal.

Temperance and self-indulgence, then, are about the pleasures animals also share — which is why they look slavish and brutish. These are the pleasures of touch and taste. And men barely use taste at all: taste is for telling flavors apart, the way wine-tasters and cooks judging a dish do, and the self-indulgent take little or no pleasure in that. Their pleasure is in the enjoyment itself, which comes entirely through touch — in eating, in drinking, in sex. Hence the wish a certain glutton is said to have made, that his throat were longer than a crane's, since his pleasure was in the touch. So the sense behind self-indulgence is the most widely shared of all the senses, and the vice looks rightly shameful, because it belongs to us not as human beings but as animals. To delight in such things and love them above all is brutish. (The most respectable touch-pleasures are set aside here — the rub-down and warm bath of the gym — since the self-indulgent man's craving touch isn't for the whole body, only certain parts.)

Of cravings, some are common to everyone, others particular and acquired. The desire for food is natural: anyone who needs it craves food, solid or liquid or both, and a young man in his prime, as Homer says, craves sex. But when it comes to this or that particular food or person, not everyone craves the same thing, and the craving isn't universal. Still, there's something natural in it, since different things please different men, and preferring certain things to whatever's at hand is universal. In the strictly natural desires few men go wrong, and all in one direction — too much. To eat or drink whatever's in front of you until you're stuffed is to overshoot the natural limit, since natural desire is just the filling of a real lack. That's why such men are called belly-mad, stuffing it past what they should; the slavish sort end up this way. But in the particular pleasures many men go wrong, and in many ways. To be "a lover of" something means taking pleasure in the wrong objects, or too intensely, or in the common vulgar way, or in the wrong manner — and the self-indulgent overshoot in all of these: they enjoy some things they shouldn't enjoy at all, things that ought to be loathed, and the things it's right to enjoy they enjoy too much, in the common way.

So excess regarding pleasures is self-indulgence, and is blameworthy. Looking at these dispositions on the side of pains, though, we find that a man isn't called temperate for enduring pains (as the brave man is) or self-indulgent for failing to. The self-indulgent man is so because he's pained more than he should be at not getting the pleasant thing — so his very pleasure causes him pain — while the temperate man is so because he isn't pained by its absence, by having to go without. The self-indulgent man craves all pleasant things, or the most pleasant, and his craving drives him to choose them over everything else. So he's pained both when he misses them and in the very craving, since all craving is painful — a strange thing, to be pained by reason of pleasure.

As for men deficient on the side of pleasure, who take less pleasure than they should, they hardly exist, since that kind of numbness isn't human: even the other animals tell foods apart and like some and dislike others. A man to whom nothing was pleasant and everything was alike would scarcely be human at all. There's no name for such a person, because he's barely real. The temperate man holds the mean. He takes no pleasure in what most delights the self-indulgent — he rather dislikes it — and none in the wrong things, none to excess in anything of the kind; he isn't pained by their absence and doesn't crave them, or only in moderation, never more than he should, never at the wrong time, and so on. The pleasant things that make for health and a good condition of body he'll go after in moderation, as he should, along with other pleasant things that don't get in the way of those and aren't unseemly or beyond his means. The man who went after these past that point would be loving such pleasures more than he should — and that's just what the temperate man is not. He keeps his desires in line with what reason directs.

Self-indulgence seems more truly voluntary than cowardice. Pleasure is the cause of the one, pain of the other, and we go toward pleasure and away from pain. Pain twists and unsettles a man's nature, while pleasure does nothing of the kind — so it's more voluntary and more justly blamed. It's also easier to train yourself against pleasures: life is full of them and the practice carries no danger, whereas with fearful things it's the reverse. And cowardice as a settled habit seems voluntary in a different way from the particular acts that build it. The habit itself is painless, but the particular moments unhinge a man with pain, so that he throws down his arms and disgraces himself — which is why some even think those moments carry a kind of compulsion. With the self-indulgent man it's the other way: the particular acts are fully voluntary, done out of craving and desire, but the resulting habit is less so, since no one craves to become an addict.

We give this vice a name — akolasia, which by its roots means "un-chastened-ness" — that we also use for the misbehavior of children, since the two cases are alike. (Which came first and lent the name to the other doesn't matter here, though plainly the later sense borrowed from the earlier.) The image is a good one: whatever reaches after base things and is apt to grow large needs chastening, and that fits the appetite and the child best of all, since children too live by craving, and the reach for pleasure is strongest in them. Unless the appetite is made obedient and put under the ruling part, it will swell out of bounds — in a fool the reach for pleasure is bottomless and indiscriminate, every indulgence feeds the habit, and if the cravings grow great and violent they'll drive out reason altogether. So they should be moderate and few, and never set against reason. An appetite in that state we call obedient and chastened. As a child should live by his tutor's orders, the appetite should live by reason's; and in the temperate man the appetite is in tune with reason, since both aim at the same mark — what is noble. The temperate man craves the right things, in the right way, at the right time, which is exactly what reason directs. Let that be our account of temperance.

Let us take up generosity next. It is held to be the mean concerning money: the generous person is praised not in war, nor in the matters that show self-control, nor in the courtroom, but in the giving and receiving of money — and chiefly in the giving. By money I mean everything whose worth can be measured in coin.

The excess and the deficiency about money are wastefulness and stinginess. We always pin "stingy" on people who care too much about money; "wasteful" we sometimes use in a looser, mixed sense, for people who lack self-control and pour money into their own runaway appetites. These are thought the worst sort, because they have several vices at once. But that is not the word's proper use. Strictly, the wasteful person is the one who has a single fault — ruining his own resources — for to be wasteful, in the root of the word, is to be one who destroys himself by his own doing. And the man who burns through his substance does in a way destroy himself, since his substance is what he lives on. That, then, is how we will use the word.

Anything that can be used can be used well or badly, and money is among the things that can be used. The person who uses a given thing best is the one who has the excellence concerned with it; so money will be used best by the person who has the excellence concerned with money — and that is the generous person. Now spending and giving are using money, while taking it in and holding onto it are simply possessing it. So giving to the right people is more the mark of the generous person than taking from the right sources and refusing to take from the wrong ones. In general, doing good to others is more the mark of excellence than having good done to you, and doing what is fine more than merely refraining from what is base — and plainly the doing of good and the doing of fine things belong to giving, while taking belongs only to receiving good or not behaving badly. Besides, we thank the giver, not the man who simply declines to take, and we praise him more. And refusing to take is easier than giving, since people are likelier to hold tight to their own than to reach for what isn't theirs. It is the givers, too, who get called generous; those who refuse to take are commended for fair dealing rather than for generosity, and for taking, people are not praised at all. And the generous are about the best-liked of all who have excellence, because they are useful — and their usefulness lies in the giving.

Every action that accords with excellence is fine and done for the sake of what is fine. So the generous person, too, will give for the sake of what is fine, and give rightly — to the right people, in the right amounts, at the right times, and with everything else that right giving involves — and he will do it gladly, or at least without pain, since whatever accords with excellence is pleasant, or at any rate not painful, and certainly not done with reluctance. The man who gives to the wrong people, or for some motive other than what is fine, should not be called generous but something else. Nor should the one who gives with pain — that shows he would rather have kept the money than done the fine thing, and no generous person feels that way. He will not take from the wrong sources either, since a man who sets no great store by money does not grab at it; and he is not one to ask favors, since a person who does others good does not readily take it from them. From the right sources — his own property, say — he will take, but as something necessary rather than fine, so that he has something to give. He will not neglect his own resources, since he wants the means to help others; and he will not give to just anyone, so that he has enough left for those he ought to give to, at the right times, and where giving is fine. It is very much in the generous person's grain even to overshoot in giving, leaving too little for himself; for it is like him to give no thought to his own interest.

Generosity is measured against a person's means, for it is not the size of the gift that makes the giving generous but the disposition of the giver, who gives in proportion to what he has. So nothing prevents the man who gives less from being the more generous, if he is giving out of less. People who have inherited their wealth rather than earned it are thought more generous, since they have never known want, and since everyone is fondest of what he himself has made — as parents are of their children, and poets of their poems. It is not easy for the generous person to be rich, since he is neither inclined to take nor to keep but to lay out, and he values money not for its own sake but for the sake of giving it away. This is why people complain that fortune leaves the most deserving the least rich. But it makes sense: you cannot have money if you take no trouble to have it, here as anywhere else. Still, he will not give to the wrong people, at the wrong times, and so on, since to do that would no longer be acting with generosity, and if he spent on such things he would have nothing left for what he ought. For, as I said, the generous person is the one who spends in proportion to his means and on the right objects, while the one who exceeds is wasteful. This is why we never call tyrants wasteful: it does not seem easy for their giving and spending to outrun their enormous holdings.

To sum up: since generosity is a mean concerning the giving and taking of money, the generous person will give and spend on the right objects, in the right proportion, in matters great and small alike, and do it gladly; and he will take from the right sources, in the right proportion. Because the excellence is a mean in both, he will do both as he ought, and right taking goes hand in hand with right giving, while taking that is not right runs against it. Should he happen to spend more than he should, or otherwise than he should, he will be vexed — but moderately, and as he ought, since feeling pleasure and pain at the right objects and in the right way is a feature of excellence. The generous person is also an easy partner where money is concerned: he is easily cheated, since he does not value money, and he is more pained at having failed to spend where he should than at having spent where he should not. He has no taste for the saying of Simonides.

The wasteful person goes wrong in these respects too: he feels neither pleasure nor pain at the right objects or in the right way, as will grow clearer as we go on. We have already said that wastefulness and stinginess are excess and deficiency, and in two things, giving and taking — for we class spending under giving. Wastefulness exceeds in giving and in refusing to take, and falls short in taking; stinginess falls short in giving and exceeds in taking, though only in small ways. Now the two sides of wastefulness do not usually go together: it is not easy to give to everyone while taking from no one, since a private person who gives like that soon runs through his means. People of this kind are the ones really thought wasteful, and such a man would seem a good deal better than the stingy one. He is easily cured — by age, and by running short of money — and he can come round to the mean, since he already has the makings of the generous person: he gives and refuses to take, only he does neither well or rightly. Train him in this, or change him some other way, and he becomes truly generous, giving to those he should and refusing to take where he should not. This is why he is not thought low in character; to overshoot in giving and in refusing to take is no sign of badness or meanness, only of folly.

So the man who is wasteful in this way is held to be far better than the stingy one, both for the reasons given and because he does good to many, while the stingy person does good to no one, not even himself. But most wasteful people, as we said, also take from the wrong sources, and on that side they are really stingy. They become grasping because they want to spend and cannot do it easily — their means soon give out, so they are forced to draw from elsewhere — and because they do not care about what is fine, they take recklessly and from any source at all, since their one wish is to give, and they are indifferent to how or from where. So their gifts are not even generous, being neither fine nor disinterested nor given in the right way. Often they make rich the people who ought to be poor: to the steady, decent sort they will give nothing, while to flatterers, or anyone who serves their pleasures, they hand over a great deal. That is why most of them have no self-restraint at all: free with their money, they lavish it on their own unbridled appetites and slide off toward their pleasures, because they do not live with an eye to what is fine. So the wasteful person, left to himself, drifts into these faults; but with some care taken of him he could reach the mean and what is right.

Stinginess, on the other hand, is incurable — old age and any kind of incapacity are thought to make people stingy — and it is more deeply rooted in human nature than wastefulness, since most people are fonder of getting money than of giving it. It also reaches far and takes many forms, since it has two parts, falling short in giving and exceeding in taking, and not everyone has it whole; sometimes it splits, and one set of people overshoot in taking while another fall short in giving. The names — close-fisted, tight, pinching, and the like — all belong to those deficient in giving; but they neither want nor will take what belongs to others, some from a real decency and a shrinking from anything base. Some keep their own out of a motive, real or alleged, of never being driven to do anything shameful — the skinflint belongs here, and everyone of that stamp, named from never letting anything go. Others hold off from their neighbors' goods out of fear, on the theory that you cannot take other people's things without their taking yours, so they would rather neither take nor give. The other set, stingy in taking, will accept anything from any source: people in degrading trades, pimps and the like, and loan sharks who lend small sums at steep interest. All of these take from the wrong sources and in the wrong amounts. What they have in common is shameful gain, since they all swallow disgrace for the sake of profit, and small profit at that. The people who take great things from the wrong sources and of the wrong kind — tyrants who sack cities and loot temples — we call wicked, impious, unjust, but not stingy. The cheat at dice, the man who strips the dead, the highway robber — these are stingy, since they go after shameful gain; both kinds put themselves to trouble and take on disgrace for profit, the one running the worst risks for plunder, the other making gain off the very friends they ought to be giving to. So both, in trying to profit from the wrong sources, go after shameful gain, and every such taking is stingy. And stinginess is rightly called the opposite of generosity: it is a greater evil than wastefulness, and people go wrong on its side more than on the side of the wastefulness we described. So much for generosity and the vices opposed to it.

Next would seem to come magnificence. This too is an excellence concerning money, but unlike generosity it does not extend to every transaction — only to expensive ones, and there it outruns generosity in sheer scale. For magnificence is, as the Greek word itself hints, fitting expenditure on a grand scale. But "grand" is relative: outfitting and captaining a warship is not the same expense as funding a public festival, and "fitting" too is relative to the man, to the occasion, and to what he is spending on. A person is not called magnificent for spending as he should on small or ordinary things — "often I gave to the wandering beggar" — but for doing it in great matters. The magnificent person is generous, then, but the generous person is not thereby magnificent. The deficiency here is called shabbiness, the excess gaudiness, tastelessness, and the like — faults not because the scale is too large for the right objects, but because they make a show in the wrong objects and in the wrong way. We will come to them shortly. The magnificent person is like a man of skill: he can see what fits and spend lavishly with taste. For, as we said at the start, a settled disposition is defined by its activities and by what it concerns.

The magnificent person's expenses, then, are large and fitting, and so are his results — for that secures spending that is not merely large but suited to the work. The work should match the expense, and the expense the work, or even exceed it. And the magnificent person will spend such sums for the sake of what is fine, which is common to all the excellences, and he will do it gladly and without stinting, since fussing over the figures is small. He asks how a thing may be done most beautifully and fittingly rather than how cheaply, and at what least cost. So the magnificent person must also be generous, since the generous person too will spend the right amount in the right way; but it is the grand scale that marks off the magnificent one, the object being the same as generosity's. And without spending more than the next man, he will make the result more magnificent. For the excellence of a possession and of a work are not the same: as a possession, the most valuable thing is the one worth most, gold for instance; but as a work, it is the one that is great and beautiful, since to behold such a thing is wonderful — and that is what magnificence is, excellence in a work on a grand scale. There are kinds of spending we call honorable: offerings to the gods, the furnishing of their temples, sacrifices, everything to do with the divine, and all the public matters people compete to do finely — funding a chorus splendidly, say, or fitting out a warship, or hosting a feast for the whole city. In all these, as we said, regard is paid to the doer's standing and means: the spending should be proportionate to these and should befit not only the work but the man doing it. This is why a poor man cannot be magnificent — he hasn't the means to spend largely and yet becomingly, and if he tries, he is a fool, since he is out of proportion and against propriety, whereas to accord with excellence a thing must be done rightly. Such spending suits people who have the resources to begin with, through themselves or their forebears or their connections, and those who are high-born or highly regarded, since all of this carries greatness and reputation.

So the magnificent person is roughly as I have described, and magnificence shows itself in expenditures of this kind, the greatest and most honorable, and among private ones in those that come only once, like a wedding, and in anything that engages the whole community or its leading people, and in receiving and sending off foreign guests, and in gifts and the returning of gifts. For the magnificent person spends not on himself but on the common good, and gifts have something of the character of offerings to the gods. It is like him, too, to furnish his house in keeping with his wealth, since even that brings a kind of credit, and to spend rather on works that last, since these are the most honorable — and to observe what fits in each case, since the same things do not suit gods and men, or a temple and a tomb. And each expense should be great of its kind, and great spending on a great object is most magnificent — though within any given field it is whatever is great there. There is a difference, too, between greatness in the work and greatness in the outlay: a very beautiful ball or flask makes a magnificent gift to a child, though its price is small and almost mean. So it is the mark of the magnificent person to do whatever he does magnificently, since work of that kind is hard to outdo and stands in fitting proportion to the cost. Such, then, is the magnificent person.

The man in excess — call it gaudiness — overspends because he spends improperly, as we said. Where small expense is called for, he lavishes much and shows off out of taste: he throws his dinner club a wedding feast, or, when he has to fund the chorus for a comedy, dresses the actors in purple for the opening scene, as the Megarians did. And all of this he does not for the sake of what is fine but to flaunt his wealth and because he thinks he'll be admired for it — spending little where he should spend much, and much where he should spend little. The shabby man, by contrast, comes up short in everything: even after spending the most, he ruins the whole effect for the want of some trifle. He dithers over every move, schemes how to spend the least, and then groans about even that, sure he is doing everything on a grander scale than he ought. Both states are faults, but they bring no disgrace, since they neither harm others nor look especially ugly.

The very name greatness of soul tells us that great things are its concern; let us first settle what sort. It makes no difference whether we look at the disposition in the abstract or at the person who has it. The great-souled person, then, is one who thinks himself worthy of great things and is — for a man who thinks it without grounds is a fool, and no one with excellence is a fool. The person who thinks himself worthy of little and is, is modest, but not great-souled, since greatness of soul implies bigness, the way beauty implies a sizable frame: small people can be neat and well-proportioned, but not beautiful. The man who thinks himself worthy of great things without being so is vain, though not everyone who overrates himself deserves the name. The one who thinks himself worthy of less than he is is little-souled, whether his real worth is great, middling, or small, since his estimate always falls short of it. The most striking case is the man of real worth, for what would he do if his worth were less? So in the size of what he claims the great-souled person is at the top, but in claiming what fits he is in the mean, since he rates himself at his true value, while the others overshoot and fall short.

Now since he rightly rates himself at a high, or rather the highest, value, his concern will be above all with one thing — and "value" here refers to external goods. We should take the greatest of these to be the one we assign to the gods, the one the powerful most desire, and the prize set on the finest deeds. That is honor; honor is the greatest of external goods. So it is in matters of honor and dishonor that the great-souled person bears himself as he should. Even without argument it is plain that the great-souled are concerned with honor, since honor is what the great think themselves chiefly worthy of, and at a certain rate. The little-souled person falls short, both as regards himself and as regards what the great-souled person is worth; the vain person overreaches as regards himself, but does not reach beyond the great-souled person. And since the great-souled person, by definition, is worthy of the greatest things, he must be the best of men, for the better a man is the more he is worth, and the best is worth the most. So the truly great-souled person must be good, and whatever is great in each excellence would seem to belong to him. It would not at all suit the great-souled person to run away flailing, or to wrong anyone — for with what aim would he do anything base, in whose eyes nothing is great? Go through the particulars and the great-souled person looks downright absurd if he is not good. He would not even deserve honor if he were bad, since honor is the prize of excellence and is given to the good. Greatness of soul, then, seems to be a kind of crown on the other excellences: it makes them greater, and cannot exist without them. This is why it is so hard to be truly great-souled — it is impossible without full goodness and nobility of character.

So honor and dishonor are above all the great-souled person's concern. At great honor from good people he will be pleased, but only moderately, as getting his due, or even a little less — for no honor can quite measure up to complete excellence; still, he will accept it, since they have nothing greater to give. But honor from ordinary people and on trifling grounds he will utterly despise, since it falls short of his deserts, and dishonor likewise, since in his case there can be no just ground for it. And though honor is his chief concern, he will also bear himself with moderation toward wealth, power, and every turn of fortune, good or bad, however it falls — neither overjoyed in good times nor unduly pained in bad. He does not even behave so about honor, and honor is the greatest of these things, since it is what makes power and wealth worth choosing, those who have them wanting honor through them. To the man who counts even honor a small thing, everything else is small too — which is why such men are thought arrogant. Strokes of good fortune are thought to feed greatness of soul: the well-born, the influential, the wealthy are held worthy of honor, since they stand higher, and whatever is superior in some good is held more worthy of honor. So such advantages do dispose people toward greatness of soul, since they bring honor from some quarters. But in truth only the good man deserves honor, though the man who has both goodness and these advantages is held still more worthy of it. People who have the advantages without the excellence are not justified in rating themselves high and are not rightly called great-souled, since complete excellence is one of the conditions of that character. Such men become arrogant and insolent — it is not easy to carry good fortune well without goodness — and, unable to carry it, and convinced of their own superiority, they look down on others and do whatever they please.
