They are imitating the great-souled person without being like him, copying him where they can: they skip the deeds that only real goodness produces and just despise other people. The great-souled person despises on good grounds, since his judgments are true, but most people do it at random.

He is not one to run small risks, nor does he go courting danger, since there are few things he prizes; but he will face great dangers, and when he does, he is lavish with his life, knowing there are terms on which life is not worth keeping. He is the sort to do favors, but ashamed to receive them, the one putting a man above, the other below. He will more than repay a favor done him, so that the original giver ends up the one in his debt and on the receiving end. Such men are thought to remember the favors they have done but not the ones done to them, since the receiver is below the giver, and the great-souled person wants to be above. He likes to hear of his own good turns but not of those done to him — which is why, in Homer, Thetis does not bring up her kindnesses to Zeus, nor the Spartans theirs to the Athenians, but only the benefits they had received. It is like the great-souled person to ask favors not at all, or very reluctantly, but to do a service readily; to bear himself loftily toward the great and the fortunate, but easily toward people of middling station — since to be above the first is hard and grand, but above the second is easy, and standing tall over the great is not ill-bred, while doing it to humble folk would be crude, like flexing your strength against the weak. He does not throw himself in honor's way, or go where others take the lead; he is slow and holds back, except where some great honor or work is at stake; he concerns himself with few things, but great and famous ones. He is open in his hatreds and his loves, since hiding them is a mark of fear, and he cares more for the truth than for appearances. He speaks and acts in the open — his contempt for others makes him blunt, so he is given to telling the truth, except when he is being self-deprecating with ordinary people — and he is reserved toward most. He cannot shape his life to please anyone but a friend, since that is servile; this is why all flatterers are lowly and all lowly men are flatterers. He is not easily impressed, since nothing is great in his eyes, nor does he bear grudges, for it is not like the great-souled person to dwell on things, least of all on wrongs — better to overlook them. He is no gossip: he will not talk about himself or anyone else, since he cares neither to be praised himself nor to have others blamed, nor again is he free with praise; and so he will not speak ill even of his enemies, except to show his contempt. He is the last man to lament over things that cannot be helped, or to ask for trifles, since that belongs to a person who takes such things seriously. He is the sort to own beautiful and useless things rather than profitable and productive ones, this being more the mark of a self-sufficient man. A slow gait, a deep voice, a measured way of speaking are thought to suit the great-souled person, since a man earnest about few things is not one to hurry, and one who counts nothing great is not one to strain — and it is anxiety that breeds the shrill voice and the quick step.

Such, then, is the great-souled person. The one in deficiency is little-souled, the one in excess is vain. These too are not thought vicious, exactly, only mistaken, since they do no harm. The little-souled person, though worthy of good things, cheats himself of his deserts; there is something wrong with him in his failing to think himself worthy of what is good, and it comes from not knowing himself, for otherwise he would reach for what he really merits, since that is good. Still, such people are thought not foolish so much as timid. But thinking so little of themselves seems to make them worse, since everyone's aims are set by what he thinks he deserves, and these men, convinced they deserve nothing, hold back from fine actions and pursuits, and from external goods as well. The vain, on the other hand, are fools, and plainly self-ignorant: they attempt honorable things as though worthy of them, and then get found out. They deck themselves out in dress and bearing and the like, and want their good fortune on display, and talk about it expecting to be honored for it. But little-souledness is more opposed to greatness of soul than vanity is, since it is the commoner failing and the worse.

Greatness of soul, then, is concerned with great honor, as we said. There seems to be an excellence concerned with honor too — as we mentioned earlier — which stands to greatness of soul roughly as generosity stands to magnificence: both keep clear of the great and dispose us rightly toward moderate and small matters. Just as there is a mean, an excess, and a deficiency in the giving and taking of money, so in reaching for honor there is the more and the less than one ought, and also the reaching from the right sources and in the right way. We blame the ambitious person for going after honor more than he should and from the wrong sources, and we blame the unambitious person for not even wanting honor for fine things. But sometimes we praise the ambitious person as manly and a lover of what is fine, and the unambitious one as moderate and self-restrained — as we noted before. Plainly, since "lover of so-and-so" can mean several things, we do not always mean the same thing by "lover of honor": as praise it means more than most people are, as blame more than a man should be. Since the mean here has no name, the extremes seem to fight over the empty ground between them. But where there is excess and deficiency there is a mean, and in fact people do reach for honor more than they should, and less, and sometimes just as they ought. This last state is the one praised, a mean concerning honor with no name of its own. Set beside ambition it looks like indifference to honor, and beside indifference it looks like ambition, and beside both it looks like both — which is not unique to this case. The extremes seem opposed to each other just because the mean has no name.

Mildness is the mean concerning anger. Since the person in the mean has no name, and the extremes nearly none either, we give the name mildness to the one in the mean, leaning toward the deficiency, which also has no name. The excess might be called irascibility, since the feeling is anger and its causes are many and various. The person who is angry at the right things and with the right people, and in the right way, at the right time, and for the right length of time, is praised — so this person is mild, since mildness is praised. The mild person means to be unruffled, not carried off by feeling, but angry only in the way, and at the things, and for the time that reason directs. He is thought to err rather toward the deficiency, since he is not quick to take revenge but more inclined to forgive. The deficiency — call it lack of spirit, or what you like — is blamed: people who do not get angry at what they should are thought fools, as are those who get angry in the wrong way, at the wrong time, or with the wrong people. A man in this state seems to feel nothing and to take no offense, and since he feels no anger, he is in no shape to defend himself. To put up with insults to yourself, and to stand by while your friends are insulted, is servile.

The excess comes in every form: people get angry with the wrong people, at the wrong things, more than they should, too quickly, and for too long. Not all of these are found in one man, of course — that would be impossible, since the evil at full strength would destroy itself and become unbearable. The hot-tempered get angry fast, at the wrong people and the wrong things and to excess, but they cool off fast too, which is their best feature: they do not bottle it up, but pay their offenders back, since their vehemence makes them show what they feel, and then it is over. The choleric are excessively quick and angry at everything, on every occasion — which is just what their Greek name means. The bitter hold their anger a long time, because they keep it pressed down, and only when they have had their revenge does it subside, since the revenge replaces pain with pleasure and so drains the anger off. If that does not happen, they carry the weight inside: because it does not show, no one can talk them out of it, and digesting anger by oneself takes time. Such people are a great burden to themselves and to their closest friends. We call those bad-tempered who get angry at the wrong objects, too much, and too long, and who are not satisfied without revenge or at least punishment. To mildness we oppose the excess rather than the deficiency, since it is the commoner — human nature being readier to take revenge than to let it go — and bad-tempered people are harder to live with. What I said before is plain here too: it is no easy thing to say how, and with whom, and at what, and how long one ought to be angry, and at what point one is right or wrong. The man who strays a little, either way, is not blamed; sometimes we praise people deficient in anger and call them mild, and sometimes we call the irritable spirited, as fit to lead. So it is hard to lay down in words just what degree or kind of lapse is blameworthy, since the decision lies in the particulars and rests with perception. But this much is clear: the mean is praiseworthy — being angry with the right people, at the right things, in the right way, and so on — while the excesses and deficiencies are blameworthy, slightly so if slight, more so if greater, and very much so when great. So we should plainly hold to the mean. Let that be our account of the states concerned with anger.

In social life — the give-and-take of words and deeds — some people are thought obsequious: out to please at all costs, they agree to everything and oppose nothing, and take it as their job never to cause anyone pain. The opposite sort are quarrelsome and contrary, opposing everything and not caring in the least whether they cause pain. Plainly both states are blameworthy, and the mean between them is praiseworthy — accepting what one should as one should, and objecting in the same spirit. This state has no name, but it is very like friendliness, since the person who has it is just the sort we would call a good friend, only with affection added. Where it differs from friendship is exactly there: it carries no feeling or affection for the people the man deals with. He takes everything as he should not out of love or hatred but simply because that is his character, and he treats strangers and acquaintances alike, intimates and outsiders alike — though fittingly in each case, since it is not right to be equally considerate of intimates and strangers, or to pain them equally. In general, then, his dealings are governed by what is fitting: he aims to avoid giving pain and to add to people's pleasure, but always with an eye to what is fine and beneficial. His concern is the pleasures and pains of social life; and wherever contributing to someone's pleasure would be dishonorable, or even harmful to himself, he will refuse and choose to cause pain instead. If a thing would bring real disgrace, or some harm, to the man doing it, while his objecting would cause only a little pain, he will not go along but hold out against it. He deals differently with the great and the ordinary, and with people according to how well he knows them, allowing for whatever differences there are, giving each his due — by himself preferring to give pleasure and wary of giving pain, but guided in the end by the consequences, by what is fine and beneficial, whichever weighs more. And he will inflict a small pain for the sake of a greater pleasure to come. So the person in the mean is roughly as I have described, but he has no name. Of those who set out to please, the one who simply wants to be agreeable, with no further motive, is obsequious; the one who does it to get something — money or what money buys — is a flatterer. And the man who is contrary in everything, as I said, is quarrelsome. Here too the extremes look opposed to each other because the mean has no name.

The mean that steers clear of boastfulness concerns much the same things and likewise has no name. Still, it is worth going over these states: by treating each separately we come to know moral character better, and we are the more convinced that the excellences are means by seeing that this holds across the board. We have already spoken of those whose social dealings aim at pleasure and pain; now let us turn to people who are truthful or false, in word and deed and in the claims they make. The boaster is thought to claim things that bring him credit when he does not have them at all, or to a greater degree than he does, while the false-modest person, on the contrary, denies what he has or plays it down. The one in the mean is a straightforward sort, truthful in life and word, owning what is his and making it neither more nor less than it is. Any of these lines can be taken with or without a further motive, but in general a person speaks and acts and lives according to his character, unless he has some special end in view. Now since falsehood is in itself low and blameworthy, and truth fine and praiseworthy, the truthful person, who is also in the mean, is praiseworthy, while both who depart from the truth are blameworthy — the boaster more so.

Let us take each in turn, and the truthful person first. I do not mean the man who keeps faith in his agreements, or in matters that touch on justice and injustice — that belongs to another excellence — but, in matters where nothing so serious is at stake, the man who is truthful in life and word simply because that is his settled state. Such a person must be counted good: someone who loves the truth as such, and is truthful where it makes no difference, will be all the more truthful where it does, since he will shun falsehood as base, having shunned it even for its own sake. And such a person is praiseworthy. Still, he leans rather toward understating than overstating, since that seems to be in better taste — exaggeration being so tiresome. The man who lays claim to more than he has with no further motive looks like a base sort, since otherwise he would take no pleasure in falsehood; but he comes off as a fool rather than a knave. The one who does it with a motive — for honor or glory, like the braggart — is not so very blameworthy; but the one who does it, directly or indirectly, for money is uglier. The braggart is a braggart not by his ability but by his choice, by his settled state and the kind of man he is — just as one liar takes pleasure in falsehood for its own sake while another lies out of a hunger for reputation or gain. Those who exaggerate for reputation claim the sort of qualities that win praise and congratulation; those who do it for gain claim qualities their neighbors can make use of, and whose absence can be hidden — being a skilled seer, say, or a good doctor. So most people pretend in this direction and exaggerate here, since these are the qualities that pay.

The false-modest, who play down their own qualities, come across as the more refined, since they are thought to speak not for gain but to avoid grandstanding. One very common trait in them is to disown the things people generally admire — as Socrates used to do. Those who lay false claim to small things, and to things whose falseness is obvious, are called poseurs and are contemptible. Sometimes this very modesty looks like boasting, as with the studied plainness of dress the Spartans go in for; both excess and the extreme of deficiency have something of boasting in them. But people who practice understatement in moderation, and about things not too plainly false, give an impression of refinement. Here it is the boaster who seems opposed to the truthful person, as the worse character.

Since life has its breaks and in them makes room for amusement with a touch of humor, it seems there is a fitting way to behave here too — a sense of the kind of thing to say and how to say it, and likewise of what to listen to. There is a difference between saying such things and hearing them. Here too there is an excess, a deficiency, and a mean. People who overdo the laughable are thought buffoons and vulgar, grabbing at a laugh any way they can, at any cost, bent on raising one rather than on saying what is seemly and sparing the target of the joke. Those who would never crack a joke themselves and are annoyed by anyone who does are thought boorish and stiff. The ones who joke in good taste are called witty — "nimble," really, since their wit is a kind of nimbleness of character, and just as we judge bodies by their movements, so we judge characters. But because the laughable lies near at hand and most people enjoy fun and joking more than they should, the buffoons too get called witty, as if they were charming. That they differ, and by a good deal, is plain from what has been said. Another thing belonging to the mean is tact: it is the tactful person who says and listens to the things that befit a decent and well-bred man, since there are things it suits such a man to say and hear by way of humor, and the humor of a gentleman differs from that of a vulgarian, as the educated man's does from the boor's. You can see this by comparing the old comedy with the new: in the old, the fun came from obscenity; in the new, more from innuendo — and that is no small difference where decency is concerned. Should we then define the man who jokes well by his saying what befits a gentleman, or by his not paining the target, or even by his giving pleasure? Or is any such definition vague, since different things are hateful and pleasant to different people? Whatever he says, he will also listen to, since a man is thought to do what he can stand to hear — though there is a limit; he will not do quite everything he will listen to, since a joke is a kind of abuse, and lawgivers forbid certain kinds of abuse and perhaps should have forbidden certain jokes too. So the refined and gentlemanly man is, as it were, a law to himself. Such is the person in the mean, whether you call him tactful or witty. The buffoon cannot resist the laughable, sparing neither himself nor anyone else so long as he gets his laugh, saying things no man of refinement would say, and some he would not even put up with hearing. The boor is useless for such company: contributing no fun of his own, he is sour with everyone who does. Yet some rest and amusement in life are generally agreed to be necessary. So the three means we have described all occur in life, and all concern the give-and-take of words and deeds. They differ in that one is concerned with truth, and the other two with what is pleasant: of these two, one deals with the humor of life, the other with the rest of social intercourse.

To call shame an excellence is not right, since it is more like a feeling than a settled state. It is defined as a kind of fear of disgrace, and its effects are much like those of the fear of danger: people who feel shame turn red, and people who fear death turn pale. Both, then, are plainly bodily in some way, which is thought a mark of a feeling rather than a settled state. The feeling, moreover, does not suit every age, only youth. We think the young should be capable of shame, since living by feeling as they do, they go wrong often, and shame holds them back. We praise the young for being modest, but no one would praise an older man for being prone to shame, since we think he ought not to do anything that calls for it. For shame, arising at base actions, does not belong to a good man at all, since such actions should not be done in the first place — and it makes no difference whether some things are disgraceful in truth and others only in opinion, since neither should be done, so that one ought not to be in a position to feel shame at all. To be the kind of man who does something disgraceful is the mark of a bad character. To be the kind who would feel shame if he did, and to count that as being good, is absurd, since shame is felt only at voluntary actions, and a good man will never willingly do anything base. Shame may be good on a condition — "if he were to do such a thing, he would feel shame" — but the excellences are good without conditions, not just in supposed cases. And granting that shamelessness, not blushing to do what is disgraceful, is base, it still does not follow that it is good to do such things and then feel shame. Self-control, likewise, is not properly an excellence but a kind of mixed state — but all that will be set out in a later book.

Our subject now is justice and injustice: what kinds of action they are concerned with, what sort of mean justice is, and between which extremes the just itself stands as a middle. We will go about it the same way we have gone about everything else in this inquiry.

Everyone uses the word justice to mean a settled state of character — the state that makes people capable of doing just things, and that makes them actually do them and want them. Injustice is the matching state, the one that makes people act unjustly and want what is unjust. Let that rough sketch stand as our starting point. I put it that way deliberately, because a state of character does not work the way a science or a skill does. We think a single science or skill covers both members of a pair of opposites — medicine knows both health and disease — but a state of character does not. Health produces only healthy actions, not their opposites; we say a man is walking in a healthy way when he walks the way a healthy man would. Still, you can often read one of two opposite states off the other, and read the states off the things they apply to. If it is clear what good physical condition is, it becomes clear what bad condition is too, and the good condition shows itself in the things that go with it, and the reverse. If good condition is firm flesh, then bad condition is flabby flesh, and whatever produces firm flesh goes with the good condition.

As a rule, if one of two opposite terms is used in more than one sense, so is the other. If "the just" has several senses, so does "the unjust." And justice and injustice do in fact seem to be used in several senses each — but because the line between the senses is so fine, it usually goes unnoticed that the word is doing more than one job. It is not obvious, the way it is when the senses of a word are wildly far apart and the eye catches the difference at once — the way the Greek word kleis names both the collarbone under an animal's neck and the bar you use to lock a door. So let us pin down how many senses the word "unjust man" carries. We call a man unjust if he breaks the law, and we also call him unjust if he grasps for more than his share and takes unequal advantage. Plainly, then, the just man will be the one who keeps the law and the one who takes only his fair, equal share. So "the just" means the lawful and the equal, and "the unjust" means the unlawful and the unequal.

Since the unjust man is also a grasping man, he grasps after good things — though not after every kind of good. He grasps after the goods that are the stuff of good and bad fortune: things that are good in the abstract, always, but not always good for the particular person who has them. People still pray for these things and chase them, when what they should do is pray that the things good in the abstract may also be good for them, and choose what is actually good for themselves. The unjust man does not always grab the larger amount, though. Sometimes he takes the smaller — when what is on offer is simply bad. But since the lesser evil counts in a way as a good, and grasping is always a grasping after good, even here he is reckoned a grasping man: a man who reaches for more good than his fair share. He is also an unequal man, which is the wider term that covers both cases.

We said the lawbreaker is unjust and the law-keeper just. Clearly, then, everything lawful is in some sense just, since by "lawful" we mean what the lawmaking power has laid down, and every such thing we call just. And the laws speak to everything, aiming either at the common good of all, or at the good of the best, or at the good of those in power — taking real excellence as the standard, or some other measure. So in one sense we call "just" whatever tends to produce and preserve happiness, and the parts of happiness, for the political community. The law also commands the actions of a brave man — not deserting your post, not fleeing, not throwing away your weapons — and the actions of the temperate man, like keeping clear of adultery and wanton excess, and the actions of the even-tempered man, like not striking others or hurling abuse. It does the same across the whole range of the virtues and vices, commanding the one and forbidding the other — rightly, if it is a good law, less well if it was thrown together carelessly.

Justice in this sense is complete virtue — though not just in itself, but as exercised toward other people. This is why justice is often thought the best of the virtues, finer than the evening star or the morning star, and why the proverb says that in justice every virtue is summed up. It is complete virtue in a special way, because to have it is to be able to exercise virtue toward others, not only on yourself. Plenty of people can manage virtue in their own private affairs but cannot pull it off in dealings with others. There is wisdom in the saying of Bias, that office will show the man — because a man who holds office is necessarily in contact with others, bound up in a community. For this same reason justice alone among the virtues is thought to be a good that belongs to someone else, since it always bears on another person: the just man does what serves another, whether a ruler or a fellow citizen. The worst man is the one whose vice infects not only himself but his friends; the best is the one whose virtue reaches not only himself but his neighbor — for that is hard. Justice in this broad sense, then, is not one part of virtue but the whole of virtue in action, and the injustice that answers to it is not one part of vice but vice entire. How this justice differs from virtue as such is clear from what we have said: it is the very same thing, looked at from a different angle. Insofar as it bears on your neighbor, it is justice; insofar as it is simply this kind of settled character, it is virtue.

But what we are really after is justice as a part of virtue — for there is such a thing, as we ordinarily speak — and likewise injustice as a part of vice. Here is the proof that this particular injustice exists. A man can act unjustly through any number of vices without grasping for more than his share: he throws away his shield out of cowardice, or hurls abuse out of bad temper, or refuses a friend money out of stinginess. But sometimes a man does a grasping thing that traces to none of those vices, certainly not to all of them — and yet to some vice, since we do blame him — and that vice is injustice. So there is a kind of injustice distinct from the injustice that is coextensive with vice as a whole, related to it as a part to the whole. And there is a corresponding "unjust" related to the unlawful, again as part to whole. Take two cases. One man sleeps with another's wife for profit and actually comes out ahead by it; another does the same thing out of sheer lust, at the cost of money and to his own harm. We would call the second man self-indulgent rather than grasping, and the first unjust but not self-indulgent. Why? Plainly because the first man gained. Every other unjust act we trace back to some particular vice — adultery to runaway appetite, deserting a comrade to cowardice, throwing a punch to anger. But if a man gains by the act, we trace it to no vice except injustice. So there is clearly a kind of injustice, distinct from and alongside the injustice that takes in all vice, sharing the same name because its definition falls in the same family. Both have their force in dealings with others; but the one operates on honor, money, safety — whatever single name might cover all of these — and is driven by the pleasure that comes with gain, while the other operates across everything the good man's conduct touches.

That there is more than one kind of justice, then — that there is one distinct from and alongside the justice coextensive with virtue — is clear. We must next find out what it is and what it is like. We divided the unjust into the unlawful and the unequal, and the just into the lawful and the equal. The broad injustice already discussed runs along the unlawful. But the unequal and the merely-more are not the same; they differ as part to whole, since everything more is unequal, but not everything unequal is more. So this unjust, and this injustice, are not the same as the earlier ones but distinct — the part as against the whole. This particular injustice is a part of the injustice coextensive with vice, and this justice a part of the justice coextensive with virtue. So what we have to discuss now is particular justice and injustice, and the particular just and unjust. Let us set aside the justice that ranks as complete virtue — virtue practiced toward others in all its forms — and the injustice that answers to it. It is plain enough, too, how to mark off the just and unjust that belong to it: most lawful acts are just the acts that naturally flow from virtue in its full sense, since the law commands living by each virtue and forbids living by each vice, and the things that produce virtue across the board are the measures laid down for a citizen's education. (Whether the education that makes a man simply good, without reference to others, belongs to political science or some other science, we can settle later — for it may be that being a good man and being a good citizen are not always the same thing.)

Of this particular justice, and the just that goes with it, there are two kinds. One has to do with the distribution of honor, money, or anything else divisible among the members of the community — for here one man's share, set beside another's, can be equal or unequal. The other is the corrective justice that sets right the dealings between one person and another. And this second kind has two parts, because some dealings are voluntary and some involuntary. The voluntary ones include selling, buying, lending at interest, putting up security, lending without interest, leaving goods on deposit, and hiring — called voluntary because the parties enter into them by their own choice. The involuntary ones either work in secret — theft, adultery, poisoning, pandering, luring away slaves, killing by stealth, bearing false witness — or are done by open force: assault, imprisonment, murder, robbery, maiming, insult, public abuse.

We said the unjust man is the unequal man, and the unjust thing the unequal thing. Plainly, then, there is a mean of the unequal — namely the equal, the exact midpoint; for wherever there is a more and a less, there is also an equal. So if the unjust is the unequal, the just is the equal — which everyone grants without needing it proved. And since the equal is a mean, the just is a mean too. Now the equal requires at least two terms. So the just turns out to be both a mean and an equal, and to be these for certain people: a mean between certain amounts — the greater and the less — equal between two parties, and just toward certain persons. The just, then, involves at least four terms: two persons for whom it is just, and two things being shared. And the equality must hold between the persons as it holds between the things, since as the things stand to one another, so must the persons. If the persons are not equal, they must not get equal shares. This is the very root of all the quarreling and grievance in the world — when equals are awarded unequal shares, or unequals are awarded equal ones. The need for this matching of ratios is plain from the common phrase "according to merit." Everyone agrees that just distribution must go by some standard of merit, even if they do not agree on what the standard is: democrats say free birth, oligarchs wealth, others noble descent, aristocrats excellence.

So the just, in distribution, is a proportional thing. Proportion is not a feature of numbers alone but of quantity in general — it is equality of ratios, and it requires at least four terms. (This is obvious in what we may call separated proportion, with four distinct terms; but it holds even in continuous proportion, where one term is used twice and counted as two, as when A is to B as B is to C — there B does double duty.) The just likewise requires at least four terms, and the ratio between the two pairs is the same, because the persons and the things are divided alike. As person A stands to person B, so thing C stands to thing D; combine them and the share that joins the first person to his thing, set against the share that joins the second person to his, keeps the same ratio. The distribution is just exactly when it joins the terms so as to preserve this ratio. Mathematicians call this kind of proportion geometric, since in geometric proportion the whole stands to the whole as each part stands to its corresponding part. So the just, in distribution, is this proportional thing, and the unjust is what breaks the proportion. When the proportion is broken, one share grows greater and the other smaller — which is exactly what happens in real life: the man who acts unjustly ends up with more of the good, and the man wronged with less. With bad things it runs the other way, since the lesser evil, set against the greater, counts as a good — the lesser evil being more worth choosing, and what is worth choosing is a good, the more so the greater the good. This, then, is one kind of the just.

The remaining kind is the corrective, which arises in dealings both voluntary and involuntary. This just has a different form from the last. The justice that governs the sharing of common property always follows the proportion just described — shares come out in the same ratio as what each person put in. The injustice opposed to it is the breaking of that proportion. But the justice in private dealings, though it is still a kind of equality, follows a different proportion — not the geometric one but the arithmetic. Here it makes no difference whether a good man has robbed a bad one or a bad man a good one, whether the adulterer is a decent man or a scoundrel. The law looks only at the harm done; it treats the parties as equals and asks merely who did the wrong and who suffered it, who inflicted the damage and who took it. So when this injustice — this inequality — has arisen, the judge tries to even it out again. When one man has been struck and the other has struck him, or one has killed and the other lies dead, the suffering and the doing have been split into unequal shares; the judge tries to restore equality by means of the penalty, subtracting from the gain. (We do apply the words "gain" and "loss" to these cases, even where they do not strictly fit — calling what the man who threw the punch got a "gain," and what the man who took it suffered a "loss" — but once the harm has been measured, the one side is called loss and the other gain.) So the equal is a mean between the more and the less, and gain and loss are the more and the less running in opposite directions: more good and less evil is gain, less good and more evil is loss. The equal, the mean between them, is the just. So the corrective just is the mean between loss and gain.

This is why people in a dispute turn to a judge. To go to the judge is to go to justice itself, for the judge is meant to be justice come alive — justice given a face. People look for a judge as a man in the middle; some even call judges "middlemen," on the idea that if they can hit the middle they will hit the just. So the just is a mean, since the judge is. The judge's job is to make things equal. It is as though a line had been divided unevenly: he takes from the longer part the amount by which it overshoots the half, and adds that to the shorter. When the whole has been split into two equal parts, then people say they have what is their own — they have gotten the equal. The equal here is the arithmetic mean between the greater and the less. This, by the way, is where our Greek words for "just" and "judge" come from: dikaion, the just, is as if to say dichaion, "in two halves," and the judge, dikastes, is the dichastes, "the halver." When you take a piece from one of two equal amounts and add it to the other, the second now exceeds the first by twice that piece; the excess of the larger over the mean must be taken from the larger, and the excess of the mean over the smaller must be added to the smaller. The words "loss" and "gain" themselves come from voluntary exchange: to have more than you started with is to gain, to have less is to lose — as in buying and selling and the other dealings the law leaves to private agreement. When the outcome leaves you with neither more nor less but exactly what you began with, people say they have their own, and neither lose nor gain. So the corrective just is a mean between loss and gain in involuntary dealings: it is having the same after the transaction as you had before.

Some people think that justice is simply reciprocity — being done to as you have done. The Pythagoreans held this; they defined the just, flatly and without qualification, as "suffering in return what you have done to another." But bare reciprocity does not fit either distributive or corrective justice — though people read it into the saying of Rhadamanthus: "If a man should suffer what he did, that would be straight justice." In plenty of cases the two come apart. If an official strikes a man, the official must not be struck back; but if a man strikes an official, he must not only be struck but punished as well. And whether the act was willing or unwilling makes a great difference. Still, in dealings of exchange it is exactly this kind of justice — reciprocity — that binds people together, but reciprocity by proportion, not by flat equality. A community holds together by proportionate give-and-take. People want either to return evil for evil — and where they cannot, they feel themselves no better than slaves — or to return good for good; and where they cannot, no exchange happens, and it is exchange that binds them. This is the point of putting the temple of the Graces in the public square: to remind people to return a favor, for that is what belongs to grace. A man who has received a kindness should repay it, and then begin a fresh round of grace by doing a kindness himself.

Exchange in due proportion can be pictured by the diagonals of a figure. Set the parties at two corners and their goods at the other two, so that each party is linked along one side to his own goods, and the line joining the parties runs opposite the line joining the goods. The builder is to take from the shoemaker the shoemaker's product and give the shoemaker his own in return. If there is first a proportional equality, and reciprocity follows, the just result we are after comes about. If not, the deal is not equal and will not hold — for there is no reason one man's product should not be worth more than the other's, and so the products must be made equal before the exchange. The same holds in every craft. Crafts would be wiped out altogether if there were no matching of what the producer makes to what the consumer takes, in amount and in quality. No exchange arises between two of the same kind — two doctors do not trade with each other — but between a doctor and a farmer, between people who are different and unequal; and these must be brought to equality before they can trade.

So everything that is to be exchanged must somehow be comparable. This is why money came in. Money is a kind of middle term: it measures everything, and so measures excess and shortfall — how many shoes are worth a house, or worth a given amount of food. As builder is to shoemaker, so a certain number of shoes must be to the house (or to the food, if a farmer takes the builder's place). Without this proportion there is no exchange and no dealing, and there is no proportion unless the goods are in some way made equal. Hence the need, as we said, for one single measure of all things. And that measure is, in truth, demand — the need people have, which holds all dealings together. If people needed nothing, or did not need each other's goods, there would be no exchange, or not the same exchange. By common agreement, money has come to stand in for demand. That is why it has the name it does: the Greek for money, nomisma, comes from nomos, custom or law — because money is what it is not by nature but by custom, and it lies with us to change its value or to make it worthless. There will be reciprocity, then, once the goods have been made equal — so that as farmer is to shoemaker, so the shoemaker's goods are to the farmer's. They must be brought into that proportion before they trade. Otherwise one side will run away with both extremes — too much profit at the other's expense. But when each has exactly his own, the parties are equal and can deal, because the same equality can hold for both. What links people in their dealings is demand, as a single common thing — shown by the fact that when one party does not want what the other has, or neither wants the other's, they do not trade at all; they trade only when one wants what the other holds, giving grain, say, for wine.

Money also serves as a kind of guarantee for future exchange: if we need nothing now, money assures us we can get goods when we do. The principle of money is that whoever brings it can take goods in exchange. Money too loses value, of course — its buying power is not always the same — but it holds steadier than the goods it stands for. This is why everything should be priced: so that exchange is always possible, and where there is exchange there is dealing. So money, like a measuring rod, makes all things commensurable and brings them to equality. Without exchange there would be no dealing, without equality no exchange, and without commensurability no equality. Strictly, things so wildly different cannot be made truly commensurable, but in reference to demand we can come close enough for all practical purposes. The common measure must be a single thing, and one fixed by agreement — which is why it is called nomisma — for that is what makes everything commensurable. In the end, all things are measured by money. Let a house be worth five minae and a bed worth a tenth of that; then it is clear how many beds equal a house — five. Plainly this is how exchange worked before money existed: it makes no difference whether you give five beds for a house or the price of five beds.

We have now said what the just and the unjust are in the abstract. With those defined, it is clear that acting justly is a mean between acting unjustly and being treated unjustly — the first being to have more than your share, the second to have less. But justice is a mean in a different way from the other virtues. It is not itself poised between two vices; rather, it aims at the mean, while injustice occupies both extremes. Justice is the settled state that makes a man able, by deliberate choice, to do what is just — to divide things between himself and another, or between two other people, so as to give himself not the larger and his neighbor the smaller share of what is worth having (and the reverse with what is harmful), but a proportionally equal share, and to do the same when judging between two others. Injustice is the matching state with respect to the unjust. Since the unjust is an excess or a deficiency of what is beneficial or harmful, in breach of proportion, injustice is both excess and deficiency, because it aims at producing both: excess, in one's own case, of what is simply beneficial, and deficiency of what is harmful; and in the case of others much the same, except that the proportion may be broken in either direction, however it happens to fall. Of the unjust act, the lesser part is being treated unjustly, and the greater part is treating others so. Let this stand as an adequate account of the nature of justice and injustice, and of the just and the unjust in general.

A man may do unjust things without yet having a settled unjust character — so we may ask whether a man becomes unjust in a given form, a thief or an adulterer, simply by doing an act of that kind. The answer, I think, is that the act alone does not settle it. A man might sleep with another's wife, knowing full well whose wife she was, and yet do it not by deliberate choice but on a surge of passion. He acts unjustly, certainly, but he has not thereby formed an unjust character. He may have stolen without being a thief, committed adultery without being an adulterer, and so on. We have already spoken of how reciprocity stands to the just. Here we should add that the justice we are looking into is both justice in the abstract and justice as it appears in political life — and political justice holds among people who share a life with a view to self-sufficiency, who are free and equal, whether equal by proportion or by number. So among people not in this position there is no political justice between them, only justice of a kind, by resemblance. For justice exists only where there is law to govern the relations of people, and law only where injustice is possible, since the giving of judgment is the act of marking off the just from the unjust. And wherever injustice is possible, acting unjustly is possible too — though not the reverse: not everyone capable of acting unjustly is therefore unjust by character; for to be unjust by character is to give oneself the larger share of what is good in the abstract and the smaller share of what is bad.

This is why we do not let a man rule, but let reason rule — because a man rules in his own interest and turns into a tyrant. A ruler is meant to be the guardian of the just, and so of the equal. If he is a just man, he seems to get no special advantage of his own, since he does not allot himself the larger share of what is good in the abstract, except as it falls to him by proportion. So he really rules for others — which is why people say justice is a good belonging to someone else. Some compensation, then, is owed him, and it comes in the form of honor and privilege; where these fall short, rulers turn into tyrants. The justice between master and slave, and between father and child, is not the same as political justice but only resembles it. There can be no injustice, strictly, toward what is simply your own; and a slave, or a child while still young and not yet broken off into a separate person, is as it were a part of yourself — and no one chooses to harm himself. So there is no injustice toward oneself, and therefore none of the political just or unjust here, which we said holds by law and among those whose nature it is to live under law — and those are people who share equally in ruling and being ruled. This is also why there is more room for justice between husband and wife than between a man and his children or his slaves: that is household justice, and it too differs from political justice.

Political justice itself comes in two kinds, natural and conventional. The natural is what has the same force everywhere and does not depend on people's accepting it or not. The conventional is what could just as well have been set up one way or the other before it was fixed, but is no longer indifferent once it has been laid down — like fixing a ransom at one mina, or sacrificing one goat rather than two sheep, or any rule passed for a particular occasion, such as the sacrifice in honor of Brasidas; in short, anything settled by specific decree. Some people think all justice is conventional, on the grounds that what exists by nature is unchangeable and has the same force everywhere — fire burns the same here as it does in Persia — whereas they see what is counted just shifting from place to place. That is not quite right, though there is something to it. Among the gods, perhaps, nothing of the just changes at all; but among us there is something that exists by nature, even granting that all of it is subject to change. Even so, we can mark off, well enough in practice, what among changeable things exists by nature and what does not but rests on convention and agreement — granting that both alike can be altered. The same distinction applies elsewhere: the right hand is naturally the stronger, yet some people can become equally skilled with both. Conventional just things can be compared to measures: the measures for wine and grain are not the same everywhere — larger where the goods are bought wholesale, smaller where they are sold. In the same way, the just things that are not natural but humanly devised are not everywhere the same, just as constitutions are not the same everywhere — though only one constitution is everywhere, by nature, the best.

Every just and lawful thing stands to the acts that embody it as a universal stands to its particulars: the acts are many, but each principle is single, since each is universal. So there is a difference between an unjust act and the unjust in the abstract, and between a just act and the just in the abstract. A thing is unjust in itself, by nature or by ordinance; once that thing has been carried out in an action, there is an unjust act — but not before; before that there is only an unjust thing. The same goes for a just act. A man is said to act unjustly or justly when he embodies these abstracts in voluntary actions; when he embodies them involuntarily, he acts neither justly nor unjustly except by accident. Whether an act counts as just or unjust depends on its being voluntary or not: when the embodying of the unjust is voluntary, it is blamed and is at the same time an unjust act; without voluntariness there is something unjust in itself but not yet an unjust act. By voluntary I mean, as before, whatever a man does that is in his own power, knowingly — not in ignorance of whom he is acting on, with what, and to what end. He must know whom he is striking, with what, and with what likely result, and none of this by accident or under compulsion. If someone seized his hand and used it to strike a third party, he does not act voluntarily, since it was not up to him. Or he may know he is striking a man, even one of those present, yet not know it is his father. Apply the same to the result and to the whole of any action. In short, what is done through ignorance, or not through ignorance but not in the agent's control or under compulsion, is involuntary. I mention this because there are many natural things we do and undergo knowingly that are still neither voluntary nor involuntary — growing old, for instance, or dying.

Accident can attach to unjust acts just as it can to just ones. A man might return a deposit, but against his will and only from fear of the consequences of refusing; we should not say he does what is just, or acts justly, except by accident. Likewise the man who fails through compulsion and against his will to return a deposit acts unjustly, or does the unjust, only by accident. Voluntary actions we do either from deliberate choice or without it — from choice when we have first deliberated, without choice when we have not. There are three kinds of harm that can be done in dealings between people. When the harm is done with ignorance, it is a mere mistake: the agent did the thing to a person he did not mean to, or did not the thing he meant, or not with the instrument or to the result he intended — he did not think he would hit the man at all, or not with this, or not this man, or did not expect this result; he meant to prick, not to wound. When the harm comes about against all reasonable expectation, it is a misfortune. When it is not against expectation but carries no malice, it is a blunder — a man blunders when the source of the error lies in himself, and meets misfortune when the source lies outside him. When he acts knowingly but without prior deliberation, it is an unjust act — for instance, whatever men do in anger or under other passions that are unavoidable or natural. In doing such harms they do act unjustly, and their acts are unjust, but they are not yet confirmed unjust or wicked men on that account, because the harm did not spring from depravity. When it does spring from deliberate choice, then the man is a confirmed unjust and depraved character.

On this principle, acts done in anger are rightly judged not to be done with malice aforethought, since the man who acts in anger is not the real instigator — the one who provoked his anger is. And the dispute in such cases is not about the facts but about who is in the right, the anger having been roused by a sense of injury. Unlike disputes over a contract, where one party must be lying unless he can plead genuine forgetfulness, here both sides agree on what happened and quarrel over which of them has justice on his side — the real aggressor, the one who laid the plot, cannot be ignorant of what he did. So one side thinks a wrong was done and the other does not. A man acts unjustly, then, if he harms another on purpose; and a man who commits such acts of injustice, in breach of proportion or of equality, is by that very fact an unjust character. In the same way a man is a just character when he acts justly by deliberate choice — and he acts justly if he acts voluntarily. As for involuntary harms, some are pardonable and some are not. Those done not merely in ignorance but from ignorance are pardonable; those done not from ignorance but in ignorance, where the ignorance is caused by some passion that is neither natural nor a fair part of human weakness, are not.

We may ask whether we have said enough about being treated unjustly and treating others unjustly. First, is the case possible that Euripides puts, strangely, when he writes: "My mother he has slain; the tale is short — either he killed her willing and himself willing, or with her will but against his own"? In other words, can a person be treated unjustly with his own consent, or must every case of being treated unjustly be against the sufferer's will, just as every act of treating someone unjustly is voluntary? And next, are all cases of being treated unjustly of one kind — involuntary — or are some voluntary and some not? The same questions arise for being treated justly. All acting justly is voluntary, so it is reasonable to expect the two — being treated unjustly and being treated justly — to line up the same way, each either voluntary or involuntary. Yet it would be odd to say that every case of being treated justly is voluntary, since some people are treated justly against their will.

One might also fairly ask whether everyone who has suffered something unjust has thereby been treated unjustly, or whether suffering works like acting: in both, a man can take part in what is just or unjust only by accident. Plainly it is the same with the unjust. Doing things that are unjust in themselves is not the same as acting unjustly, and suffering them is not the same as being treated unjustly. The same holds for acting justly and being treated justly, since no one can be treated unjustly unless someone else acts unjustly, and no one treated justly unless someone else acts justly. Now if acting unjustly is simply harming someone voluntarily — knowing whom you harm, with what, and how — and if the man who lacks self-control harms himself voluntarily, then it would seem a man could be treated unjustly with his own consent, and could treat himself unjustly. (This is in fact one of the questions raised: whether a man can treat himself unjustly.) Or again, a man might, through his own lack of self-control, be harmed by another acting voluntarily — another case, it seems, of being treated unjustly with one's consent. The solution, I think, is that our definition of being treated unjustly is incomplete. We must add, to harming with knowledge of the person, the instrument, and the manner, the further condition that it is against the wish of the man harmed. So a man can be harmed and can suffer what is in itself unjust voluntarily — but treated unjustly voluntarily no one can be, since no one wishes to be harmed, not even the man who lacks self-control. He acts against his own wish, for no one wishes for what he does not think good, and the man without self-control does not do what he thinks he ought. And a man who gives away his own property — as Homer says Glaucus gave Diomedes "gold armor for bronze, the worth of a hundred oxen for the worth of nine" — is not treated unjustly, since the giving rests entirely with him, whereas being treated unjustly does not: there must be someone else doing the wrong. So it is clear that being treated unjustly is not voluntary.

Two points remain that we set out to discuss. First, in a faulty distribution, is the man who acts unjustly the one who awarded the larger share against proper merit, or the one who got it? And second, can a man treat himself unjustly? On the first: if it is the distributor who acts unjustly and not the man with the larger share, then when a person knowingly and willingly gives more to another than to himself, he is treating himself unjustly — which is what decent, moderate men are thought to do, since it is a mark of the fair-minded man to take less than his due. But the case is not quite as stated. The man who gave away the larger share did get more of some other good — reputation, say, or the simple honor of the thing. And the difficulty dissolves by the definition of unjust treatment: the man suffers nothing against his own wish, so on that score at least he is not treated unjustly; at most he is harmed. It is also clear that the one who acts unjustly is the distributor, not the man who ends up with the larger share. For what makes an act unjust is not merely that the unjust attaches to what a man does, but that he does it voluntarily — and the source of the action lies with the distributor, not the receiver. Besides, "doing" is said in several senses: in one sense lifeless things kill, or a hand does, or a slave at his master's command; the receiver in our case does not act unjustly but does things that are in themselves unjust. Again, if a man makes a wrong award in ignorance, he does not act unjustly in the eye of the law, nor is his judgment unjust — though it is unjust in a sense, for the legally just and the primary, natural just are not the same. But if he gave the wrong judgment knowingly, then he too grasps at a larger share — of gratitude from the one party, or of revenge against the other. So the man who judges wrongly from such motives gets more, in exactly the way a man does who takes a cut of the unjust gain itself: the judge who wrongly awarded a field did not get land but money for his unjust verdict.

People suppose that acting unjustly is entirely up to them, and conclude that acting justly must be just as easy. It is not. To sleep with a neighbor's wife, or strike a neighbor, or pass money from your hand — that is easy and up to you. But to do these things from a certain inner disposition is neither easy nor wholly up to you. In the same way, people think there is nothing clever in knowing what is just and unjust, since it is no great feat to grasp what the laws talk about. They forget that these are just acts only by accident: to be truly just, the acts must be done and apportioned in a certain way, and that is a harder task than knowing what is good for health. There it is easy enough to know about honey, wine, hellebore, cautery, and the knife — but knowing how to apply them for health, to whom, and when, is the whole work of being a doctor. The same mistake makes people think the just man is no less able to act unjustly — that he can do every one of these acts just as readily, indeed more readily, than the unjust man: he too can lie with a woman or strike a man, and the brave man can throw away his shield and turn and run any direction he likes. True. But cowardice and injustice are not the mere doing of these things, except by accident; they are the doing of them from a certain inner state — just as practicing medicine and healing are not the mere using of the knife or the drug, but the using of them in a certain way. The principles of justice operate among those who share in what is good in the abstract and who can have too much or too little of it. Some beings can never have too much — the gods, perhaps. For others, the incurably wicked, no amount of these goods does any good at all; everything harms them. For others still they are good up to a point. So justice has its place among human beings.

We have next to speak of equity and the equitable — how equity stands to justice, and the equitable to the just. Looked at closely, they are neither flatly identical nor different in kind. Sometimes we praise the equitable, and the man who embodies it, and we even transfer the word to other things as a term of praise in place of "good," showing that the more equitable a thing is, the better. At other times, following the argument out, we reach a puzzle: if the equitable is something apart from the just and yet praiseworthy, then either the just is not good, or the equitable is not just — since by assumption they differ; or if both are good, they are the same thing. That is a fair statement of the difficulty. But it all reconciles, and there is no real contradiction. The equitable is just; it is better than one kind of just, but it is not better than the just as though it were a different kind of thing. The just and the equitable are the same, and both being good, the equitable is the better of the two.

What creates the difficulty is this: the equitable is just, but not the just that goes by the letter of the law — rather, it is a correction of that. And the reason is that every law is framed in universal terms, while there are some things about which it is not possible to lay down a correct universal rule. So where a universal rule is needed but cannot fit every case, the law takes the general run of cases, fully aware that it does not capture them all. And it is no less right for that, since the fault lies not in the law, nor in the lawmaker, but in the nature of the case — for that is just how the material of conduct is. So when the law states a general rule, and a case turns up that the rule does not fit, then it is right, where the lawmaker has fallen short and erred by speaking without qualification, to correct the gap — to rule as the lawmaker himself would rule if he were present, and as he would have written into the law had he foreseen the case. This is why the equitable is just, and better than one kind of just — not better than the just in the abstract, but better than the error that comes of speaking in unqualified terms. The very nature of the equitable is this: a correction of law where law falls short by reason of its generality. It is also why not everything can be settled by law: there are matters about which no law can possibly be laid down, so that we need a special ruling for the particular case. For the measure of what is indeterminate must itself be indeterminate — like the leaden rule the builders of Lesbos use, which bends to the shape of each stone instead of staying rigid; just so, the special ruling bends to the facts of the case. It is clear, then, what the equitable is: it is the just, and better than one kind of just. And it is clear who the equitable man is — the man inclined to choose and do such things, who does not stand on his rights to a fault but is willing to take less than his share even when the law is on his side. This settled state is equity, a species of justice and not some separate state of character.

The answer to the other question we raised — whether a man can treat himself unjustly — follows from what we have said. One class of just things is what the law commands in accordance with virtue in its fullest sense: the law, for instance, does not bid a man kill himself, and whatever it does not bid, it forbids. So whenever a man does harm in violation of the law, voluntarily — knowing whom he harms and with what — and not in return for a harm done to him, he acts unjustly. The man who kills himself in a rage does this voluntarily, against right reason, which the law does not allow. So he acts unjustly — but toward whom? Toward the city, not toward himself, since he suffers it with his own consent, and no one can be treated unjustly with his own consent. This is why the city punishes him: a certain dishonor attaches to the suicide, as to one who has wronged the city. A man cannot treat himself unjustly in the other sense either — the sense in which a man is unjust who does unjust acts without being thoroughly bad. (These are different: the unjust man is bad in a way, as the coward is, without being charged with badness in the full sense, so he does not act unjustly in that full sense.) For if he could, the same thing would have been taken from and added to the same person at once — which is impossible; the just and the unjust always require more than one person. Besides, an unjust act must be voluntary, deliberately chosen, and unprovoked — for the man who harms in return for harm first suffered is not thought to act unjustly — whereas here the man would be doing and suffering the same thing at the same moment. It would also imply that a man could be treated unjustly with his own consent. And on top of all this, no man can act unjustly without his act falling under some specific wrong: a man cannot seduce his own wife, burgle his own house, or steal his own property. In the end the whole question is answered by what we settled about being treated unjustly with one's own consent.

It is plain, too, that being treated unjustly and treating others unjustly are both bad — the one is having less than the mean, the other having more, like health in medicine and good condition in training. Still, treating others unjustly is the worse of the two, for it involves wickedness and deserves blame — wickedness either complete, or close to it, since not every voluntary wrong amounts to injustice — whereas being treated unjustly involves no wickedness or injustice on the sufferer's part. In itself, then, being treated unjustly is the lesser evil, though by accident it may turn out the greater. Such accidents are beyond the reach of any precise statement: a doctor calls pleurisy a greater bodily evil than a bruise, yet by accident the bruise may prove the greater, if a man takes a fall, is bruised, and so is captured by the enemy and killed. Finally, there can be justice of a sort toward oneself — not in the strict sense, between a man and himself, but by metaphor and likeness, between the parts of his nature; and not justice of every kind, only the kind that holds between master and slave, or between the head of a household and his dependents. For throughout this inquiry we have treated the rational part of the soul as distinct from the irrational. Looking to these parts, people suppose there can be injustice toward oneself, since a man can suffer, in one part, against the impulses of another part that are truly his own — and so they think there is a kind of justice between these parts, as between ruler and ruled. Let this stand as our account of justice and the other moral virtues.

We have already said that one should choose the mean, and avoid both the excess and the deficiency, and that the mean is fixed by the right principle. It is time to spell out what that principle is. In every settled state of character we have described, and in all the others too, there is a kind of target the person who has reason keeps his eye on as he tightens or slackens his effort; and there is a standard that marks off the mean states, which lie between an excess and a deficiency and accord with the right principle. To say this much is true, but it is not yet definite enough. In any field that calls for care and method — anywhere skill or knowledge is brought to bear — it is true to say that we should neither work nor rest too much or too little, but in the right measure, as the right principle directs. Yet a person who had only this would be none the wiser, the way he would be none the wiser if he asked what to apply to his body and were told, "Whatever medicine prescribes, and in the way the doctor directs." So with the states of the soul: it is not enough to say truly that the mean lies where the right principle says it does; we have to lay down what the right principle actually is, and how to define it.

When we sorted the excellences of the soul, we said there are two kinds: those of character and those of the intellect. We have gone through the excellences of character; now we turn to the intellectual ones, after a few words about the soul itself. We said before that the soul has two parts, one that has reason and one that does not. Now we must divide the part that has reason in the same way. Let us suppose it has two parts: one by which we grasp the kind of things whose first causes cannot be otherwise than they are, and one by which we grasp the kind of things that can be otherwise. For when objects differ in kind, the parts of the soul that are naturally suited to each must differ in kind too, since it is by some likeness and kinship to their objects that these parts know them. Call the first part the part that knows, and the second the part that calculates — for to deliberate and to calculate are the same thing, and no one deliberates about what cannot be otherwise. So the calculating part is one part of the soul that has reason. We have to find the best state of each of these two parts, for that best state is the excellence of each — and the excellence of each is relative to the work it has to do.

There are three things in the soul that govern action and truth: perception, intellect, and desire. Perception originates no action; we can see this from the fact that animals have perception but take no part in action. What affirmation and denial are in thought, pursuit and avoidance are in desire. So, since excellence of character is a settled state that issues in choice, and choice is desire that has been deliberated, the reasoning must be true and the desire right if the choice is to be good, and what reason affirms the desire must pursue. This is thinking and truth that bear on action. For the part of the intellect that only contemplates, and is concerned with neither action nor production, doing well or badly is just hitting the truth or missing it — that is the work of any intellectual faculty. But for the part that is both practical and intellectual, doing well is reaching the truth that answers to right desire. Now the origin of action — the thing that sets it going, not the goal it aims at — is choice, and the origin of choice is desire together with reasoning aimed at some end. This is why there is no choice without intellect and thought, and none without a certain moral character, since acting well and its opposite require both thought and character. Thought by itself moves nothing; only thought aimed at some end and bearing on action moves anything. (Thought that governs production is a separate matter, since everyone who makes something makes it for the sake of something further; what is made is not an end in itself but only a means to something else and for someone. What is done, though, is an end in itself, since acting well is itself the end, and that is what desire reaches for.) So choice is either desiring thought or thinking desire, and a being capable of that origin is a human being. Nothing already done and past can be chosen; no one chooses to have sacked Troy. For no one deliberates about the past, only about what is still to come and can be otherwise, whereas what has happened cannot be made not to have happened. Agathon was right: "This alone is denied even to a god — to make undone whatever has been done." So truth is the work of both intellectual parts of the soul, and the excellence of each is the state in which it best reaches the truth.

Let us start again, then, and speak of these excellences. Suppose there are five states by which the soul reaches truth, in affirming or denying — five and no more: craft, scientific knowledge, practical wisdom, philosophic wisdom, and intuitive understanding. (Judgment by supposition and opinion are left out, since by them we can be wrong.) What scientific knowledge is becomes clear if we are exact about it and not misled by loose resemblances. We all assume that what we know in the strict sense cannot be otherwise than it is; with things that can be otherwise, the moment they pass out of our sight we cannot tell whether they still hold or not. So the object of scientific knowledge holds of necessity, and is therefore eternal, since whatever exists of strict necessity is eternal — and eternal things have no beginning and no end. Again, all scientific knowledge can be taught, and what it covers can be learned. And all teaching starts from what is already known, as we also say in the Analytics — sometimes by working out the consequences (deduction), sometimes by gathering the universal from instances (induction). Induction is the source of first universals, while deduction reasons from them. So there are starting points that deduction reasons from but cannot itself prove, and these are taken in by induction. Scientific knowledge, then, is a settled capacity to demonstrate — with all the further marks we set out in the Analytics. A person knows in the strict sense when he is confident in a certain way and the starting points are clear to him. If they are not clearer to him than his conclusion, his knowledge will be only incidental. Let that stand as our account of scientific knowledge.

What can be otherwise than it is comes in two kinds: things to be made, and things to be done. Making and doing are different (we have shown this elsewhere), so the reasoned state apt for doing is distinct from the reasoned state apt for making, and neither falls under the other — doing is not making, and making is not doing. Since building is a craft, and is essentially a reasoned state apt for making, and since there is no craft that is not such a state and no such state that is not a craft, craft and the reasoned state apt for making true things are the same. Every craft is concerned with bringing something into being — with the know-how of making some thing that may or may not come to be, and whose origin lies in the maker and not in the thing made. Craft has nothing to do with things that are or come to be by necessity, or with things that arise by nature, since these have their origin in themselves. And since making and doing are different, craft belongs to making, not to doing. In a way craft and luck deal with the same matters, as Agathon says: "Craft loves luck, and luck loves craft." So craft, as we said, is a settled state, conjoined with true reason, that is apt for making; and its opposite, lack of craft, is a settled state conjoined with false reasoning — both bearing on what can be otherwise.

We can get at the nature of practical wisdom by looking at the kind of person we call practically wise. It seems to belong to the practically wise person to be able to deliberate well about what is good and useful for himself — not in some narrow line, like what makes for health or strength, but about what makes for living well as a whole. A sign of this is that we call people wise about some particular thing when they calculate well toward some worthwhile end in a matter where there is no fixed rule. So, broadly, the person who is good at deliberating will be practically wise. But no one deliberates about what cannot be otherwise, or about things that are not within the reach of his own action. So, since scientific knowledge requires strict demonstration, and the matters practical wisdom deals with admit of being otherwise — for all matters of deliberation can be otherwise, and there is no deliberating about what holds by necessity — practical wisdom is neither scientific knowledge nor craft. Not knowledge, because what is done can be otherwise; not craft, because doing and making differ in kind. What is left is that it is a true and reasoned state apt for action, concerned with what is good and bad for a human being. For the end of making is always something beyond the making, but the end of doing cannot be, since acting well is itself the end. This is why we count Pericles and people like him as practically wise: they can see what is good for themselves and for people in general — and that, we think, is the mark of someone able to run a household or a city. It is also why we give self-mastery the name we do in Greek, a word that means "what preserves practical wisdom" — for what self-mastery preserves is exactly this kind of judgment about one's own true good. Pleasure and pain do not destroy or distort every judgment — not the judgment that the angles of a triangle add up to two right angles — but only judgments about action. For the starting points of action are the ends they are done for, and to a person corrupted by pleasure or pain the starting point at once goes dark: he no longer sees that he should choose and do everything for the sake of that end and because of it. Vice destroys the starting point. So practical wisdom must be a true and reasoned state apt for action, having to do with what is good for a human being.

There is more. A craft can be done better or worse, but practical wisdom admits of no such degrees. And in a craft, a person who goes wrong on purpose is the better craftsman; in practical wisdom, as in the excellences of character, he is the worse. So plainly practical wisdom is an excellence of a certain kind and not a craft. Of the two parts of the soul that have reason, it must be the excellence of the part that forms opinion — the part we earlier called calculating or deliberative — since opinion, like practical wisdom, deals with what can be otherwise. And it is not merely a reasoned state, as is shown by this: a reasoned state of that kind can be forgotten, while practical wisdom cannot.

Scientific knowledge is a grasp of universals and of what holds by necessity, and every chain of demonstration, and so all such knowledge, rests on first principles. The faculty that takes in the first principles of what falls under scientific knowledge cannot itself be scientific knowledge, or craft, or practical wisdom. Not scientific knowledge, since the object of knowledge is reached by demonstration; not either of the other two, since they deal only with what can be otherwise. Nor can it be philosophic wisdom, since the wise person must in some matters rely on demonstration.
