So if the states by which we reach truth and are never deceived, in dealing with what is necessary or even with what can be otherwise, are scientific knowledge, practical wisdom, philosophic wisdom, and intuitive understanding — and the first three cannot grasp first principles — then it must be intuitive understanding that does so.

We use the word for philosophic wisdom mainly in two ways. First, in the crafts, we ascribe it to those who have carried their craft to the highest finish — we call Phidias a wise sculptor, Polyclitus a wise statue-maker, meaning by "wisdom" here nothing but excellence in a craft. Second, we think some people wise in general, not in any one line or about any one thing, the way Homer says in the Margites: "The gods had made him neither a digger nor a plowman, nor wise in anything else." So it is clear that philosophic wisdom must be the most exact form of knowledge. The wise person must not only know what follows from first principles but also have the truth about the first principles themselves. So philosophic wisdom is intuitive understanding combined with scientific knowledge — knowledge, with its head on, of the highest things. I say the highest things, because it would be absurd to suppose that statecraft, or practical wisdom, is the best kind of knowledge, unless a human being were the best thing in the universe. Now "healthy" and "good" mean different things for people and for fish, but "white" and "straight" are always the same; so everyone would grant that wisdom is always the same, while what counts as practical wisdom shifts. For we give the name to whatever looks well after its own interest — which is why people even call some animals practically wise, the ones that plainly have a power of foresight about their own survival. And it is plain that philosophic wisdom and statecraft cannot be the same thing. If we called the faculty that looks after our own interest "wisdom," there would be many wisdoms, one for each kind of creature, since there is no single faculty that looks after the good of all animals at once — any more than there is one art of medicine for every living thing. It is no answer to say that human beings are superior to the other animals, since there are many things more divine in their nature than a human being — the heavenly bodies that make up the universe, most obviously. So philosophic wisdom is intuitive understanding and scientific knowledge together, trained on the highest things by nature. This is why people call Anaxagoras, Thales, and men of that stamp wise, but not practically wise: they can see them ignorant of their own good, and they say that what these men know is extraordinary, marvelous, hard, and even superhuman, but useless — because it is not the human good they are after.

Practical wisdom, by contrast, is concerned with human affairs and with what can be deliberated about. We say the chief work of the practically wise person is to deliberate well, and no one deliberates about what cannot be otherwise, or about anything that has no end, and an end that is some good attainable by action. The person who is good at deliberation without qualification is the one who, by calculation, can hit on the best of the goods attainable by action for a human being. Nor does practical wisdom deal with universals alone; it must also recognize particulars, since it is concerned with action, and action is about particulars. This is why some people who lack the general knowledge are more effective in action than others who have it — above all those who go by experience. If a man knows that light meats are easy to digest and healthy, but not which meats are light, he will not produce health; the man who knows that chicken is light and healthy is far likelier to. Since practical wisdom is concerned with action, it should have both kinds of knowledge — or, if only one, the knowledge of particulars rather than of universals. Still, here too there will be a governing kind and a subordinate kind. Statecraft and practical wisdom are the same state of mind, but they are not the same in their point of view. Of practical wisdom exercised over a city, the master form is legislation; the subordinate form, dealing with particulars, keeps the common name "statecraft," and its business is action and deliberation, since a decree is something to be acted on, the last step in this kind of deliberation. That is why people say only these men are really governing, since they alone act — standing to the lawgivers as workmen do to a master builder. But practical wisdom is thought to be most properly the kind concerned with oneself, the individual, and this kind takes over the common name; the others are called household management, legislation, and civic government, the last divided into the deliberative and the judicial. Now knowing one's own good is one kind of knowledge, but it varies widely; and people commonly think the man who knows and minds his own affairs is practically wise, while those who busy themselves with the public are meddlers. Euripides puts the sentiment in a character's mouth: "How am I wise, who might have lived at ease, an idle number in the ranks, sharing the common lot? For Zeus hates the busy and the over-clever." People generally seek their own good and think that is their proper business — and from this opinion comes the idea that such men are the practically wise. Yet it may well be that a person's own good cannot be secured apart from his household and his city. And how a man should manage even his own affairs is sometimes far from clear, and has to be worked out.

What I have said is borne out by the fact that the young can become geometers and mathematicians, wise in such matters, but are not thought capable of practical wisdom. The reason is that practical wisdom is concerned with particulars, which become known through experience, and a young person has no experience, since experience takes time to acquire. One might also ask why a boy can become a mathematician but not a natural scientist or a philosopher. Is it not because mathematics works by abstraction, while the starting points of those other fields come from experience? The young can repeat the words of natural science but do not really grasp them, whereas the objects of mathematics are clear and plain. Again, in matters of action, error can lie in the general rule, in the course of deliberation, or in the particular fact — for instance, the general rule "all heavy water is bad," or the particular fact "this water is heavy." And it is clear that practical wisdom is not scientific knowledge, since it bears on the last particular, as we said, which is the object of action. It stands opposite to intuitive understanding: understanding takes in the principles that no reasoning can prove, while practical wisdom is concerned with the last particular, which no scientific knowledge can grasp but only perception — not perception by one of the five senses, but the same kind by which we perceive that the last figure in geometry is the triangle, where too we have to stop. But that is perception more than practical wisdom, or perception of a different sort.

Inquiring and deliberating are different, though deliberating is a kind of inquiring. We should work out what good deliberation is — whether a kind of scientific knowledge, or opinion, or a knack for a lucky guess, or something else again. It is not scientific knowledge, since people do not inquire about what they already know, and good deliberation is a kind of deliberation, and the person deliberating is inquiring and calculating. Nor is it a lucky guess, since a lucky guess comes without reasoning and in a flash, while people deliberate a long time — as the saying goes, you should carry out quickly what you have resolved on, but deliberate slowly. Quick wit is yet another faculty, a species of lucky guess, and good deliberation is not opinion of any kind. Since the person who deliberates badly goes wrong and the one who deliberates well does it rightly, good deliberation is plainly a kind of rightness — but not rightness of knowledge, nor of opinion. Knowledge cannot be called right, since it cannot be wrong; and rightness of opinion is just truth, and what opinion is about is already settled and definite. Yet good deliberation is not without reason. So it must be rightness of thinking, since thinking is not yet an assertion. Opinion is not an inquiry but an assertion already made, while the person deliberating, whether well or badly, is still inquiring and calculating. Good deliberation is a kind of rightness in deliberation, so we have to start from what deliberation is and what it is about. Now "rightness" has several senses, and we plainly do not mean every kind. The weak-willed person, or the bad one, will by calculation reach what he set out to reach, so in a sense he has deliberated rightly — but what he gets is a great evil. To have deliberated well, though, seems to be a good thing, since the rightness of deliberation that counts as good deliberation is the kind that hits on something good. But even this can be reached by false reasoning — you can land on the right result through the wrong means, by a faulty middle term — so this is still not good deliberation, getting what you should but not by the proper route. Again, one man reaches a result after long deliberation, another quickly, and that quickness is not yet good deliberation either; good deliberation is rightness measured against what is beneficial, reaching the right end, in the right way, at the right time. Finally, one can deliberate well in general or toward a particular end. Good deliberation in general is the kind that goes right toward the end without qualification; good deliberation in a particular case is the kind that goes right toward a particular end. So, since deliberating well is the mark of the practically wise, good deliberation is rightness about what serves the end that practical wisdom truly grasps.

There is also the faculty of understanding, and its absence, by which we call people understanding or not. Understanding is not the same as scientific knowledge or opinion in general — if it were, everyone would have it — nor is it any one special science, like medicine, which is about health, or geometry, which is about magnitudes. It is not about what always exists and cannot change, nor about whatever happens to come to be, but about the things a person might be in doubt about and deliberate over. So it deals with the same matters as practical wisdom; yet the two are not the same. Practical wisdom issues commands — its end is what one should do or not do — while understanding only judges. (When we put "good" in front of it in Greek, "good understanding" means exactly the same as plain "understanding.") Understanding is neither the having of practical wisdom nor the getting of it. Just as we use the word for "grasping" when a learner puts his knowledge to use, so understanding is using the opinion-forming part of the soul to judge the matters practical wisdom deals with, when someone else states them — and judging not just any way, but judging well. The faculty we call good judgment, by which we call people sympathetic and fair-minded, is the correct discernment of the decent person. A sign of this is that we say the decent person above all is one who makes allowances, and making allowances in some cases is decent. Indeed the word for forgiveness is sympathetic judgment that discerns rightly what is fair — and by "rightly" I mean the judgment of a truthful person.

All these states naturally point in one direction, just as ordinary speech leads us to expect. We speak of good judgment, understanding, practical wisdom, and intuitive understanding, and we credit the same people with good judgment and intuitive understanding whom we call practically wise and understanding. For all these faculties are concerned with the last things — with particulars. A person is understanding, and has good judgment, in virtue of being able to decide the matters that fall to the practically wise, since fairness is common to all good people in their dealings with others. And all matters of action belong to the particulars, the last things; the practically wise person has to recognize them, and understanding and good judgment are likewise about actions, which are particulars. Intuitive understanding takes in the last things at both ends, since both the first terms and the last are grasped by understanding and not by reasoning. In demonstration, understanding takes in the unchanging first terms; in action, it takes in the last term, the one that can be otherwise — the minor premise. These are the starting points of the end aimed at, for the universal is built up out of particulars. To grasp these we must have perception, and that perception is intuitive understanding. This is why these states are thought to be natural gifts. No one is held to be wise by nature, but people are held to have good judgment, understanding, and intuitive understanding by nature — a sign of which is that we think they come with certain times of life, and that a given age brings intuitive understanding and good judgment, as if nature were the cause. So intuitive understanding is both a beginning and an end, since demonstrations start from these and are about these. We should therefore pay as much attention to the undemonstrated sayings and opinions of experienced and older people, and of the practically wise, as to demonstrations — for experience has given them an eye to see rightly.

We have now said what practical wisdom and philosophic wisdom are, what each is concerned with, and that each is the excellence of a different part of the soul. But someone might ask what use they are. Philosophic wisdom, he could say, studies none of the things that make a human being happy, since it produces nothing. Practical wisdom does have that to recommend it — but why do we need it? Its province is what is just and fine and good for a human being, and these are the things the good person does as a matter of course; we are no more apt to do them for knowing them, since the excellences of character are settled states — just as we are no healthier or fitter for knowing what medicine and training say, since these terms describe what shows health, not what produces it. And if we say it is by becoming good, not by knowing what is good, that one becomes practically wise, then practical wisdom will be no use even to those who are already good, and none to those who are not — since it makes no difference whether they have it themselves or follow others who have it. We might be content to do here as we do with health: we want to be healthy, but we do not therefore set about learning medicine. On top of this, it would be strange if practical wisdom, lower in rank than philosophic wisdom, were to govern it — and govern it it does, since whatever produces a result rules and directs in its own field. These are the questions we must now take up; so far we have only raised them.

First, then, we say that both of these are choiceworthy in themselves, simply because each is the excellence of a part of the soul — even if neither produced any result at all. Next, they do in fact produce a result: philosophic wisdom produces happiness, not the way medicine produces health, but the way health itself does. For wisdom is a part of excellence as a whole, and by being possessed and exercised it makes a person happy. Further, a human being's work is fully done in virtue of practical wisdom together with excellence of character: excellence of character makes the aim right, and practical wisdom makes the means to it right. (The fourth part of the soul, the merely nutritive one, has no such excellence, since nothing is in its power to do or leave undone.) As for our not being more apt to do fine and just things by having practical wisdom, we must go a little further back and take this as our starting point. We say that people can do things that are in themselves just without being just — when they do what the law requires unwillingly, or out of ignorance, or for some other motive, and not for the sake of the things themselves — and yet they do what they ought, all that the good person should. So it seems that to be a good person one must do each act in a certain frame of mind: from choice, and for the sake of the acts themselves. Now it is excellence of character that makes the choice right, but carrying out whatever that choice naturally requires belongs not to excellence but to another faculty. We must pause and speak about this more plainly.

There is a faculty people call cleverness, of such a nature that it can do whatever serves a given aim and hit it. If the aim is fine, the cleverness is praiseworthy; if it is base, the same faculty is mere unscrupulousness. This is why we call both the practically wise and the unscrupulous clever. Practical wisdom is not the same as this faculty, but it does not exist without it. This eye of the soul does not reach its proper state without excellence of character, as we have said and as is plain. For the reasonings that govern action have a starting point of the form "since the end, the chief good, is such-and-such" — fill in the blank with whatever you like, since we only want to show the shape — and what should fill that blank is seen only by the good person, because vice distorts the moral vision and deceives us about the starting points of action. So it is clear that a person cannot be practically wise without being good.

We must look again, then, at excellence of character, since here too there is a close parallel: just as cleverness stands to practical wisdom, so natural virtue stands to full, mature virtue — a relation of resemblance, not identity. People think each of the moral dispositions belongs to us somehow from birth: we are inclined toward justice, self-mastery, and courage straight from the start. Yet we look for goodness in the full sense as something beyond these, and we expect these dispositions to belong to us in a different way. Children and even animals have these natural states, but without intelligence they are plainly harmful. We can see this much by experience: a powerful body deprived of sight stumbles badly when it moves, just because it cannot see, and it is the same here. But once intelligence is added, it transforms the way a person acts; and the disposition, which only resembled virtue before, will then be virtue in the full sense. So just as the opinion-forming part of the soul has two forms, cleverness and practical wisdom, the part concerned with character has two, natural virtue and full virtue — and the second of these cannot be formed without practical wisdom. This is why some say that all the virtues are just forms of practical wisdom. Socrates was partly right and partly wrong: wrong to think the virtues simply were practical wisdom, but right that they do not exist without it. A sign of this is that everyone now, in defining virtue, after naming the state and what it is about, adds "in accordance with the right principle" — and the right principle is the one set by practical wisdom. So everyone seems to sense that the state in accordance with practical wisdom is virtue. But we must change their formula slightly: virtue is the state that not merely accords with the right principle but actually involves it — and the right principle in such matters is practical wisdom. Socrates thought the virtues were forms of reasoning, since he took them all to be knowledge; we say they involve reason. From all this it is clear that one cannot be good in the strict sense without practical wisdom, nor practically wise without goodness of character.

This also answers the argument that the virtues can be had separately, on the grounds that one and the same person is not by nature equally disposed to all of them at once, so that he will have acquired one before another. With the natural virtues this is possible; but with the virtues that make a person good without qualification it is not, since they all come together with the single faculty of practical wisdom. It is plain, too, that even if practical wisdom were not concerned with action, we would still need it, because it is the excellence of a part of the soul — and that no choice can be right without practical wisdom and goodness of character, since the one supplies the right end and the other makes us do what leads to it. And practical wisdom is not the master of philosophic wisdom, the higher part of the soul — any more than medicine is the master of health. Medicine does not use health but looks to how it may come about; it gives orders for the sake of health, not to health. To say otherwise would be like saying that statecraft governs the gods because it gives orders about everything in the city.

Let us start again from a fresh point. There are three states of character to avoid: vice, lack of self-control, and brutishness. The opposites of the first two are clear enough — virtue answers to vice, self-control to its lack. As the opposite of brutishness it makes sense to set down a virtue beyond the human, a heroic and godlike excellence. So Homer has Priam say of Hector that he was so outstanding "he seemed not the son of a mortal man, but of a god." And if, as people say, men become gods through some surpassing height of excellence, then the state opposed to the brutish would plainly be of that order. For just as a beast has neither virtue nor vice, neither does a god; a god's condition is something more precious than virtue, and the brute's is something different in kind from vice.

Now a godlike man is rare — the Spartans, when they admire someone past all measure, call him seîos anēr, "a divine man" — and the brutish man is rare too. You find brutishness mostly among barbarians, though some cases come from disease or mutilation; and we also fling the word at men whose vice runs past every ordinary bound. We'll come back to that condition later. Vice we have already treated. For now the task is lack of self-control, along with its near relations softness and self-indulgence, set against self-control and endurance on the other side. We should not take any of these to be the very same states as virtue and vice, nor yet as wholly different in kind.

We'll proceed as before: lay out the common opinions, work through the puzzles they raise, and then, if we can, leave standing the most credible of the views people hold — or at least the greater and weightier part of them. For we'll have done enough if the difficulties are untangled and the respected opinions survive. Roughly, the common opinions come to this. Self-control and endurance are counted good and praiseworthy; lack of self-control and softness, low and blameworthy. The self-controlled man is taken to be the man who stands by what he has reasoned out, the man without self-control the one who abandons it. The man without self-control acts at the urging of his feelings, knowing it is wrong, while the self-controlled man, knowing his cravings are wrong, refuses on the strength of reason to follow them. The temperate man is thought to have both self-control and endurance — though some say anyone with these is temperate and others deny it. Some people run together the man with no self-control at all and the merely weak-willed man; others keep them apart. The man of practical wisdom, it is sometimes said, cannot be weak-willed, and sometimes that even shrewd, capable men can be. And finally, people are called weak-willed not just flatly but with a qualification — weak-willed about anger, say, or honor, or money. Those are about the common opinions.

Here is the first puzzle. When a man fails of self-control, what is the state of the knowledge he violates? Some say he cannot fail while genuinely knowing, in the strict sense, what is right. It seemed absurd to Socrates that knowledge could be present in a man and yet something else master it and drag it around like a slave. Socrates denied weakness of will outright: no one, he held, acts against what he judges best — failures come only from ignorance of what is best. But this collides head-on with the plain facts, and we have to ask, if the failure does involve ignorance, what kind of ignorance it is. For it is obvious the man does not think his act right before the feeling takes hold of him.

Some agree with Socrates in part. They grant that nothing can overpower knowledge, but deny that no one acts against his own conviction of what is better; so they say it is not knowledge the weak man yields against, but only opinion. But if it is mere opinion and not knowledge — if the conviction opposing the craving is faint, a matter of half-belief, as in someone who is genuinely unsure — then we might excuse him for not holding out against strong desire. Yet real wickedness is not to be excused, nor is anything that deserves blame. Is it practical wisdom, then, that does the opposing, since that is the firmest principle of all? Absurd: the same man would then be both practically wise and weak-willed, and no one would say it belongs to practical wisdom to do, of one's own accord, the gravely wrong thing. Besides, we have shown that the practically wise man is marked precisely by acting, not merely knowing, since he is at home in the particulars and possesses the other virtues as well.

More puzzles. If the self-controlled man must have strong and bad cravings, then he is not the same as the temperate man, who has no such cravings — yet the self-controlled man must, for if his desires were good, the state restraining him from acting on them would be bad, and self-control would not always be good; and if they were weak and harmless, there would be nothing impressive in resisting them. Again, if self-control made a man stand by every opinion whatsoever, it could be a bad thing — by a false opinion, say; and if weakness made him drop every opinion, there would be cases where weakness is good. Think of Neoptolemus in Sophocles' Philoctetes: he is praised for not standing by the lie Odysseus talked him into, because it pained him to be false. Sophistical reasoning makes trouble too: a man can find himself fettered by an argument he cannot refute yet cannot accept, since the conclusion offends his judgment. And on the "mere opinion" view, foolishness joined to weakness might come out as a kind of goodness: a man's settled view is that the good thing is bad and must not be done, and his weakness then makes him act against his view — so he ends up doing the good after all. These tangles tell us the account needs fixing.

So let us examine, first, whether the weak-willed man acts knowing what is right; and if he does, in what sense. The real starting point is this. To say it is true opinion, not knowledge, that he violates changes nothing, since some people hold opinions with no doubt at all and take themselves to know — Heraclitus believed his own views as firmly as anyone believes what he strictly knows. Here is the better answer: "knowing" has two senses. We say a man knows both when he has the knowledge but isn't using it and when he is actively using it. There is all the difference between doing wrong while holding knowledge you aren't drawing on, and doing wrong while actually exercising it; the second would be strange, the first is no anomaly at all.

Push further. Action involves two kinds of premises, a universal and a particular, and a man may well have both yet act against his knowledge by using the universal without the particular — and it is the particulars that action is about. The universal itself can split in two: "dry food is good for every man" and "I am a man," with the further premise "this food here is dry" — and whether this food is dry he may either not know or not be attending to. Across these senses the difference is enormous, so that knowing in one sense and acting wrongly is nothing to wonder at, while in another sense it would be astonishing. And men can hold knowledge in yet another way. We see people who have knowledge and don't use it — who in a sense have it and in a sense don't — when asleep, or mad, or drunk. The man in the grip of passion is in just that condition. Anger, lust, and the like visibly alter even the body, and in some they bring on a kind of madness; so the weak-willed man is in a state like the drunk's or the sleeper's. That he recites the right principle proves nothing about his using it: men under passion can reel off proofs and quote Empedocles' verses the way beginners string words together before they grasp the sense, or the way an actor speaks his lines. They are saying the moral truth, not exercising it.

Look at the mechanics of action. Every action follows from a kind of syllogism, with a universal premise and a particular one that perception takes in; and where the two combine, the mind must affirm the conclusion, and in matters of doing, the man must act on it at once. Suppose the universal is "everything sweet should be tasted" and the particular "this is sweet": a man who can act, and isn't stopped, must straightaway taste. Now suppose there is in him one universal forbidding him to taste, and at the same time the universal "everything sweet is pleasant" with its particular "this is sweet" — and that this last is the live one, while desire is present. The one principle tells him to keep away; desire drives him on, since desire can set each of the body's parts in motion. So he fails, and in a sense under the direction of reason and opinion — opinion not in itself opposed to right reason, but only by accident, since it is the desire, not the opinion, that runs counter to right reason. This is also why beasts are never called weak-willed: they have no grasp of universals, only of particular images and impressions.

How the ignorance lifts, and the weak man recovers his knowledge, is the same story as for the drunk man and the sleeper, and belongs to the natural scientists to explain. But since the particular premise is an opinion about something perceived, and it is this that governs action — the man under passion either does not have this premise, or has it in a way that amounts not to knowing but to merely mouthing it, like the drunk reciting Empedocles. And because the particular term is not universal, and is not thought to yield knowledge the way the universal does, the result Socrates was after does, in a way, come out true: it is not knowledge in the strict and proper sense that gets dragged about by the passion — that knowledge stays untouched — but the knowledge that comes through perception. So much for whether the weak man acts with knowledge, and how.

Next: is there such a thing as being weak-willed without qualification, or is everyone weak-willed only about some particular thing — and if there is the unqualified kind, what is it about? Plainly self-control and its lack, like endurance and softness, are about pleasures and pains. Now things that give pleasure are of two sorts: those that are necessary, and those choiceworthy in themselves but admitting of excess. The necessary ones are the bodily pleasures — food, drink, sex, the rest of touch and taste. The others are not necessary but are worth choosing for their own sake: victory, honor, wealth, and such fine or pleasant things. When men go too far after these, against the right reason within them, we do not call them weak-willed flatly, but with the addition — weak about money, honor, anger — because they are really a different sort of character, called weak-willed only by a likeness, the way we tack "Olympic victor" onto a man's name and his account shifts only slightly. And a sign of the real difference: weakness about the bodily pleasures is blamed not as mere error but as a vice, while these other cases are not.

It is the man whose object is bodily pleasure — who chases the pleasures and shrinks from the pains of touch and taste, not by deliberate choice but against his own choice and judgment — who is called weak-willed without any qualifier, just as "soft" is used only of these and not of the others. We put this man, the man with no self-control at all, the self-controlled man, and the temperate man together in one class, because they share the same field of pleasures and pains; they differ in how they stand to it — two of them act on deliberate choice, two against it. So we should count the man more wholly given over to his passions who chases excessive pleasures and flees moderate pains while feeling little or no real desire, than the man driven by overwhelming desire — for what would the first do with the added goad of youth and the violent pain of going without?

Some desires and pleasures are noble and good in kind — recall that pleasant things divide into the naturally choiceworthy, the naturally to-be-avoided, and the indifferent in between, like money and gain and honor. For all of these, and for the indifferent ones, men are blamed not for feeling or wanting or liking them, but for overdoing it in any way — for being more eager than they should about honor, or even about their own children or parents. These are good objects, and men are praised for caring about them; but the caring can run to excess, as when someone, like Niobe, would even fight the gods, or doted on his father like Satyrus, nicknamed "father-lover" for the foolishness of it. There is no real depravity here, since each object is by nature worth choosing; only the excess is wrong and blamable. And there is no weakness of will here in the strict sense, since that is not merely something to avoid but something blameworthy. Because the condition resembles weakness of will, the word gets used with the object attached, the way we call a man a bad doctor or a bad actor whom we would never call simply bad. So we reserve the bare terms — self-control and its lack — for the field that the temperate man and the man with no self-control share, and use them of anger and the rest only by resemblance.

Some things are naturally pleasant — some to everyone, some to particular kinds of creature or person — while others become pleasant only through injury, or habit, or a corrupted nature; and there are states of character to match each. Take the brutish: the woman they say would rip open pregnant women and devour the unborn; the savage tribes near the Black Sea, some eating raw flesh, some eating human flesh, some lending their children for one another's feasts; or the stories told of Phalaris. These are brutish states. Others come from disease or madness — the man who sacrificed and ate his mother, the slave who devoured his fellow's liver. Still others come from disease or from habit: pulling out one's hair, gnawing one's nails, eating coal or dirt. Where nature is truly the cause, no one would call a man weak-willed, any more than for the diseased states; he is simply outside that frame. To have any of these urges is something apart from vice, as brutishness is apart from it; mastering them is not self-control in the proper sense, nor being mastered by them weakness of will, but only by resemblance. So there is brutish and there is morbid weakness of will, but only the human kind earns the name without qualification.

Now to the claim that weakness about anger is less disgraceful than weakness about appetite. Anger, it seems, does listen to reason after a fashion, but mishears it — like a hasty servant who runs off before he has heard the whole order and gets it wrong, or a dog that barks at any noise before checking whether it's friend or foe. Reason or some impression signals an insult or a slight, and anger, reasoning in its rough way that it must fight such a thing, flares up at once. Appetite is different: let reason or perception merely say "this is sweet," and appetite rushes off to enjoy it. So anger follows reason in a way, and appetite not at all; the appetite-driven man is the more disgraceful, since the angry man yields, after a fashion, to reason, while the other yields to nothing but his craving. And we more readily forgive a man for following natural desires, the ones common to all — and anger and irritability are more natural than appetites for what is excessive and unnecessary. (Recall the man who beat his father and pleaded, "My father beat his, and his beat his, and this boy here will beat me when he grows up — it runs in the family"; and the old man being dragged along who told his son to stop at the door, since that was as far as he had once dragged his own father.) Anger, besides, is not sly — it is out in the open — whereas appetite is the schemer; they call Aphrodite "weaver of deceits" and her girdle the thing that "cheats even the shrewd mind." So weakness about appetite, being the more devious and unjust, is the more disgraceful, and is weakness of will in the full sense, and a kind of vice; whereas the angry man acts in pain, and no one is insolent in pain.

So weakness about appetite is more disgraceful than weakness about anger, and the field of self-control and its lack is bodily appetites and pleasures — but among these we must mark the differences already drawn: some proper to mankind and natural in kind and degree, some brutish, some born of injury and disease. Only the first are the field of temperance and the utter lack of self-control, which is why we never ascribe either to beasts, except by metaphor when one whole species outdoes another in insolence or destructiveness or greed; beasts have no deliberate choice, no power to reason things out, and stand apart from us as madmen do. Brutishness is not as low in the scale as vice, but it is more to be feared — not because the highest principle has been corrupted, as in a man, but because the creature has no such principle at all. It is like asking which is worse, a thing without life or a thing with it: the harm done by what has no source of action in it is always the smaller, and intellect is exactly such a source. A bad man can do ten thousand times the harm of a bad beast.

Turn now to the pleasures and pains of touch and taste, and to standing firm against them or giving way. A man may yield where most people would hold out, or hold out where most would yield: in pleasures, that makes him weak-willed or self-controlled; in pains, soft or enduring. Most men fall somewhere between, leaning a little to the worse side. The man who chases excessive pleasures by deliberate choice, for their own sake and nothing further, is the man with no self-control at all — incapable of regret, and so incurable, since a man who feels no remorse cannot be cured. (The man who takes too little pleasure is his opposite; the temperate man holds the mean.) Of those who go wrong without choosing it, one is led on by pleasure, the other gives way because he flees the pain of denying his craving — and these are not the same. Everyone would call a man worse for doing something base with little or no desire than under a violent one, just as we judge a man worse for striking in cold blood than in anger: "What would he do if passion had hold of him?" Of these two, the one is really softness, the other weakness of will proper.

Self-control is opposed to weakness of will, endurance to softness; for enduring is holding out under strain, self-control is outright mastery, and holding out is to mastering as not being beaten is to winning — so self-control is the more worth having. The man who caves where ordinary people easily stand firm is soft and self-indulgent — the sort who lets his cloak trail in the mud rather than take the trouble to lift it, who plays the invalid without thinking himself wretched though he acts the part. If a man gives way to violent, extreme pleasures or pains, that is no wonder, and we forgive him if he put up what fight he could — like Philoctetes bitten by the snake in Theodectes' play, or men straining to hold in laughter who burst out helplessly. The wonder is when a man caves to what ordinary people can resist, unless his failure comes from his birth or a disease (some Scythian royal lines are soft by constitution, and there is the natural difference between the sexes). The man enslaved to amusement, by the way, is usually thought to lack self-control, but he is really soft — amusement is relaxation, a kind of rest, and he overdoes the resting.

Weakness of will comes in two forms, the impulsive and the weak. In the weak kind a man makes resolutions and fails to keep them under the pull of feeling; in the impulsive kind he is swept off by feeling because he never formed a resolution at all — whereas some men, like those who tickle themselves first to be ready for it, see the temptation coming, brace themselves and their reason, and do not give way. The impulsive form runs strongest in the quick-tempered and the moody, the one because his passions are too fast, the other because they are too violent, to wait on reason; both lurch after whatever notion strikes them. And the man with no self-control at all, as we said, does not feel regret, since he stands by his choice; the weak-willed man is all regret. So the earlier puzzle resolves: the first is incurable, the second curable. Settled vice is like a chronic disease, dropsy or consumption; weakness of will is like an acute attack. Vice is continuous, and its victim does not notice it; weakness is not, and he does. As Demodocus said of the Milesians, "They are not fools, but they do the kind of things fools do" — so the weak-willed are not unjust, but they do unjust things.

To sum the comparison: the weak-willed man chases bodily pleasure to excess against right reason, but holds no settled conviction that he should; the man with no self-control does hold such a conviction, since chasing pleasure is, to his mind, exactly his line. So the first is easy to talk round, the second is not. For virtue and vice respectively save and destroy the governing principle, and in action the end we aim at is the principle, as the axioms are in mathematics; in neither field does argument teach us the starting point — it is excellence, native or trained, that holds the right view of it. The man who holds it rightly is the temperate man; the man with no self-control is his contrary. There is also the man swept off against right reason by passion — mastered so far that he cannot act on reason, but not so far as to be convinced he ought to pursue such pleasures without limit. That is the weak-willed man, better than the man with no self-control and not simply bad, because in him the best part, the principle, is preserved. Set against him stands the man who keeps to his resolutions and is not shaken from them by passion. From all this it is plain that self-control is a good state and its lack a bad one.

Is a man self-controlled for standing by any conclusion and choice whatever, or only by the right one? And weak-willed for abandoning any conclusion and choice, or only a true one? Surely it is true conclusions and right choice the two are essentially defined by, and any old conclusion only incidentally. If a man pursues one thing for the sake of another, it is the second he pursues in his own right, the first only along the way; so it is the man who holds to, or lets go of, the true opinion who is self-controlled or weak-willed in the full sense. There are also people with a knack for clinging to their own opinions — the stubborn, hard to budge, not easily turned. They look a bit like the self-controlled, the way a spendthrift looks like the generous man or the reckless like the brave, but they differ on many counts. The self-controlled man does not shift for passion or craving, yet will gladly be persuaded when there is reason to; the stubborn man will not be moved by reason, though plenty of his kind are in fact led by their pleasures. The opinionated, the ignorant, and the boorish are all stubborn — the opinionated from pleasure and pain, since they relish a kind of victory in never being talked round and resent having their verdicts overturned. So they actually resemble the weak-willed more than the self-controlled. And some men depart from their resolutions not from weakness but for a noble reason, like Neoptolemus, who broke his resolution to lie because being truthful was, in his eyes, the finer thing. Not everyone who acts for pleasure's sake lacks self-control or is base or weak-willed — only the man who acts for a base pleasure.

Since there is also a man who takes less pleasure than he ought in bodily things and fails to stand by his reasoning, the self-controlled man is the mean between him and the weak-willed man: the weak man falls away through a little too much, this man through a little too little, while the self-controlled man stands firm and shifts for nothing but his own conclusions. Self-control being good, both contrary states are bad; but because the deficient one is rarely seen, self-control gets treated as the opposite of weakness alone, just as temperance is treated as the opposite of the utter lack of self-control alone. Many terms are used by likeness, and so people speak of the temperate man's "self-control": the two share the trait of never acting against right reason for bodily pleasure, but the self-controlled man has bad desires and the temperate man does not, and the temperate man is so made that he feels no pleasure against his reason at all, while the self-controlled man feels it but does not give in. Likewise the weak-willed man and the man with no self-control resemble each other though they are distinct: both pursue bodily pleasures, but the latter thinks it the proper thing to do and the former does not.

The same man cannot be both practically wise and weak-willed, since practical wisdom, as we showed, includes goodness of character, and is not knowledge only but the readiness to act — which the weak-willed man lacks. The merely shrewd man, though, can well be weak-willed; and the reason some are now and then taken for practically wise yet weak-willed is that shrewdness sits very close to practical wisdom in its intellectual side and parts from it only in the choice. The weak-willed man is not like the man who knows and is using his knowledge, but like the man who has it and is overpowered by sleep or wine. He acts of his own will, since in a sense he knows what he is doing and where it leads, but he is not a settled bad man, since his choice is sound — he is, at most, half bad. Nor is he unjust, for he does not act by design: of the two forms, one does not keep to his resolutions and the other, the man of violent passions, never forms any. So he is like a city that passes all the right laws and has excellent statutes but acts on none of them — proving Anaxandrides' gibe, "the city willed it, that cares nothing for laws" — whereas the bad man is like a city that does act on its laws, but its laws are bad.

Both self-control and its lack are conditions beyond the run of men: the one keeps to reason more, the other less, than most people can manage. And of the two forms of weakness, the kind found in men of violent passion is more easily cured than the kind found in men who resolve and break their resolutions; those weak by habit are easier to cure than those weak by nature, since habit is easier to change than nature — and the very closeness of habit to nature is what makes it hard, as Evenus says: "Long practice, friend, in the end becomes a man's own nature." We have now said what self-control is, and weakness of will, and endurance, and softness, and how these states stand to one another.

The next subject is pleasure and pain — and it belongs to the student of human affairs to examine them, since he is the one who fixes the end against which we call each thing good or bad. We cannot pass them by. We said that virtue and vice of character are both bound up with pains and pleasures, and most people hold that happiness must include pleasure — which is why they call the blessed man makarios, from a root meaning to rejoice. There are three views to confront. Some say no pleasure is good, in itself or by result, since good and pleasure are not the same. Others say some pleasures are good but most are bad. A third party grants that every pleasure is good, but denies that pleasure could be the chief good.

The case that pleasure is simply not good runs like this. Every pleasure is a perceived process toward a natural state, and no process is of the same order as the end it aims at, just as building is not of the same order as the finished house. The temperate man, besides, stays clear of pleasures; the practically wise man pursues freedom from pain, not the getting of pleasure; pleasures get in the way of thought, the more so the more intensely they are felt; pleasure answers to no art, though every good is the product of some art; and children and beasts chase pleasures. The case that not all pleasures are good points out that some are shameful and reproached, and some are positively harmful, since some pleasant things bring on disease. And the case that pleasure is at any rate not the chief good says it is no end but a process toward one. That is a fair report of the views in circulation.

But none of these arguments shows that pleasure is not good, or not the chief good, as the following will make plain. First, good is of two kinds, the unqualified and the relative, and so too are the natures and states that embody it — and likewise the movements and processes. Among those reckoned bad, some will be bad without qualification yet not bad relative to a given person, perhaps even worth his choosing; some not even worth choosing for him except at certain times or briefly, though not in themselves. And some are not pleasures at all, only seem so — all those bound up with pain and undertaken as a cure, like the "pleasures" of the sick. Next, since good is either an activity or a state, the processes that restore us to our natural state are pleasant only incidentally, by way of that restoration; the real activity lies in the desires of the part of us that is already sound. For there are pleasures with no admixture of pain or desire at all — the activity of contemplation, for one, where nothing in our nature is lacking to be filled. A sign of this: the same thing is not pleasant while the natural state is being refilled and once it is whole. When we are whole, what pleases us is what is pleasant in itself; while we are being restored, even the contrary things please — sharp and bitter things that no one would call pleasant by nature, so that the pleasures from them are not natural pleasures either.

Next, it does not follow, because (as some argue) the end must be better than the process that produces it, that there is always something better than a given pleasure. For not all pleasures are processes or even come with a process — some are activities, and are themselves ends; they arise not from our coming to be something but from our using what we already are. And the end is not in every case distinct from the process; that holds only for processes that complete a natural state. This is why it is wrong to call pleasure "a perceived process." Better to say "the unimpeded activity of a natural state" — "activity" for "process," and "unimpeded" for "perceived." People take it for a process because they think it good in the fullest sense, confusing activity with process, though the two are distinct. As for the objection that some pleasures are bad because some pleasant things harm the health — that is like saying some healthy things are bad for business. In that sense both are "bad," but not bad without qualification: even hard thinking can damage the health. What harms practical wisdom, or any state, is not the pleasure proper to it but some foreign pleasure; the pleasure of thinking and of learning only makes us think and learn the more.

Next: "no pleasure is the work of any art." What else would you expect? No activity is the work of an art — only the capacity for the activity is — though the perfumer's and the cook's arts are in fact taken to serve pleasure. As for "the temperate man avoids pleasures," "the practically wise man pursues freedom from pain," and "children and beasts pursue pleasures" — one answer covers all three. We have already said in what sense all pleasures are good in themselves and in what sense not all are; it is the latter that beasts and children pursue, the ones tied to desire and pain, the bodily pleasures and their excesses, the very ones the man with no self-control is given over to. And it is freedom from the pain that goes with these that the practically wise man seeks, and these that the temperate man avoids — for plainly the temperate man has pleasures of his own. Further, pain is agreed to be an evil and to be avoided — some of it bad in itself, some as a hindrance — and the contrary of what is to be avoided as evil is good; so pleasure must be a good. Speusippus' attempted answer, that pleasure is the contrary of pain the way the greater part of a quantity is the contrary of the lesser, both being opposed to the equal, does not hold; he cannot mean that pleasure is a species of evil.

And even granting that some pleasures are low, there is no reason a particular pleasure should not be very good, just as a particular kind of knowledge can be very good even though some kinds are low. Indeed it may follow — since every state has its unimpeded activity, and happiness is the unimpeded activity of all of them or of some one — that this activity, when unimpeded, must be worth choosing for its own sake; and pleasure is exactly that. So the chief good could be a pleasure of some kind, even if most pleasures are, let us grant, low in themselves. That is why everyone thinks the happy life pleasant and weaves pleasure into happiness — and reasonably, since no impeded activity is complete, and happiness is something complete. This is why the happy man needs, in addition, the goods of the body, external goods, and good fortune, so that on these counts he is not hampered. Those who say a man is happy on the rack, or fallen into great disasters, so long as he is good, are talking nonsense, whether they mean to or not. And because fortune is needed besides, some take good fortune itself to be happiness — wrongly, for fortune in excess is itself a hindrance, and perhaps no longer deserves the name of good, being good only so far as it serves happiness.

That every creature, beast and man alike, pursues pleasure is some sign that it is in a way the chief good — "there is something in what all men say." But since no single nature or state is, or is thought, best for all, men do not all pursue the same pleasure, though pleasure they all pursue. Perhaps what they pursue is not what they think or would say, but really one and the same thing, since in everything there is something divine. The bodily pleasures, though, have taken the name to themselves, because they are the kind we meet most often and all of us share; and because to many people these are the only ones they know, they suppose these the only ones there are.

It is plain, too, that unless pleasure and its activity are good, it cannot be true that the happy man's life is pleasant: why would he want pleasure, if it is not good, when he could live even with pain? For if pleasure is not good, then pain is neither good nor evil, and there would be no reason to avoid it. And the good man's life is no more pleasant than any other unless his activities are. We must look as well at the bodily pleasures, for the sake of those who say that some pleasures — the good ones — are highly worth choosing, but not the bodily ones, the field of the man with no self-control. If so, why are the contrary pains bad? The contrary of bad is good. Perhaps the necessary bodily pleasures are good in the sense in which what is not bad is good — or good only up to a point. States and movements that admit no excess of the better admit no excess of pleasure either; those that admit excess of the one admit it of the other. The bodily pleasures do admit excess, and it is by pursuing the excess, rather than the necessary measure, that the bad man becomes bad. Food, drink, and sex give pleasure to everyone, but not to everyone in the right way and degree. With pain it is the reverse: he avoids not excessive pain but pain at all — for it is only relative to excessive pleasure that pain at all becomes its contrary.

It is not enough to state the truth; we should show how the false view arises, since that strengthens conviction — when we can give a plausible reason why what is not true strikes people as true, they hold the truth more firmly. So we must say why the bodily pleasures appear more worth choosing than the rest. The first reason is that bodily pleasure drives out pain; men feel pain in excess and so pursue pleasure in excess, generally bodily pleasure, as a remedy. These remedies grow violent — which is the very reason they are pursued, since they make their impression by being set against their opposite. And there are two reasons, already given, why bodily pleasure is thought not good. Some such pleasures belong to a low nature, whether inborn, as in beasts, or acquired by habit, as in bad men; and others are cures of some deficiency, and of course it is better to be in the healthy state to begin with than to have it come on later. (Some pleasures do accompany a nature being brought to completion, and these are good by result.)

Their very violence, again, makes the bodily pleasures sought by men who can relish no others — men who manufacture their own thirsts. When the thirsts are harmless we do not blame it; when harmful, it is base. They have nothing else to take pleasure in, and to many people the neutral state, free of both pleasure and pain, is in itself distasteful, for living is some kind of effort, as the natural scientists testify when they tell us that seeing and hearing are painful, only we have grown used to it. In youth the constant growth produces a state like a mild drunkenness, and youth is pleasant; the melancholic by temperament constantly need a cure, since the body is forever fretting them, and live in chronic violent craving. Pleasure drives out pain — not only the directly contrary pleasure but any strong one — and this is how men come to have no self-control, to be bad. But the pleasures with no admixture of pain admit no excess; these belong to things pleasant by nature and not merely by result. By things pleasant "by result" I mean the curative ones, thought pleasant because the cure is worked by whatever part of us is still sound; by "pleasant by nature" I mean what sets a healthy nature in action.

No single thing is invariably pleasant to us because our nature is not simple but composite, so that we are perishable beings with something in us at war with the rest: when one part acts, that action is against the other part's nature, and only when the two are in balance does what is done feel neither pleasant nor painful. For a being whose nature was simple, one and the same activity would always be the most pleasant. This is why God enjoys a single, simple pleasure forever — for there is an activity not only of motion but of rest, and pleasure lies more in stillness than in movement. "Change is the sweetest of all things," the poet says, and it is true only because of some flaw in us: the man easily changed is a bad man, so the nature that craves change is bad, being neither simple nor good. We have now had our say about self-control and its opposite, and about pleasure and pain — what each is, and how the one set is good and the other bad. It remains to speak of friendship.

After the virtues, friendship is the natural next subject, for friendship is either a virtue itself or something bound up with virtue, and beyond that it is one of the things life most needs. No one would choose to live without friends even if he had every other good thing in the world. In fact the rich, and people who hold power and office, are thought to need friends most of all. What good is such prosperity if you are stripped of the chance to do good to others, which is done above all, and most admirably, for friends? And how could prosperity be kept safe without friends? The greater it is, the more precarious. In poverty too, and in every other kind of trouble, people think their friends are the one refuge they have.

Friendship helps the young to keep from going wrong, and the old to be cared for and to make up for what their failing strength leaves undone, and those in their prime to act nobly — "two going together," as Homer says, for two are better able to think and to act than one. It seems, moreover, to be planted in us by nature: a parent feels it toward its offspring and the offspring toward the parent, and not only in human beings but in birds and most animals; members of the same race feel it toward one another, and human beings toward other human beings especially, which is why we praise those who love their fellow men. You can see in traveling how every man is kin and friend to every other.

Friendship also seems to be what holds communities together, and lawgivers seem to care about it even more than about justice; for concord is something close to friendship, and concord is what they aim at most, while what they most try to drive out is faction, which is its enemy. Where people are friends, there is no need of justice besides, but where they are merely just, they still need friendship; and the truest form of justice is thought to be a kind of friendly thing. Friendship is not only necessary but admirable. We praise those who love their friends, and having many friends is counted to a man's credit. Some even hold that to be a good man and to be a friend come to the same thing.

Yet there is no shortage of disputed points about it. Some lay it down that friendship is a kind of likeness, and that like is friend to like — hence the sayings "like to like" and "birds of a feather." Others say the opposite: that two of a trade never agree. Some push the question higher and answer it in terms of nature. Euripides says the parched earth loves the rain, and the heavy sky, swollen with rain, loves to fall upon the earth. Heraclitus holds that what opposes helps, that the finest harmony comes out of differences, and that everything comes to be through strife. Empedocles, against them, says that like reaches for like. These questions about nature we may set aside; they belong to another inquiry. We will look at what is properly human — what concerns character and feeling.

Here, for instance, is one such question: does friendship arise among all people without distinction, or is it impossible for bad men to be friends? And another: is there only one kind of friendship, or several? People who think there is only one, on the ground that friendship admits of degrees, are arguing from too little; for things that differ in kind can also admit of degrees. (We have discussed that elsewhere.)

These points will come clear once we have settled what it is that is the proper object of friendship. For it is thought that not just anything is loved, but only what is lovable — which is to say, what is good, or pleasant, or useful. And the useful, it would seem, is whatever brings about some good or some pleasure; so that the good and the pleasant are the lovable things as ends in themselves. There is a question here: do men feel friendship for what is good without qualification, or for what is good to themselves? The two sometimes come apart — and the same goes for the pleasant. It seems that each man feels it toward what is good to himself; that without qualification the real good is lovable, and to each man what is good to him. So it comes to this: each man feels friendship not for what is good, but for what strikes him as good to himself. This makes no real difference, though, since what is truly lovable will also strike him that way.

There are, then, three grounds on which men feel friendship. But we do not use the word for fondness toward lifeless things, since there is no return of the feeling, and no wishing of good to the object. It would be absurd to say a man wishes his wine well; if anything, he wishes it kept sound — for his own use. Toward a friend, they say, one should wish good for the friend's own sake. When someone wishes good to another this way and it is not returned, we call him merely well-disposed; for friendship, as they define it, is mutual goodwill. But should we not add that the goodwill must be known to both? Many people feel goodwill toward those they have never met but believe to be decent or useful — and the other might feel just the same toward them. They are plainly well-disposed to one another, then; but how can we call them friends when neither knows how the other feels? To be friends, then, they must have goodwill toward each other, must wish each other good on one of the grounds named, and must each know the other feels it.

Since the grounds of friendship differ in kind, so do the feelings and the friendships. There are three kinds of friendship, equal in number to the things that can be loved; for in each there can be mutual goodwill that both are aware of. Now those who are friends wish each other good on the ground of their friendship. So those whose ground is usefulness do not love each other for themselves, but only for the good that comes to them from each other. The same holds for those whose ground is pleasure: they love witty people not for their character but because they find them pleasant. Friends of utility, then, love what is good to themselves; friends of pleasure, what is pleasant to themselves — not loving the friend for being who he is, but for being useful or pleasant.

These friendships, then, are matters of incidental result, since the man is not loved for being who he is but for supplying some advantage or some pleasure. Friendships of this kind are easily dissolved when the parties stop being what they were; for once the others are no longer pleasant or useful, the feeling stops. And usefulness is not a lasting thing but shifts from moment to moment; so when the ground of the friendship is gone, the friendship dissolves with it, since it existed only for the sake of that ground. This kind of friendship is found mostly among the old (who at that age pursue not what is pleasant but what is profitable), and among such of the young and the prime-aged as chase advantage. People like this do not even live much in each other's company; sometimes they are not even pleasant to each other, and they have no wish for such company unless there is profit in it, since they please each other only so far as there is hope of gain. With these we usually rank the friendship of host and guest.

The friendship of the young is thought to rest on pleasure, since they live by feeling and chase above all what is pleasant to them and present to the moment; and as their age changes, so do their pleasures. This is why they form and break friendships fast — the friendship shifts as the pleasant object shifts, and that kind of pleasure shifts quickly. The young are also much given to love, which is largely a matter of feeling and rests on pleasure; so they fall into friendships and drop them quickly, changing often within a single day. But they do want to spend their days and live in close company with their friends, for that is how they get what they want from the friendship.

The complete friendship is the one between people who are good and alike in their goodness. These wish each other good in the same way, just insofar as they are good — and good is what they are in themselves. Those who wish good to their friends for the friends' own sake are friends most of all, for they feel this on their friends' own account and not as some incidental result. So this friendship lasts as long as they are good, and goodness is a lasting thing. Each is good without qualification and good for his friend as well, since good men are both good in themselves and useful to one another. They are pleasant to each other too, for good men are pleasant both in themselves and to one another; each takes pleasure in the actions that suit his own nature, and good men's actions are of one kind, or at least alike.

A friendship like this, then, is naturally lasting, since it brings together everything friends should have. Every friendship is for the sake of good or pleasure — either without qualification or relative to the one who feels it — and rests on some likeness; and in this kind all these belong to the friends themselves, for here they are alike, and the rest follows. In it there is the good without qualification and the pleasant without qualification, and since these are most of all the objects of friendship, the feeling and the state of friendship are at their strongest and best in people of this sort. Such friendships are likely to be rare, since such men are rare. Besides, they take time and familiarity; for as the proverb says, men cannot know each other until they have eaten the proverbial salt together, nor can they admit one another to intimacy, much less be friends, until each has shown himself to the other to be worthy of friendship. People who strike up friendly exchanges quickly may wish to be friends, but they are not friends unless they are also lovable and know it of each other. A wish for friendship comes quickly; friendship itself does not.

This friendship, then, is complete both in time and in every other respect, and each gets from the other the same or nearly the same — which is how it should be between friends. The friendship based on pleasure is a copy of this one, since good men are pleasant to each other; and so is the friendship based on usefulness, since good men are useful to each other. Among such people friendships last longest when the same thing comes to each from the other — pleasure, say — and not merely the same thing but from the same source, as with two witty people, and not as with a lover and the one he loves. These two do not draw their pleasure from the same thing: the lover from looking at the beloved, the beloved from the attentions paid him. So when the bloom of youth fades the friendship sometimes ends too, since the lover no longer enjoys the sight and the beloved no longer gets the attentions. But many do stay friends, if from long company they have come to love each other's character, being alike in temper.

Where lovers exchange not pleasure but profit, the friendship is both weaker and shorter-lived. People who are friends for advantage break apart when the advantage ends; they were never really friends of each other but of the gain. So it turns out that bad men can be friends to each other for pleasure or profit, and good men to bad, and a neutral character to anyone at all; but for each other's own sake, plainly, only the good can be friends — for bad men take no pleasure even in each other except where there is some advantage in it. The friendship of the good is also the only kind proof against slander, since it is not easy to believe a third party against someone you have long tried and tested. Between good men there is mutual trust, the conviction that a friend would never wrong you, and all the other things expected in a friendship worthy of the name. In the other kinds there is nothing to stop such suspicions.

I call these friendships, because people commonly give the name of friends to those tied by profit (as political language allows, since alliances between states are thought to be made for advantage) and to those tied by pleasure (as children are). So we may perhaps be allowed to call such people friends too, and to say there are several kinds of friendship: first and foremost that of the good, insofar as they are good, and the rest by resemblance to it. People tied otherwise are friends in the way that something good and some likeness arises to them (remember that the pleasant is good to those who love it). But these secondary friendships do not often combine; the same people do not become friends both by advantage and by pleasure, for these incidental things rarely come together.

Just as men are called good in respect of an inner state in one case and of activity in another, so it is with friendship. Those who live together take pleasure in each other and do each other good; but those who are asleep or far apart are not exercising the friendship, though they are in the kind of state from which they would act in a friendly way if they did act. Distance has no direct effect on the friendship itself; it only blocks its exercise. Still, if the absence runs long, it is thought to make even the friendship forgotten — hence the saying that lack of contact has dissolved many a friendship. Neither the old nor the sour-tempered seem suited to friendship, for there is little pleasure in them, and no one can spend his days with what is painful, or even not pleasant, since to avoid pain and reach for pleasure is one of the most obvious facts of our nature.

People who think well of each other but are not in the habit of each other's company are more like men of goodwill than friends; for nothing is so characteristic of friends as living together. Those in need want help, and even the fortunate want company — they are the last people made for a solitary life. But you cannot pass your time together unless you are pleasant to each other and take pleasure in the same things, which is thought to belong to the friendship of companions.

The friendship between the good, then, is friendship in the fullest sense, as has been said often. For what is good or pleasant without qualification is thought to be lovable and worth choosing, and to each man whatever is such to him; and the good man is lovable to the good man for both reasons at once. (Loving is like a feeling, friendship like a settled state; for the feeling can have even lifeless things for its object, but returning friendship involves choice, which comes from a settled state. And men wish good to those they love for the friends' own sake, not as a mere feeling but as a matter of character.) In loving his friend the good man loves his own good, since the good man, once in this relation, becomes a good to the one he is joined with. Each loves his own good and pays his friend back in equal measure, in wishing well and in pleasure — for equality is said to be a bond of friendship. All this belongs most of all to the friendship between good men.

Among the sour or the elderly, friendship is less apt to spring up, since they are harder to deal with and take less pleasure in society and company, which are thought to be especially friendly and to breed friendship. That is why the young make friends quickly and the old do not (no one becomes a friend to those he takes no pleasure in), and likewise the sour-tempered. Such people may have goodwill toward one another — they wish each other well and help each other in need — but they are not quite friends, since they neither spend their time together nor take pleasure in each other, which are thought the marks of friendship most of all.

It is not possible to be a friend to many people in the complete way, any more than to be in love with many at once. That is a kind of excess, and its nature is to have a single object; it is not easy for one man to be very pleased with many people at the same time, nor perhaps to find many who are really good. And one needs experience and close familiarity, which is very hard. But it is quite possible to please many on the score of advantage and pleasure, since there are many such people and the services take little time. Of the two lesser kinds, the one that most resembles the complete friendship is the one based on pleasure, where the same thing comes from both and they take pleasure in each other or in the same things — as in the friendships of the young, since these have the most generosity of spirit in them. The friendship for advantage is the bond of tradesmen.

The very fortunate have no need of useful friends, but they do need pleasant ones, since they want people to share their lives with; what is painful they can bear for a short time, but no one could endure it without break — not even the supreme Good itself, if it were painful to him in particular. So they look for pleasant friends; though perhaps they ought to require that these be good as well, and good to themselves in particular, since then they would have all that friendship needs. Men in power are often seen to keep several distinct friends — some useful to them, some pleasant — but rarely both in one person; for they do not actually look for friends who are at once pleasant and good, nor useful for honorable ends. To get what is pleasant they look for witty men, and again for men clever at carrying out any task put to them; and these two skills are seldom found in the same man. We have already said that the good man is at once pleasant and useful. But such a man will not be a friend to someone above him in rank unless he is also above him in goodness; otherwise, being outdone in rank, he cannot make things even by a proportionate return of friendship. And men who unite high station with goodness are not common.

Now all the kinds of friendship mentioned so far rest on equality, since either the same thing comes to both and they wish the same things to each other, or else they trade one thing for another — pleasure, say, for profit. (We have said that this last kind is weaker and shorter-lived, and that it is their likeness and unlikeness to the same thing — the friendship based on virtue — that makes them seem now to be friendships and now not. They look like friendships through their likeness to that one, the one having the pleasant and the other the useful, both of which belong to it as well; and they look unlike it through their unlikeness, which is that the true kind is above slander and lasting, while these change quickly and differ in many other ways.)

But there is another form of friendship, the kind in which one party stands above the other: father and son, older and younger, husband and wife, ruler and ruled. These differ among themselves; the friendship of parents toward children is not the same as that of ruler toward ruled, nor is the father's toward the son the same as the son's toward the father, nor the husband's toward the wife the same as hers toward him. For the function, and so the excellence, of each of these is different, and so are the grounds on which they feel friendship; their feelings and their friendships, then, are distinct. The same things do not come to each from the other, nor should they be looked for; but when children render to their parents what is owed to those who gave them life, and parents to their children what is owed to their offspring, the friendship between them will be lasting and fair.

In all friendships between unequals the affection should be proportionate: the better, or the more useful, and so on, should be loved more than he loves in return; for when the affection matches the merit, a kind of equality results, and equality is thought to belong to friendship. (Equality in friendship is not the same as in justice, though. In justice the proportionate equal comes first and the numerically equal second; in friendship it is the reverse.)
