That equality is required is shown plainly when a wide gap opens — in goodness, or in vice, or in wealth, or anything else; for then people are no longer friends, and do not even think they have a right to be. The clearest case is the gods, who are most superior in every good thing. It is plain too with kings, for those far beneath them do not feel entitled to be their friends, and very insignificant men do not feel entitled to be friends with men of great excellence or wisdom.

There is no fixing the exact point up to which such friends can remain friends; many points of agreement can fall away and the friendship still hold, but when one party is set very far off — as a god from men — it can no longer continue. This has raised a puzzle: do friends really wish their friends the very greatest goods, such as to become gods? For if the wish came true, they would no longer have them for friends — and so would lose a good, since friends are a good. If, then, it was rightly said that a friend wishes good to his friend for the friend's own sake, the friend must be understood to stay the kind of being he now is; so one wishes him the greatest goods of which, as a human being, he is capable. And perhaps not even all of these, since each man wishes good most of all for himself.

Most people, out of love of honor, seem to want to be loved rather than to love, which is why they are fond of flatterers — a flatterer being an inferior friend, or one who pretends to be a friend and to love more than he is loved; for to be loved is thought to be close to being honored, which is what most people are after. Yet men seem to choose honor not for its own sake but incidentally. The common run delight to be honored by those in power because of the hope it raises — they think they will get from them whatever they happen to want — so they enjoy the honor as a token of benefits to come. Those who crave honor from good men, men who really know their worth, want to confirm their own opinion of themselves; they take pleasure in the conviction that they are good, resting on the verdict of those who say so. But men delight in being loved for its own sake, and so it may be judged higher than being honored, and friendship choiceworthy in itself.

Friendship seems to consist in loving rather than in being loved, as is shown by the joy mothers take in loving. Some give their children to others to raise and, knowing them, go on loving them without ever seeking it returned, if both cannot be had; they seem content to see their children doing well and to keep on loving them, even though the children, out of ignorance, never give them any of a child's regard or love in return. Since friendship lies more in loving than in being loved, and those who love their friends are the ones we praise, loving seems to be the excellence of friends. So in those in whom it is present in proper measure, the friends are steady and the friendship lasting. This is the way unequals can best be friends, since loving in proportion can make them equal.

Equality and likeness are a bond of friendship, especially likeness in goodness; for good men, being steady in themselves, are steady toward others too, and neither ask degrading favors nor do them — rather, they hold them off. It belongs to the good neither to go wrong themselves nor to let their friends go wrong. The bad have no steadiness in them; they do not even stay like themselves for long, and become friends only for a short while, taking delight in each other's badness. Friends for profit or pleasure hold together somewhat longer — as long as they can give each other pleasure or gain. The friendship of profit seems to form most of all out of opposites: the poor man becomes the friend of the rich, the ignorant of the well-informed, each wanting what he lacks and giving something else in exchange. Here too we might rank the lover and the beloved, the beautiful and the plain. This is why lovers sometimes look ridiculous, demanding to be loved as intensely as they love; if they were equally lovable they might have the right, but when they have nothing of the kind it is absurd. Perhaps, too, the opposite does not reach for its opposite for its own sake, but only incidentally; what it really wants is the mean, since it is good for the dry not to become wet but to reach the mean, and so with the hot, and the rest. But let us set these questions aside; they are somewhat off our path.

As was said at the start, friendship and justice seem to have the same field and to hold between the same people; for in every community there is thought to be some justice, and some friendship too. People call those friends whom they share a voyage or a campaign with, and likewise those joined with them in other ways. The friendship reaches just as far as the community does, and so does the justice. This bears out the proverb that friends' goods are shared, since friendship rests on community. Brothers and close companions share everything, while others share their property only in part — some more, some less, since friendships too differ in degree. The claims of justice differ as well: they are not the same between parents and children as between brothers, nor between companions as between mere fellow-citizens, and so on through all the kinds of friendship.

The kinds of injustice differ accordingly, and wrongs grow worse when done to friends. It is worse to rob a companion than a fellow-citizen, worse to refuse help to a brother than to a stranger, worse to strike your father than anyone else. Justice naturally increases with the closeness of the friendship, since both hold between the same people and reach equally far. All communities are like parts of the political community, since in them men band together for some advantage and to procure some of what life needs; and the political community itself is thought to have come together, and to last, for the sake of advantage. This is what lawgivers aim at, calling just what is in the common interest. The other communities aim at advantage in particular areas: a ship's crew at what comes from the voyage, undertaken to make money or the like; comrades in arms at what comes from war, whether wealth or victory or political standing; members of a tribe or deme in the same way.

Some communities seem to form for the sake of pleasure — religious societies, say, or dining clubs, which exist for sacrifice or company. But all of these fall under the political community, since its aim is not the advantage of the moment but advantage for the whole of life; with this in view, members hold sacrifices and the gatherings that go with them, to render honor to the gods and to win themselves a rest from toil along with pleasure. For it seems that the old sacrifices and assemblies came after the harvest as a kind of offering of first fruits, since that was the season of most leisure. So all the kinds of community are parts of the political one, and the corresponding kinds of friendship will follow upon these communities.

There are three kinds of political constitution, and an equal number of deviations from them — corruptions, so to speak. The constitutions are kingship, aristocracy, and a third based on a property qualification, which it seems fitting to call timocracy, though most people simply call it a polity. The best of these is kingship, the worst timocracy. The deviation from kingship is tyranny: both are rule by one, but they differ enormously, since the tyrant looks to his own advantage and the king to his subjects'. For a man is no true king unless he is self-sufficient and superior in all good things; and such a man, needing nothing, will not look to his own advantage but to his subjects', while one who is not in this position is a king chosen by lot for the occasion. Tyranny is the very opposite of this kingship, for the tyrant pursues his own good. Here the inferiority is clearest, and what is worst is the opposite of what is best. The slide to tyranny comes from kingship, tyranny being the corruption of monarchy — the bad king turns tyrant.

From aristocracy the slide is to oligarchy, through the vice of the rulers, who distribute the city's goods against right proportion, giving themselves all the good things or the greater share, and keeping the offices always in the same hands, making wealth their idol; so a few rule, and bad men instead of the best. From timocracy the slide is to democracy, since they border on each other: timocracy too is meant to be rule by the many, and all in the same property class are equal. Democracy is the least bad of the deviations, since it departs least from the form of its constitution. These, then, are roughly the changes the constitutions undergo, these being the smallest in degree and the easiest to make.

You can find likenesses and, as it were, models of these even in the household. The bond between a father and his sons has the shape of kingship, since the father cares for his children; this is why Homer calls Zeus father, kingship being meant to be a fatherly rule. Among the Persians, though, the father's rule is tyrannical, for they treat their sons as slaves. (The rule of master over slaves is tyranny in kind, since here it is the master's interest that is regarded.) This last seems as it should be, but the Persian custom mistaken, since different subjects call for different rule. The bond of husband and wife has the shape of aristocracy, for the husband rules by merit and in matters proper to a husband, leaving to the wife what befits her. When the husband lords it over everything, he turns the relation into oligarchy, doing so against right proportion and not as the better of the two. Sometimes the wives rule, being heiresses; here rule goes not by merit but by wealth and power, as in oligarchies. Timocracy finds its likeness in the bond of brothers, who are equal except as age sets them apart — so if they are very different in age, the friendship is no longer a brotherly one. Democracy shows up most in households without a head, where all are equal, or where the proper head is weak and everyone does as he pleases.

For each form of constitution there is plainly a friendship, reaching just as far as the justice does. The friendship of a king toward his subjects is one of superiority in benefit, since he does his subjects good — assuming he is a good king and looks after their welfare, as a shepherd tends his flock; hence Homer calls Agamemnon shepherd of the people. The fatherly friendship is of this same kind, only that it surpasses the king's in the greatness of the benefits, since the father is the cause of his children's being — thought the greatest benefit — and of their nurture and upbringing. (These are credited to ancestors generally too.) By nature a father rules his sons, ancestors their descendants, a king his subjects. These friendships hold between superior and inferior, which is why parents are not only loved but honored. And the justice between these parties is not equal but proportionate, just as the friendship is.

Between husband and wife there is the same friendship as in an aristocracy, for the relation goes by merit: the better person has the greater good, and each has what befits — and so too the justice between them. The brotherly friendship is like that of companions, since brothers are equal and close in age, and such people generally share like feelings and like characters. Like this too is the friendship of a timocracy, where the citizens are meant to be equal and fair, so that rule passes from hand to hand and is shared on equal terms — and the friendship matches. In the deviant forms, just as the justice is small, so is the friendship, and least of all in the most perverted; in tyranny there is little or no friendship. For wherever ruler and ruled have nothing in common, there is no friendship, because there is no justice; the case is rather like that of a craftsman and his tool, or soul and body, or master and slave. All these are benefited by those who use them, but toward lifeless things there is neither friendship nor justice — nor toward a horse or an ox, nor toward a slave as a slave, since they have nothing in common. A slave as such is a living tool, a tool a lifeless slave.

As a slave, then, there is no friendship toward him; only as a man. For there is thought to be some justice between any man and any other who can share in law and be party to an agreement, and so some friendship too, insofar as he is a man. So in tyrannies friendship and justice reach only a little way, but in democracies they reach furthest, since those who are equal have much in common.

Now all friendship rests on community, as has been said; but one might set apart from the rest the friendship of kindred and that of companions, while the friendships of fellow-citizens, fellow-tribesmen, shipmates, and the like seem more peculiarly to rest on community, since they plainly exist by an agreement, stated or implied. Among these we may rank the friendship of host and guest. The friendship of kindred is itself of many kinds, and all of them seem to depend on the parental: parents love their children as a part of themselves, and children love their parents as deriving from them. But parents know that their children are theirs more surely than children know they come from their parents, and the source is more closely bound to what it produces than the offspring to what made it. For whatever comes from oneself is one's own — a tooth, a hair, anything at all, to the one it belongs to — while the source is not its own, or less so. Then there is the length of time: parents love their children from the moment they exist, but children love their parents only after time has passed and they have gained understanding or perception. These same points show why mothers love more than fathers.

Parents, then, love their children as themselves, since what comes from them becomes a kind of second self by being separated off; and children love their parents as having sprung from them. Brothers love one another from having sprung from the same source, for their sameness with that source makes them the same with each other — hence the phrases "same blood," "same root," and the like. In a sense they are the same thing even in distinct individuals. Being raised together and being near in age are a great help to friendship, for a man likes one of his own age, and people used to each other become companions; this is why the friendship of brothers resembles that of companions. Cousins and other relatives get their bond from these — from their common origin — and the bond is stronger or weaker according to how close they stand to the common ancestor.

The friendship of children toward parents, and of men toward the gods, is friendship toward something good and above us; for these have done the greatest benefits, being the cause of our existence and nurture, and of our upbringing once we were born. And a friendship of this kind has more of the pleasant and the useful in it than friendship between people unrelated by blood, in proportion as their life is more shared. In the brotherly friendship there is everything there is in that of companions, and more in the case of the good, and of those who are alike — more in proportion as they are more closely tied, having from birth a feeling for one another to start with, and being more alike in character, since they spring from the same stock, have grown up together, and have been brought up alike; and they have had the fullest chance, over time, to test one another, and so can rely on the proof most securely.

Between husband and wife there seems to be a friendship by nature; for man is by nature more given to pairing than to political life, inasmuch as the household comes before the city in time and is more necessary, and procreation is something he shares with the other animals. The other animals come together only this far, but human beings live together not only to have children but for life in general; for from the start the tasks are divided, some belonging to the man, others to the woman, so that they supply each other's needs, each putting what is its own into the common stock. For these reasons this friendship is thought to combine the useful and the pleasant; and it will rest on virtue too, if they are good, since each has a virtue and they can delight in this in each other. Children too are thought to be a bond, which is why the childless part more easily; for children are a good shared by both, and what is shared holds people together. How a man should live with his wife — or, in general, one friend with another — seems to be just the question of how it is just for them to live; for plainly the justice between friend and friend is not the same as between strangers, or companions, or chance fellow-travelers.

There are, then, as was said at the start of this book, three kinds of friendship, and in each there can be friends on equal terms and friends in a relation of superior and inferior; people alike in goodness become friends, and the better with the worse, and likewise the pleasant; and again people become friends for advantage, either balancing their usefulness exactly or differing in it. Those who are equal should be made equal in the friendship and the rest by their very equality, and those who are unequal by rendering friendship in proportion to the other's superiority.

Complaint and blame arise either only, or chiefly, in the friendship of utility. For those who are friends through goodness are eager to do each other good, since that is what goodness and friendship produce; and when men vie with each other in this, there can be no complaint or quarrel, since no one is annoyed at someone who feels friendship for him and does him good — if he has any refinement, he repays him with kind acts. And even if one outdoes the other, he will not blame his friend, since he is getting what he aimed at, for what each aims at is the good. Nor can there be much quarreling between friends for pleasure's sake; for if they enjoy living together, both get what they want, and a man would look ridiculous to blame another for not pleasing him, when it is in his power to stop spending time with him.

But the friendship of utility is full of complaint. Since the parties use each other for advantage, they always want more, and think they are getting less than their due, and complain that they are not getting as much as they deserve; while those who do the good can never come up to what the receivers want. It seems that, just as the just is of two kinds — the unwritten and the written — so the friendship of utility is of two kinds, the moral and the legal. The richest source of complaints is when people contract and discharge obligations in different keys. The legal kind is on stated terms — either purely commercial, hand to hand, or more gentlemanly as to time, but still by agreement a fixed return for a return. In the legal kind the obligation is clear and beyond dispute; the friendly element is the delay in calling it in. (For this reason, in some places no suit is allowed for such debts, on the view that those who have dealt on trust must abide the outcome.)

What may be called the moral kind is not on stated terms; a man gives as to a friend, and so on. But he still expects to get an equivalent back, or even more, as though he had not given but lent; and he too will complain, because he does not get the obligation discharged in the same key in which he contracted it. This happens because all men, or most, wish for what is honorable but, when it comes to the test, choose what is profitable; and doing good disinterestedly is honorable, while receiving benefit is profitable. In such cases one should, if able, return something proportionate to the good received, and do it willingly; for one ought not to make a man a disinterested friend against his will. One should act, that is, as having made a mistake at the outset in taking a kindness from one from whom one should not have taken it — he being no friend, and not acting disinterestedly — and should discharge oneself as though one had received a kindness on stated terms. A man would agree, if he could, to repay it, and if he could not, even the doer would not expect it; so if he can, he ought to repay. But one ought at the start to find out from whom one is receiving the kindness, and on what understanding, so that one can accept it on those terms or not.

A disputable question is whether one should measure a kindness by the good done to the receiver, and make that the standard of repayment, or by the kind intention of the doer. Those who have received kindnesses often plead, to play them down, that they got from their benefactors things that were small for them to give, or things they could have got from others; while the doers insist they gave the best they had, what could not be got elsewhere, and in time of danger or other straits. May we not say that, since utility is the ground of the friendship, the advantage to the receiver must be the standard? For he is the one who asked the kindness, and the other helps him in his need on the understanding that he will get an equivalent; so the help is exactly proportionate to the advantage the receiver gained, and he should repay as much as he gained, or even more, that being more honorable. In friendships based on goodness this question is never raised; here the intention of the doer seems the proper standard, since virtue and character depend above all on intention.

Quarrels also arise in friendships between unequals, because each thinks himself entitled to the greater share — and when this happens, the friendship breaks up. The better man thinks the greater share belongs to him by right, since more is always awarded to the good man; and likewise the more useful one. "A useless man," they say, "should not share equally; it becomes a tax, not a friendship, unless the fruits of the friendship are reaped in proportion to the work done." Their idea is that, as in a money partnership those who contribute more take more, so it should be in friendship. The needy man and the less good make the opposite claim: it is the very business of a good friend, they say, to help those in need — else what use is a good or powerful friend, if one is to reap no advantage from him?

Each seems to make a right claim, and each is entitled to get more out of the connection than the other — only not more of the same thing. The superior man should get more honor, the needy man more profit; for honor is the reward of goodness and of doing good, while profit is the relief of need. This is plainly the principle in political communities: a man who contributes no good to the common stock gets no honor, since the public's property goes to the man who does the public good, and honor is the public's property. One cannot both make money out of the public and receive honor from it as well, for no one will take the smaller share in everything. So to the man who loses out in money they award honor, and money to the man who can be paid by gifts; for, as has been said, observing due proportion equalizes and preserves the friendship.

The same rules, then, should govern dealings between unequal friends: to the man who does another good in money or in goodness, that other should repay honor, returning what he can; for friendship asks what is possible, not what is strictly owed. Strict repayment is not possible in every case, as in the honors paid to gods and to parents — no one could ever make the due return — and a man is thought good if he pays respect according to his means. For this reason it would seem never to be allowable for a son to disown his father, though a father may disown a son. The debtor is bound to pay, and a son can never, by anything he does, fully repay the benefits first conferred on him, so he is always in debt; but the one to whom something is owed may release his debtor, and so the father may release the son. At the same time, it must perhaps be granted that no father would ever cut himself off from a son utterly, except in a case of extreme depravity; for, quite apart from the natural friendship, it is human not to push away the help a son might give. But for the son, if depraved, helping his father is a thing to be shunned, or at least one he will not be eager to do; most men are willing enough to receive a kindness but reluctant to do one, as unprofitable. Let this be enough on these matters.

segments.text: In every friendship between unequal partners, it is proportion that keeps things even and holds the bond together, as we have already said. In a civic friendship, for instance, the shoemaker is paid for his shoes at a certain rate, and so is the weaver, and everyone else; here money has been supplied as a common measure, and everything is referred to it and measured by it. But in the friendship of lovers the complaint sometimes comes from the lover that for all his devotion his love is not returned — though he may have nothing in him worth loving; and just as often it comes from the one who is loved, that the suitor who once promised the world now delivers nothing. These quarrels happen because the lover's friendship rests on pleasure and the beloved's on advantage, and the quality each wants is not there in the other. Since these were the grounds of the friendship, the friendship dissolves once the grounds give out: the two never loved each other but only loved qualities in each other, and those qualities do not last, so neither does the bond. Friendship grounded in character, by contrast, exists for its own sake and is not after anything, and so it lasts — as we have already said.

Quarrels also break out when the partners get a different return than the one they wanted, because getting something other than what you were after feels like getting nothing at all. There is the well-known story of a man who promised a musician more and more in proportion to how well he played; but when the musician came the next morning to claim what he was owed, the man said he had already paid pleasure for pleasure. If that had been the deal both intended, fine. But if one wanted entertainment and the other wanted money, and one got his object while the other did not, the exchange is not square — because each fixes his mind on what he happens to want, and is willing to pay for that specific thing.

So who should set the rate — the one who gives first, or the one who receives? At first glance the one who gives first seems to leave it up to the other. This, they say, is exactly what Protagoras did: when he had taught a man something, he would have the learner judge for himself what the knowledge was worth, and then he took that much. In such cases some people follow the rule, "a friend should be content with the agreed reward."

People are rightly blamed, though, who take the money up front and then do nothing they said they would, having promised far past their power. The Sophists are perhaps forced into this, since no one would pay a cent for what they know once they had it; but if they have already taken the fee for a job and not done it, the blame is fair.

Where no terms are fixed in advance for the mutual services, those who give the first service freely will not raise the question — as we said before — because it belongs to friendship grounded in goodness to take its measure from the other's intention, and that intention is the mark of a true friend and of goodness itself.

The same rule seems to hold for the relationship between teachers and students of philosophy: here the value of what is given cannot be measured in money, and no equivalent price can be set on it, so perhaps it is enough to repay what one can — as with the gods or with one's parents.

But where the first gift was made openly for some return, the best course is for the repayment to be one both sides agree is proportionate; and where that cannot be reached, then for the receiver to set the value is not only necessary but fair. For when the giver gets back what matches the benefit he conferred — or what he would have paid for the pleasure he got — then he has had his worth from the other. We see this is the rule in buying and selling, too; and in some places the law allows no suit on voluntary agreements, on the principle that once a man has trusted another he must be content to settle the debt in the same spirit he made it. The thinking is that the trusted party should fix the value rather than the trusting one. For people who own a thing and people who want it do not value it the same: what is mine, and what I am giving up, always looks to me worth a great deal. Still, since the return is set by the receiver's estimate, he should perhaps measure what he received not by what he values it at now that he has it, but by what he valued it at before he got it.

Other questions arise as well — for instance: Does a father have an unlimited claim on your obedience and service, or should you obey your doctor when you are sick? And in electing a general, should fighting ability be the only thing considered?
Likewise: should you do a favor for a friend, or for a good man? Should you repay a benefactor, or give to a comrade, when you cannot do both?

Surely the honest answer is that none of these can be settled with precision, because they vary in every direction — in how much is at stake, in what is noble, in what is necessary. It is obvious, at least, that no single person can have every claim on us at once. As a general rule, returning a kindness is a higher duty than doing an unasked favor for a comrade: paying a debt binds you more than making a gift. And yet even this admits exceptions. Which is the higher duty — for a man who has been ransomed out of the hands of robbers to ransom his ransomer in turn, whoever he is, or to repay him in cash on demand though he was never himself captured; or, instead, to ransom his own father? It would seem a man should ransom his father even before himself.

So, as we said, the debt should generally be paid; but if in a particular case the gift weighs far heavier — as nobler or more urgently needed — then we must let that decide. Sometimes, too, repaying an existing debt would not even be a fair exchange: suppose the original benefactor helped a good man knowing he was good, while this good man has to repay someone he now believes to be a scoundrel. And in some cases there is no obligation to lend back to a man who lent to you: suppose a bad man lent to you taking you for good, expecting to be repaid, while you, being good, have no hope of repayment from him, since he is bad. Either the case really is as we have described, and then the claim is not equal; or it only seems so — and even then, in acting this way, people are not to be judged as doing wrong. As we have often said, all statements about feelings and actions can be exact only so far as their subject is exact. It is obvious enough that not everyone has the same claim on us, and that a father's claims are not unlimited — just as not every kind of sacrifice is offered to Zeus. Since the claims of parents, brothers, comrades, and benefactors all differ, we must render to each what belongs to and befits each.

And this is in fact what people do. To weddings they invite their relatives, because they share a common stock, and so share in everything bound up with it; and to funerals they think relatives ought to gather before others, for the same reason. As for support, it seems our first duty is to our parents, since we are in their debt, and it is nobler to help the authors of our existence in this than to help ourselves. Honor we owe our parents as we owe it to the gods — but not every kind of honor, and not the same to a father as to a mother; nor the honor due a man of learning or a general to a father, but the honor that is a father's due, and likewise for a mother. To all our elders we owe the honor that suits their age: rising when they enter, giving up our seat, and the rest. To comrades and brothers we owe frankness and a free share in all we have. And to kin, fellow tribesmen, fellow citizens, and everyone otherwise tied to us, we should keep trying to render what is due, weighing what belongs to each by closeness, goodness, or familiarity. With people of the same kind the weighing is easier; with people of different kinds it takes more effort. But that is no reason to give up the attempt; we must draw the distinctions as far as we can.

There is also the question of whether or not to dissolve friendships when the partners no longer remain what they were when the bond was formed. Where the motive was advantage or pleasure, there is surely nothing wrong in breaking off once those qualities are gone, since it was the qualities the two were friends of, and when these fail it is only natural the feeling should fail too.

A man does have grounds for complaint, though, if the other was really attached to him for advantage or pleasure but pretended it was for his character. As we said at the start, the most common source of quarrels between friends is precisely this — that they are not friends on the grounds they suppose. When a man has deceived himself, imagining he was loved for his character while the other gave no sign of it, he has only himself to blame. But when he has been deceived by the other's pretense, he has every right to complain of the man who deceived him — more right, even, than against a counterfeiter, in proportion as what was counterfeited here is more precious.

But suppose a man takes up another as good, and the other turns out, and is found out, to be a scoundrel — is he still bound to be his friend? Surely not; it is impossible. Not everything can be an object of friendship, but only what is good; and so there is no obligation to befriend a bad man, and indeed one should not, for one ought not to love what is evil or grow like what is base — which is what would happen, since, as we said before, like is friend to like.

Should the break, then, come at once? Not in every case — only where the friend is incurably corrupt. Where there is a chance of reform, we are bound to come to the rescue of a friend's character even more than his money, in proportion as character is the better thing and the closer to friendship. Still, a man who does break off is not to be judged as acting wrongly; he was never the friend of a person like the one his friend has now become, and since the man has changed and cannot be brought back, he withdraws.

Take the reverse case. Suppose one partner stays as he was when the friendship formed, while the other grows in goodness and far outstrips him. Should the improved man treat the other as a friend? Surely he cannot. It is clearest where the gap is widest, as in the friendships of boys: if one of two boyhood friends stays a boy in mind while the other becomes a man of the highest character, how can they be friends, when they no longer enjoy the same things or love and hate the same things? They will not share these toward each other, and without that, as we assumed, they cannot be friends, since they cannot live a shared life — and we have already spoken of those who cannot. Should the improved man, then, treat his old friend exactly as if the friendship had never existed? Surely he ought to remember their old closeness, and, just as we think ourselves bound to do favors for friends before strangers, so to those who were friends and are no longer we should grant something on the score of the past — as long as the cause of the break was not sheer depravity on their part.

Now the friendly feelings we show toward our friends, the feelings by which we recognize friendship, seem to have grown out of the feelings we have toward ourselves. People define a friend as one who wishes and does good — or what he takes to be good — to another for that other's sake; or as one who wishes his friend to exist and to live for the friend's own sake, which is what mothers feel toward their children, and what estranged friends feel toward each other; or as one who shares a life with another and chooses the same things; or as one who grieves and rejoices along with his friend, which again is true above all of mothers. By one or another of these marks people generally identify friendship — and every one of them the good man has toward himself, and the rest of us have insofar as we take ourselves to be good. (For, as we said, goodness, the good man, is the measure for everyone else.)

For the good man is at one with himself, and with every part of his soul he desires the same things. He wishes for himself what is good, and what he believes to be good, and he acts on it — since it is the mark of a good man to work at what is good — and he does it for his own sake, that is, for the sake of the thinking part of him, which is generally held to be a man's true self. He wishes himself to live and be kept alive, and above all that thinking part by which he is what he is, because existence is a good to a man who is good. It is for himself that each man wishes good things; no one, imagining he might become someone other than he is, would choose for that new self to have everything — a god already has the chief good, but he has it as the being he actually is — and the thinking part must be judged to be each man's self, or at least most truly so. And the good man wishes to go on living with himself, because he can do it with pleasure: his memories of past actions are full of delight, his hopes for the future are good, and good hopes are pleasant. His mind is well stocked with things to contemplate. And he grieves and rejoices most of all with himself, because what gives him pain and pleasure stays the same from day to day, not one thing today and another tomorrow — for he is not, so to speak, a man of regrets. Since each of these feelings is something the good man has toward himself, and since a friend feels toward a friend as toward himself — a friend being, in fact, another self — friendship is held to be one of these feelings, and those in whom they are found are reckoned friends. Whether or not there can really be friendship of a man toward himself is a question we will set aside; there can be thought to be, insofar as two or more of these conditions are met, and because the highest friendship, as the word is ordinarily used, resembles the feeling a man has toward himself.

It might be objected that these same conditions seem to show up even in ordinary, low men. The answer is that they share in them only so far as they please themselves and take themselves to be good. In the thoroughly corrupt and wicked these feelings are not found, really or even in appearance — one might almost say they are not found in bad men at all. For bad men are at war with themselves, craving one set of things while wishing, in cool reason, for another, exactly like men who lack self-control: they choose what is harmful but pleasant over what they themselves believe to be good; or, out of cowardice and laziness, they shrink from doing what they are convinced is best for them; and those who have done many terrible things, driven by their own depravity, come to hate and flee their own lives, and so kill themselves. The wicked seek out others to spend their days with precisely so as to flee themselves, since alone they are haunted by ugly memories and can look forward only to more of the same, but in company they drown it out. Having nothing in themselves to love, they feel no friendship toward themselves.

Nor can men of this stamp rejoice and grieve along with themselves, because their soul is torn by faction: one part, on account of the corruption in it, is pained at being denied certain things, while the other and better part is pleased; the one drags them this way and the other that, as if tearing them apart. They cannot literally feel pleasure and pain at once, but a little later the man is sorry he was ever pleased, and wishes those things had never pleased him at all — for the wicked are full of regret. It is plain, then, that the wicked man cannot stand even to himself as a friend, since he has nothing in him to be a friend of. And if to be like this is utterly miserable, then a man should flee wickedness with all his strength and strive to be good, for so he can be a friend to himself and come to be a friend to another.

Goodwill resembles friendship but is not the same thing. It can be felt toward people we do not know, and without their being aware of it, which friendship cannot. (This too we have said before.) And it is not even affection, since it carries no intensity or longing, which affection brings with it. Affection takes time and familiarity, but goodwill can spring up all at once — as it does toward athletes in a contest: spectators come to wish them well and share their hopes, though they would not lift a finger to help, because, as we said, the feeling arose suddenly and is only a surface liking.

Goodwill seems, rather, to be where friendship starts — the way pleasure taken through the eyes is where love starts. No one falls in love without first being pleased by the look of the beloved, yet being pleased by the look does not by itself amount to loving; that comes only when he aches for the beloved when she is gone and longs for her presence. In the same way, men cannot become friends without first passing through goodwill, but those who feel goodwill do not necessarily go on to friendship: they have only an inert wish for the good of the people they feel it toward, and would not act with them or put themselves out for them. So, speaking loosely, one might call goodwill a dormant friendship, which, once it has lasted a while and ripened into familiarity, becomes friendship in fact — though not the kind whose object is advantage or pleasure, since those motives cannot produce even goodwill. The man who has received a kindness returns it with goodwill toward his benefactor, and rightly so; but the man who wishes another well because he hopes to get something through him has goodwill not toward that person but toward himself, just as he is no real friend if he courts him for his own ends. In general, goodwill arises on the ground of some goodness and worth, when one man strikes another as fine, or brave, or the like — as we said happens with athletes in a contest.

Concord, too, is plainly a feature of friendship, and so is not the same as mere agreement of opinion, which can hold even between people who do not know each other. Nor do we usually say people are in concord just because they agree on any old point — say, on a question of astronomy, where agreement has nothing to do with friendship. We say a community is in concord when its people agree about what is to their advantage, settle on the same policy, and carry out what they decided together. So concord is about matters of action — and about the important ones, those that affect both parties, or, in a single state, everyone. A community is in concord when all agree, say, that the offices should be elective, or that they should ally with Sparta, or that Pittacus should rule (assuming he was willing). But when each man wants the power for himself, as the brothers do in the Phoenician Women, they fall out and form factions. Concord is not merely each man holding the same idea, whatever it may be, but holding it about the same object — as when both the common people and the men of sense want the best men in office, so that everyone gets what he is after. Concord, then, is a civic friendship, just as it is said to be, since its subject is what is advantageous and bears on the conduct of life.

Concord exists among the good. They are in concord with themselves and with one another, standing, if I may put it so, on the same ground: the wishes of such men hold steady and do not ebb and flow like the tide in the strait, and they wish for what is just and advantageous and pursue it in common. The bad can no more be in concord than they can be true friends, except to the slightest degree; they grab for more than their share of what is profitable while shirking the work and service the common good demands. Each wanting these things for himself, each is jealous of his neighbor and gets in his way; and since no one watches over the common good, it is lost. They end up quarreling, each insisting the other do his part while refusing to do his own.

Benefactors are generally thought to feel more friendship for those they help than the helped feel for them — a fact that gets debated as running against what one would expect. Most people explain it by saying the one party are debtors and the other creditors: just as with actual loans, where debtors wish their creditors gone while creditors are anxious to keep their debtors alive, so those who have done kindnesses want the people they helped to go on living, in hopes of a return, while those people are in no hurry to repay. Epicharmus would probably say that the people who give this explanation are judging from their own meanness — and yet it is true to human nature, since most people do have short memories on this score and would rather receive a kindness than do one.

But the real cause seems to lie in nature, and the case is not parallel to the creditor's. There is no affection in the creditor for the debtor's person, only a wish to keep him around for the sake of the return; whereas those who have done kindnesses genuinely feel friendship and love for the people they have helped, even when those people neither are nor ever could be of any use to them. The same is true of craftsmen: every one of them loves his own work more than that work, if it came alive, could ever love him back. It is most of all true of poets, who are devoted to their poems and love them like their own children. The benefactor's case is like this: the person he has helped is his own handiwork, and so he loves him more than the handiwork loves its maker. The reason is that existence is, to everyone, something worth choosing and worth loving; and we exist by activity — by living and acting; so a man who has made something exists, in a manner of speaking, by his act of making it. He loves his work, then, because he loves existing — which is only natural, since the work makes actual, out in the open, what was there before only as a possibility.

There is more. The benefactor has something noble in his deed, so that he can take pleasure in the man in whom that noble thing now resides; but the one who received the benefit has nothing noble in his relation to his benefactor, only something advantageous — which is both less pleasant and less an object of friendship. Pleasure comes from carrying out a present action, from looking forward to a future one, and from remembering a past one; but the keenest pleasure, and the one we love most, attends the action while it is being done. Now the benefactor's deed endures, since what is noble is lasting, while the advantage to the one helped passes away. And there is pleasure in recalling noble deeds, but little or none in recalling advantageous ones — though, oddly enough, the reverse holds for looking forward to them. Besides, to feel friendship is like acting on someone, while to be its object is like being acted upon; so the friendly feeling, and everything that goes with it, belong to the party who is, in the benefaction, the more active. One more thing: everyone loves most what has cost him effort to produce — people who made their own money are fonder of it than those who inherited it. Receiving a kindness costs no effort; doing one costs a great deal. This is also why mothers love their children more, since their share in producing them costs the most pain, and they know more surely that the children are theirs — and this feeling, too, would seem to belong to benefactors.

There is also the question of whether a man should love himself most, or someone else. People find fault with those who love themselves above all, and call them self-lovers as a reproach. The bad man, it is thought, does everything for his own sake, and the worse he is the more thoroughly he does so — people accuse him of never doing a thing that is not in his own interest. The good man, by contrast, acts from a sense of the noble, and the better he is the more he does, and he acts for his friend's sake, careless of his own interest. But the facts do not square with these theories — and no wonder. We also say a man should love most the one who is most his friend, and the one who is most a friend is the one who wishes another good for that other's own sake even where no one will ever know. Now these conditions — and all the rest by which we recognize a friend — belong first and foremost to a man in relation to himself, since, as we said, all the friendly feelings flow out to others from feelings that have the self as their first object. And all the proverbs back this up: "one soul," "friends hold all in common," "friendship is equality," "the knee is nearer than the shin." Every one of these is most fully true of a man in relation to himself, since he is most of all a friend to himself, and so is bound to love himself most.

It is reasonable to ask which of the two views to follow, since both have something to be said for them. With theories of this kind the right course is probably to sort out how far each is true, and in what sense. If we could pin down what each side means by "self-loving," the matter would clear up.

Those who use the word as a reproach give the name to people who assign themselves the larger share of money, honors, and bodily pleasures. For most people grasp after these things and take them in earnest as the best things there are, which is why they are fought over. Those who are greedy for them gratify their appetites and their passions in general — the irrational part of the soul. Most people are like this, and so the word "self-lover" took its meaning from the majority, who are low and bad; and people of that kind are justly reproached. It is plain that the crowd usually applies the term to those who give themselves the larger share of such things. For suppose a man were eager, more than anyone else, to do what is just, or self-controlled, or in any way virtuous — to secure for himself, in short, what is noble: no one would call him a self-lover, or blame him for it.

And yet such a man might be judged the truer self-lover. He assigns himself the noblest and best things; he gratifies the part of his nature that has the rightful authority, and obeys it in everything. Just as a city, or any other system, is most truly identified with its sovereign part, so is a man; and so the man who loves and gratifies this part is most truly a self-lover. We also call a man self-controlled or not according to whether his intellect is in command, which plainly implies that this part is what each man is; and the actions we most credit a man with having done himself, of his own will, are the ones done with reason. So it is clear that this part either wholly or chiefly is the man, and that the good man loves it above all. He is therefore a self-lover in the highest degree — but of a kind other than the one we reproach, as far above it as living by reason is above living at the beck of passion, and as aiming at the truly noble is above aiming at apparent advantage.

Everyone approves and praises those who throw themselves into noble action; and if everyone competed for the noble and strained to do what is finest, the community as a whole would have all it needs, and each individual would have the greatest of goods — virtue. So the good man should be a self-lover, since by doing what is noble he will both benefit himself and do good to others; but the bad man should not be, since by following his low and evil passions he will harm both himself and his neighbors. In the bad man, what he does and what he ought to do pull apart, while the good man does what he ought, because intellect always chooses what is best for itself, and the good man obeys his intellect.

It is true of the good man, too, that he does many things for the sake of his friends and his country, even to the point of dying for them if need be. He will throw away money, honors, and all the goods men compete for, while clutching the noble for himself. He would rather have one year of intense joy than many tame ones, one great and noble life than a long ordinary one, one great and noble act than many small ones. This is perhaps what happens to those who die for their country and their friends: they choose great glory for themselves. They will give away their own money so that a friend may receive more — the friend gets the money, but the man himself gets the noble, and so assigns himself the greater good. It is the same with honors and offices: he will hand them all to his friend, because doing so reflects honor and praise back on himself; and with good reason he is held a fine character, since he chooses the noble before everything else. He may even surrender the chance to act to his friend, and to have been the cause of a friend's doing something may be nobler than to have done it himself. In short, in everything we praise, the good man plainly assigns himself the larger share of the noble. In this sense a man ought to be a self-lover; in the vulgar sense, he ought not.

There is also a question about the happy man: will he need friends or not? Some say that the blessed and self-sufficient have no need of friends, since they already have everything good, and, being self-sufficient, want nothing more — whereas a friend's whole office, they say, is to be a kind of second self and supply what a man cannot get for himself. Hence the line, "when fortune favors us, what need of friends?" On the other hand, it looks absurd to hand the happy man every other good and yet deny him friends, who are reckoned the greatest of external goods. And if it is more the mark of a friend to do kindnesses than to receive them, and if doing good belongs to the good man and to virtue, and if it is nobler to do kindnesses for friends than for strangers, then the good man will need people to be the objects of his kindness — which raises the further question of whether friends are needed more in good fortune or in bad, since the unlucky man needs people to help him and the fortunate man needs people to help. And it would be strange, besides, to make the happy man a solitary, since no one would choose to have every good in the world on the condition of being alone. Man is a social animal, made by nature to live with others; the happy man has this nature too, since he has everything that is good by nature; and plainly the company of friends and good men is better than the company of strangers and ordinary people. So the happy man does need friends.

What, then, did the first speakers mean, and in what way are they right? Surely it is that most people mean by "friends" those who are useful — and of course the happy man will not need those, since he already has every good; nor will he need friends for pleasure, or only slightly, since his life is already pleasant and wants no pleasure imported from outside. And because he needs no friends of these kinds, he is thought to need none at all. But this is probably not true. As we said at the start, happiness is a kind of activity, and an activity is plainly something that has to come into being, not something already in hand like a piece of property. If being happy lies in living and being active, and the good man's activity is in itself excellent and pleasant, as we said early on; and if what is our own is among the things that please us; and if we can see our neighbors better than ourselves and their actions better than our own — then the actions of good men who are our friends are pleasant to the good, since they hold both of the things naturally pleasant. So the man at the height of happiness will need friends of this kind, since he wants to contemplate actions that are good, and that are in a sense his own — which the actions of a friend, being a good man, are.

Besides, the common view requires that the happy man live a life pleasant to himself. Life alone is a heavy thing, since it is hard to keep working continuously by oneself, but easier in company and in relation to others; so the activity, being pleasant in itself, will be more continuous — which is just what the happy man's should be. For the good man, in that he is good, takes pleasure in actions that accord with virtue and is pained by those that spring from vice, exactly as a musical man delights in fine music and is grated on by bad. And, as Theognis says, virtue itself can be improved by practice, from living with the good.

On further and more searching grounds it will appear that the good friend is naturally a thing the good man should choose. We have said that whatever is naturally good is also in itself good and pleasant to the good man. Now living, in animals generally, is defined by the power of perception, and in man by the power of perception or of thought — and the power is always to be referred to its actual exercise, since that is the main thing — so that to live is, above all, to perceive or to think. Living is in itself one of the things that are good and pleasant, for it is something definite and complete, and whatever is such belongs to the nature of the good; and what is naturally good is good to the good man, which is why it seems pleasant to everyone. (We must not bring in a life that is corrupt and depraved, or one spent in pain, for such a life is something indefinite, like the qualities running through it; what is to be said about pain will be clearer later.)

If living is in itself good and pleasant — and it appears to be, since all desire it, and the good and the deeply happy above all, their lives being the most worth choosing and their existence likewise — then consider this. The one who sees perceives that he sees; the one who hears perceives that he hears; the one who walks perceives that he walks; and in every other case there is some power that perceives the fact that we are active, so that when we perceive, we perceive that we perceive, and when we think, we perceive that we think. But to perceive that we perceive or think is to perceive that we exist, since existence was defined as perceiving or thinking. And to perceive that one is alive is in itself a pleasant thing, since life is by nature good, and to perceive that something good is present in us is pleasant. So living is worth choosing, and to the good especially, since existence is to them good and pleasant: they take pleasure in their inner awareness of what is in itself good.

But the good man stands toward his friend as toward himself, since a friend is another self; and so, just as his own existence is worth choosing to each man, his friend's existence is worth choosing too, or nearly so. We said that one's existence is worth choosing because one perceives oneself to be good, and any such perception is pleasant in itself. So a man should be fully aware of his friend's existence as well, which comes about through living with him — sharing in his words and his thought; for this is what "living together" means for human beings, not merely feeding in the same place, as it does for cattle. If, then, for the deeply happy man his own existence is in itself worth choosing, being naturally good and pleasant, and his friend's existence is nearly as much so, then a friend too must be among the things worth choosing. And whatever is worth choosing a man must have, or else he will be deficient in just this respect. So the man who is to measure up to our idea of the happy man will need good friends.

Should we, then, make our friends as many as possible? Or, just as it has been well said of acquaintances, "have not many, yet do not be without," so with friendship might we adopt the same rule — that a man should be neither without friends nor burdened with a great many? For friends meant for use, the rule fits perfectly well, since repaying the services of many is hard work, and a whole life would not be long enough to do it. More of them, then, than your own life can handle become a nuisance and a hindrance to living well, and we do not want them. And of friends meant for pleasure, a few are quite enough, like a little seasoning in food. But of good friends, should we make as many as we possibly can? Or is there a limit to the number, as there is to the number that makes a city? You cannot make a city out of ten men, and if you swell the number to a hundred thousand it is no longer a city; though the right number is perhaps not some single figure but anything between certain bounds. So with friends too there is a limit — perhaps the largest number with whom one could keep up a shared life, since that is reckoned among the surest marks of friendship, and it is plain you cannot share your life with many, cannot divide yourself among many. And they must also be friends to one another, if they are all to live a common life, which is a hard thing to find in many men at once. It is hard, too, to enter into the joys and sorrows of many people, since one would likely have to rejoice with this one and grieve with that one at the same moment.

So perhaps the thing is not to seek as many friends as possible, but only as many as are enough for a shared life — since it would seem impossible to be much of a friend to many at once. For the same reason one cannot be in love with many at once: love is a kind of excess of friendship, and that points at a single object; and all strong feelings must be limited in the number they are felt toward. The facts seem to bear this out. Not many become friends in the way of close companionship; all the famous friendships of that kind are between two people. Those who have many friends and meet everyone on intimate terms seem to be no one's friend, except in the way of ordinary fellow-citizens — the people we call ingratiating. In the ordinary way of fellowship a man can indeed be a friend to many without being ingratiating, by being genuinely good; but one cannot be a friend to many for their virtue and for their own sakes. It is much to be content with even a few such.

Again: are friends needed more in good fortune or in bad? They are wanted in both. The unfortunate need help, and the fortunate need people to live with and to do kindnesses to, since they have a desire to act well toward someone. Having friends is more necessary in misfortune, which is why useful friends are wanted then; and having them in good fortune is nobler, which is why the fortunate seek out good men, since it is better to do kindnesses for these and to live with them. Even in misfortune the very presence of friends is pleasant, for the grieving are comforted by their friends' sympathy.

This raises the question whether friends actually take up part of the weight of our troubles, or whether it is only that their presence is pleasant, and the awareness of their sympathy, that lessens the sufferer's pain. We need not settle which of these, or what other cause, produces the relief; at any rate the relief is a plain fact. But the presence of friends probably has a mixed effect. Simply to see friends is pleasant, especially to a man in misfortune, and it helps lighten his grief, since a friend with any tact comforts by his look and his words, knowing the sufferer's temper and what gives him pleasure and pain. But to see a friend grieved at one's misfortunes is itself painful, since everyone shrinks from being a cause of pain to his friends. That is why men of a manly nature are careful not to drag their friends into their suffering, and, unless a man is utterly hardened to others' pain, he cannot bear the pain he thus causes his friends; in short, he does not let others wail with him, not being given to wailing himself. Women, and the men who are like them, like having others groan along with them, and love such people as friends and fellow-mourners. But plainly it is our duty in all things to imitate the better character.

The advantage of friends in good fortune, on the other hand, is the pleasant company and the awareness that they are glad at our success. It would seem, then, that we should call friends in readily when fortune is good, since it is noble to be ready to do others good, but reluctantly when fortune is bad, since we should make others share our troubles as little as possible — which is the point of the saying, "my own misfortune is enough." The best occasion to call them in is when, at little trouble to themselves, they can be of great use to the one who needs them. Conversely, it is perhaps fitting to go to friends in their misfortunes unasked and eagerly, since kindness is a friend's office, above all toward those in need who do not demand it as a right — which is both more creditable and more pleasant for both. And in their good fortune we should go readily if we can help it along in any way, since men need their friends for this too; but we should be slow to share in the benefits, since eagerness to receive an advantage is not creditable. One should perhaps take care, though, not to seem sullen in turning down a friend's sympathy or help, as occasionally happens. So the presence of friends turns out to be, in every circumstance, worth choosing.

May we not say, then, that just as the sight of the beloved is what lovers prize most, choosing that sense above all the others because love "is kindled by the eyes and fed by gazing," so for friends a shared life is what is most worth choosing — friendship being a communion? Again, as a man is to himself, so he is to his friend; and toward himself the perception of his own existence is worth choosing, so it is so toward his friend as well. Their friendship, besides, is acted out in a shared life, and so with good reason they desire it. Whatever each man takes existence to be, or whatever it is for the sake of which he chooses to live, that is what he wishes to do alongside his friends. And so some men drink together, others gamble, others train or hunt together, others do philosophy together — each spending his days with his friends in whatever he loves most in life; for wishing to share their lives with their friends, they do and take part in the things they think will bring that about. So the friendship of the wicked turns out depraved: being unstable, they share in bad things, and grow depraved by being made alike. But the friendship of the good is good, and grows by their company; they even improve, it seems, by acting together and correcting one another, for each takes an imprint from the other in the things that please them — whence the poet's line, "from the good you will learn good things."

What comes next, it seems, is pleasure. For nothing is bound up more tightly with our kind than this: it is by the two rudders of pleasure and pain that we steer the young, and learning to enjoy and to hate the right things is held to count for more than almost anything in the shaping of a good character — for these feelings run the whole length of a life, pulling us toward virtue and a life that goes well, since men reach for what is pleasant and shrink from what hurts. A subject this large we cannot simply walk past, the more so because people disagree about it so sharply. Some call pleasure the chief good outright; others go to the far end and call it thoroughly bad — a few because they honestly believe it, but others, I suspect, on a theory that even if pleasure is not bad it is useful to say it is, since the crowd is its slave, and dragging men toward the opposite extreme may land them somewhere near the middle.

I doubt the wisdom of that. When it comes to what men feel and do, theories carry less weight than facts, and the moment a theory clashes with how people actually live it is not merely scorned — it drags the truth down with it. Let the man who runs pleasure down be caught once reaching for it, and the crowd, unable to make fine distinctions, takes his lapse as proof that pleasure is exactly the universal good he denied. So honest talk about these things is the useful kind, not only for knowing but for living, because what squares with the facts is believed, and what is believed moves the wise to live by it. Enough of that, though; let us turn to what people actually say about pleasure.

Eudoxus held that pleasure is the chief good, on the grounds that everything reaches for it, rational and irrational alike. In each case, he argued, what a thing chooses is good for it, and what it chooses most is best; so the fact that all are drawn to one thing shows that one thing is best for all. "Each finds its own good," he said, "the way it finds its own food, and what is good for all, the target of every aim, is the chief good." His arguments were trusted less for themselves than for the man behind them, for he was thought a model of self-command, so no one supposed he praised pleasure because he loved it — he was simply saying what he believed. He thought the point was made just as well from the opposite side: since pain is something everything avoids, its contrary must be something everything chooses. And he urged that what we choose for nothing beyond itself is the most choiceworthy thing of all, and that pleasure is plainly of this kind, since no one ever asks what a man is pleased *for* — taking pleasure to be worth having in itself. Add it to any other good, he said — to a just act, to self-command — and you make that good more worth choosing; and a thing can only be increased by what is good.

But that last argument seems to prove only that pleasure belongs among the goods, not that it stands above the rest, since *every* good is more choiceworthy paired with another than taken alone. In fact Plato uses just this argument the other way, to show pleasure is *not* the chief good: the life of pleasure is more choiceworthy combined with wisdom than without it, but if the mixture is better, then pleasure by itself is not the chief good — for the chief good is the one thing that cannot be made more choiceworthy by any addition. So whatever can be improved by combination with some other good is ruled out. As for those who object that "what everything aims at need not be good," I cannot see much in it. What everyone believes, we say *is so*; and the man who pulls that ground from under us has nothing steadier to put in its place. If only the brute animals desired pleasure he might have a point — but the rational desire it too, and even in the lower animals there may be some natural good above themselves that aims at the good proper to them.

Nor does the worry hold that pleasure cannot be good because pain is bad — that evil can be opposed to evil, and both to what is neither. True in general, but not here. If both pleasure and pain were bad, both would be things to avoid; if neither, neither would be — yet plainly men avoid the one as bad and choose the other as good, so the opposition is complete. And it is no objection that pleasure is not a *quality*: neither are the activities of virtue, neither is happiness, and these are surely goods. Some say the chief good is bounded but pleasure unbounded, because it admits of more and less. But if they mean the feeling itself, the same could be said of justice and the other virtues, in respect of which a man is plainly called more or less just, more or less brave. And if they mean the pleasures themselves, perhaps they have missed the real cause — that some are pure and some are mixed. Health is bounded and still admits of degrees; why not pleasure?

Then comes the charge that the chief good is complete while every movement and coming-to-be is incomplete, and that pleasure is a movement or a coming-to-be. But it is not even a movement. Every movement has a speed, fast or slow — if not in itself then relative to something — yet pleasure has neither. A man may *become* pleased quickly, as he may grow angry quickly, but he cannot *be* pleased quickly, nor quickly relative to anyone else, though he can certainly walk or grow fast or slow. And how could pleasure be a coming-to-be? A thing comes to be from what it later dissolves back into — but pleasure has no such partner, for what pain destroys is not what pleasure builds up. They say pain is a falling-short of what nature requires and pleasure the filling of it; but those are states of the *body*, and if pleasure were really a refilling, the thing being refilled would feel the pleasure — the body — which no one believes. The notion grew, I think, out of the pleasures and pains of eating: men feel a lack, suffer for it, and then enjoy the filling. But not every pleasure is like that. The pleasures of mathematics involve no prior pain at all; nor do many of the pleasures of smell, or many sounds, sights, memories, hopes. Of what could these be a filling, when there was no emptiness to fill?

What of the disgraceful pleasures people bring up? We can answer that these are not really pleasant — not pleasant simply because they are pleasant to the corrupt, any more than what tastes sweet to the sick is really sweet, or what looks white to the man with diseased eyes is really white. Or we can say the pleasures are choiceworthy, only not from *those* sources — as wealth is good, but not as the wages of treason; or health, but not at the price of eating something vile. Or, better still, that pleasures differ in kind: the pleasure that comes from noble things is a different thing from the pleasure that comes from base ones, and you cannot have the just man's pleasure without being just, or the musician's without being musical. The very difference everyone draws between a friend and a flatterer shows as much — the friend aims at your good in the friendship, the flatterer only at your pleasure, and we reproach the one and praise the other, as men with different ends. No one, after all, would choose to live his whole life with a child's mind, however much he enjoyed what children enjoy, or to take pleasure in doing something utterly shameful, even on the guarantee of never being pained for it. And there are many things we would work hard for even if no pleasure came of them at all — seeing, remembering, knowing, having the virtues. That pleasure follows on these by nature changes nothing; we would choose them with no pleasure attached. So this much is plain: pleasure is not the chief good, and not every pleasure is worth choosing, but some are worth choosing in themselves, differing in kind by the source they spring from. So much for the common talk about pleasure and pain.

What pleasure actually is, and what sort of thing, comes clearer if we start again from the beginning. Seeing seems to be complete at any moment of it; it lacks nothing that could be added later to round out its nature. Pleasure is like that. It is a whole, and you could not find, at any instant, a pleasure whose nature would be completed by lasting longer. This is why it is not a movement. Every movement takes time and aims at some end — the building of a house is finished only when the builder has made what he set out to make, either in the whole stretch of time or in a given part of it. The lesser movements inside it are each incomplete in their own stretch, and different in kind from the whole and from one another: setting the stones is one movement, fluting a column another, raising the temple a third, and only the last is complete, lacking nothing for its end — laying the foundation and cutting a single triglyph are incomplete, each being the movement of a mere part. So with walking and the rest: motion from here to there comes in kinds — flying, walking, leaping — and even within walking the where-from and where-to differ across the whole course and within any part of it, for a man is not just crossing a line but crossing a line *in a place*, and this place is not that one.

I have dealt with movement exactly elsewhere; here it is enough to say that it is not complete at any given moment, and that most movements are incomplete and differ in kind, since their whence and whither make different species of them. But pleasure is complete in its whole nature at any moment whatever. So pleasure and movement must be two different things, and pleasure belongs among things that are whole and complete. The same follows from this: a thing cannot move except over some stretch of time, but pleasure needs no stretch — what is there at the very present instant is a kind of whole. So men are wrong to call pleasure a movement or a coming-to-be. Those words fit only what is divisible and not a whole: there is no coming-to-be of an act of seeing, none of a point, none of a unit, and none of these is a movement either. And so there is none of pleasure, for it is, one might say, a whole.

Now every faculty of perception is set to work on the object that answers to it, and works best when the faculty is in good condition and the object is the finest within its range — for that is about what we mean by perfect activity, whether we credit the faculty itself or the thing the faculty resides in. In each case, then, the best activity is that of the best-conditioned faculty upon the best of its proper objects; and this activity will also be the most complete and the most pleasant. For pleasure goes with every perceiving faculty, and likewise with every act of thought and contemplation; and the most pleasant is the most complete, and the most complete is the work of the best faculty on the finest of its objects. Pleasure completes the activity — but not the way the faculty and the object complete it, by being its causes, any more than health and the physician are causes of being well in the same sense.

Pleasure completes the activity not as a settled state already in it, but as a kind of bloom laid over the top — the bloom on those in the flush of youth. So long as the object of thought or perception is what it should be, and the faculty that judges or takes it in is what it should be, there will be pleasure in the activity; for when the thing apt to act and the thing apt to be acted on are alike and stand in the right relation, the same result follows of its own nature. Why, then, does no one feel pleasure without a break? Because we tire — no human faculty can keep up unbroken exertion, and so the pleasure flags too, since it rides on the activity. It is the same reason some things delight us when new and less so afterward: at first the mind is roused and works at full stretch, the way men stare hard at a thing they have just caught sight of; later the working slackens into something careless, and the pleasure dulls with it. One might conclude that everyone reaches for pleasure because everyone reaches for life, and life is an activity, and each man works at and with the things he loves best — the musical man works at music with his hearing, the studious man at problems with his mind, and so on. Pleasure completes the activities, and so completes the life men reach for; no wonder they reach for pleasure too. (Whether we choose life for the sake of pleasure or pleasure for the sake of life we may leave aside — the two are yoked together and will not come apart, since there is no pleasure without activity, and every activity pleasure completes.)
